title: Meet Feather, the startup building the ‘Android of robotics’ for developers
snippet: Feather is betting on a customizable, $30,000 platform built for software developers.
fullText:
If there is one thing robotics founders and investors agree on, it’s that the “ChatGPT moment” where a general-purpose robot can seamlessly adapt to any environment has not arrived. Opinions vary on whether the breakthrough is just around the corner or a decade away.

Feather Robotics, a humanoid startup founded last year, is developing a robot for either timeline. Unlike Tesla or Figure, which are tackling the lofty mission of building both the body and a foundational “brain” that isn’t yet widely deployed, Feather provides the hardware and software toolkit for developers to tackle real-world tasks now.

“You can’t buy a Tesla robot today and develop on top of it,” Feather co-founder Hoa Mai told TechCrunch. “We realized that this is not how most companies became successful. Hardware players like Nvidia or Apple started with a product that worked and was deployable, and then they added complexity over time.”

In 2025, after his previous humanoid startup was sold to 1X, Mai (pictured above, left) teamed up with Parsa Bakhtiari (pictured above, right), a former Tesla Model 3 engineer who at one point reported directly to Elon Musk, to build what the duo hopes will become the Android of robotics.

That vision was attractive to Gradient Ventures, which backed Feather at its inception, leading the startup’s previously announced $7.6 million pre-seed round.

Since then, Feather has rolled out a modular robotic system that allows developers to customize the hardware for different use cases, such as adjusting arm lengths. The startup has already begun selling to customers, surpassing $1 million in revenue.

Although Feather is not disclosing its customers, it said that its robots are working as cooks in restaurants and cleaning up science labs. On the software side, the hardware can run models from any leading robotics AI provider, including Nvidia, Skild, or Physical Intelligence.

“We’ve been selling small quantities of these robots, and now that we resolved like almost all the issues over the last year of field testing, we’re getting ready for a big product launch,” Mai said.

According to Darian Shirazi, general partner at Gradient, Feather doesn’t have direct competitors in the U.S. He breaks down the current hardware robotics landscape into three categories: startups like Sunday building domestic household robots, heavyweights like Figure and Tesla aiming for general-purpose machines, and Feather, which, he believes, is the only U.S. startup developing a modular humanoid platform.

Mai admits that Feather took a page from Chinese robotics companies like Unitree. But with new foreign-made models restricted from entering the U.S. market, Feather is now uniquely positioned as a homegrown option of its kind.

Feather’s other advantage is its price. The robot costs $30,000, which is about half the price Unitree’s H2 Edu.

Shirazi believes the market size at that price could be very large. “You would hire a laborer for $50,000 to $60,000 a year, you’d have to train [them]. They’d have to have HR. They’d have to have all these different support mechanisms,” he said. “You can now buy a Feather robot to do that.”

Feather is also operating extremely efficiently, having spent only a fraction of its pre-seed funding, according to Shirazi.

The startup’s big bet, of course, is that the value in robotics will come from an ecosystem developed around the hardware.

“If we think about the market size today for physical AI companies, it’s very small,” Mai said. “But if you think about how many physical AI application companies will probably exist in five years, we expect it to be in the thousands.”

Feather hopes to be the platform that powers all of them.

title: Meta announces camera-free glasses, dedicated Muse AI gadget, more
snippet: Meta announced today a series of AI-powered devices, including the Muse Charm, a palm-sized gadget designed specifically for its new Muse AI assistant. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Meta announced today a series of AI-powered devices, including the Muse Charm, a palm-sized gadget designed specifically for its new Muse AI assistant. Here are the details.

Meta kicked off its Meta Connect 2026 event today, its yearly showcase for new AI technologies, wearables, and VR products.

Last year, the biggest announcement was the Meta Ray-Ban Display, the company’s first smart glasses with a built-in display that can show messages, navigation, Meta AI responses, and more.

At the time, Meta’s AI-powered glasses lineup was already gaining significant traction, with Meta and EssilorLuxottica going on to sell more than 7 million units for the year.

Since then, Meta’s camera-equipped glasses have faced growing scrutiny over privacy and ethics, as there has been no shortage of discussions involving privacy, ethics, and the general pushback on AI.

Today, Meta announced the Ray-Ban Meta Audio, its first pair of camera-free smart glasses, which starts at $349 and will be available beginning October 13.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio retains features such as music and podcast playback, calls, and live translation, offering many of the same audio features as Meta’s camera-equipped glasses. They also support Muse, Meta’s recently launched personal AI agent.

That said, Meta also announced the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) tonight, featuring a slimmer design, up to nine hours of battery life, and a new action button, while retaining the 12MP camera and 3K video recording introduced with the previous generation.

The new action button can be customized in the Meta AI app to provide one-touch access to Meta AI or other features, such as live translation. The Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is available today, starting at $449.

In tonight’s event, the company also announced the Meta VR Glasses, a roughly 100-gram VR headset designed to look and feel more like a pair of glasses. The device features what Meta calls a “5K Infinite Display built on micro-OLED panels,” built-in Meta AI, eye and hand tracking, and a separate pocketable puck that handles processing, battery, and storage.

Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as a personal cinema, gaming device, and workspace. They are also the first IMAX Enhanced-certified VR device, with support for 3D movies and immersive live sports.

Alongside the Meta VR Glasses, the company also introduced a new hologram feature that can create a photorealistic avatar that reflects a user’s real-time expressions and reactions during video calls.

Meta says that a version of the feature is also coming to Meta Ray-Ban Display, where users can create a digital version of their face for hands-free video calls, beginning with WhatsApp.

The Meta VR Glasses will go on sale in spring 2027 for $1,299.99.

Rounding up tonight’s glassware news, Meta also expanded its own Meta Glasses lineup with two new styles, Capri and Nova, a new collection designed with LISA, and the $249 Meta Adventurer, its most affordable pair of smart glasses yet.

The company also introduced a limited-edition Meta Fury model and a new Ivory colorway for its Kylie Jenner collaboration.

At tonight’s event, Meta also announced the Muse Charm, a palm-sized device built specifically around its recently launched Muse personal AI agent. Meta launched Muse earlier this month, and the app has since risen to the No. 1 spot on both the U.S. App Store and Google Play.

According to Bloomberg, the Muse Charm was developed by Meta’s new design lab, led by former Apple interface design chief Alan Dye, alongside the company’s Superintelligence AI group.

The Muse Charm, which Meta refers to as a “holdable,” features a roughly 2-inch OLED touchscreen with a customizable Muse character at the center of the interface. Users can change its appearance, outfits, voice, and other attributes, and interact with Muse directly through the device.

The device also includes front- and rear-facing cameras, speakers, microphones, 5G connectivity, and a USB-C port. The cameras can capture photos and videos, but Bloomberg reports they are primarily intended to provide Muse with visual context for analysis and AI-assisted actions, rather than to serve as traditional cameras.

Users set up and sync the Charm through the Muse app on iPhone or Android. Two Charm devices can also recognize and interact with each other when placed nearby.

Meta plans to begin selling the Muse Charm in December. The company has not yet announced a price, but Bloomberg reports that it is expected to cost roughly as much as a smartwatch.

title: Oh no, here come the AI Tamagotchis
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m watching yet another Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave review (watch this for context), getting started on my Booker Prize shortlist read-through, and reading as much as I can about Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” now that it’s the longest-running #1 hit of all time. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe. more…
fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m watching yet another Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave review (watch this for context), getting started on my Booker Prize shortlist read-through, and reading as much as I can about Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” now that it’s the longest-running #1 hit of all time. 

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Meta may no longer be a metaverse company, but it’s trying its damndest to be a hardware company. At last night’s Meta Connect event, the company unveiled a bunch of new AI wearables, including the third-generation Ray-Ban Meta camera glasses, the camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, a wider rollout of its Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, and a next-gen VR product called, appropriately, Meta VR Glasses, coming in the spring of 2027.

	

All of these are interesting in their own way, particularly the VR Glasses, which are basically Galaxy XR/Vision Pro competitors in a much smaller form factor and considerably lower cost ($1,299). Meta’s found considerable traction with its bevy of wearables despite growing pushback from privacy advocates and regular people who don’t want to be filmed with “perv glasses.” The audio-only product, which boasts Dolby Atmos support, is a direct response to that, but the company is still iterating on the baseline camera hardware while promising software updates will prevent misuse.

But the really interesting announcement came in the form of a Tamagotchi-like doohickey called the Muse Charm that runs Meta’s popular new Muse AI agent, which has seen massive growth as an app on Android, iOS, and Mac. The hardware has a 2-inch OLED touch display, a camera and microphones, a 5G modem, and runs a proprietary OS that Meta says will connect to retailers like Walmart and Best Buy.

AI agents are no longer novel — I’ve been testing them all summer in the form of apps like Poke, Tolan, Instinct, Town, and others — but Muse has taken off because it’s free, fast, and genuinely useful. Meta is also building it into everything it owns, from Instagram to WhatsApp, and is soon adding the ability to chat with an agent through video.

At the beginning of 2024, we had a few months of hand-wringing over AI gadgets like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI Pin, but they failed because the models were not even close to being ready for the tasks promised in the marketing. Now, AI agents are more than capable of chasing down a refund, booking a concert, or buying an anniversary gift, and Meta’s preemptive jump into the space will only heighten expectations for OpenAI’s rumored hardware product that’s expected to debut in 2027.

I regret to inform you, though: I think the Museagotchi looks pretty damn cute.

As Android XR nears, smart glasses are only getting more popular despite Meta backlash. 

✉️ Inbox

Adobe Premiere for Android launches for free with layered video editing, YouTube templates. I feel like we’ve been waiting years for Premiere on Android, and it’s finally here. And free, which is pretty great.

Samsung has delayed its Android 17 update. By a week. We’ll be fine.

Qualcomm announces the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Qualcomm is going to five blades this year with its new dual flagship chip strategy. The Elite Gen 6 is the standard one, with the Extreme boasting “advanced agentic AI” capabilities.

Oppo Find X10 series goes official with triple 200MP cameras, 8,000 mAh battery. I can’t even with this phone. Monster specs and a ridiculous camera array, sure. But a battery that size? I need it right now.

Xiaomi 18 Pro series goes official with ‘privacy screen,’ 8,500 mAh battery, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Oh, I guess 8,000 mAh wasn’t big enough.

Android Auto rolls out game support, no longer in beta. I know that this exists just to compete with Tesla, but I genuinely don’t know why this is legal.

Motorola Signature 27 is a proper flagship with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. This phone will probably cost $2,000 but holy smokes does it look worth it.

Motorola Signature 27 officially gets a North American launch in the ‘coming months’

Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Sol & Luna both launch today with lower costs. I’ve been testing both of these models and if this is what “pacing the frontier” looks like, we’re all doomed (in a good way).

Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra leak shows another side, confirming minimal changes. A $1000+ Android tablet? In this economy?

Nest Doorbell has been triggering Gemini’s American accent, no matter what language you speak. This is genuinely the funniest thing I’ve heard all week. Only Google could make this happen.

YouTube announces Custom Feeds, GIF comments, and ‘Your podcast lineup’. YouTube’s making some interesting announcements in the face of increasing competition from Netflix in the “clips” space.

YouTube Music adding corner access to ‘Ask Music’ with Gemini

Google Beam 3D meeting booths coming to co-working spaces. Remember the sci-fi-esque video conferencing booths that Google debuted a few years ago under the Starline name? Well, they’re still a kajillion dollars, but they seem popular enough to be expanding to co-working spaces in Atlanta, Chicago, New York City, and Palo Alto.

Google Maps update shows traffic lights and stop signs at your next turn on Android Auto, more

Microsoft launches 12-inch Surface Pro with Snapdragon X2 Plus & 5G, 13-inch Surface Laptop too

➡️ FWD:

I’m going to do a bit of shameless self-promotion today and share a few cool things that the 9to5 video team has been working on.

Our Googlebook hands-on video is close to 500k views, and for good reason: Jordan absolutely crushes it with his deep dive into the highs, lows, and oddities of Google’s latest hardware launch.

Damien does a spectacular job detailing life with Google’s $899 Pixel 11, noting that “there is a good phone underneath the price hikes,” but that $100 bump really overshadows the battery and camera improvements.

Finally, I was back on The Sideload with my buddy, Will Sattelberg, where we had the privilege of talking to Kevin Michaluk and Jeff Gadway of Clicks, which is about to release its long-awaited Communicator smartphone this December. It was a really fun conversation that gets a bit philosophical about why we use technology and what it really means to disconnect in today’s world. 

And if you missed my Cc: questions with Kevin from Tuesday’s Inbox edition, you can catch up with them here.

🗑️ Trash

Disney+ is raising its prices for the fourth time in four years. The popular Disney+ Premium plan with no ads now runs $21.49, a 13% bump over yesterday’s price.

Just this year, Netflix, Peacock, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV, YouTube Premium, and Paramount Plus got more expensive, and it seems that every streamer is making their ad-free tier as unenticing as possible to lure people back to ads.

I’m pretty close to canceling Netflix — my kids watch a fair amount of its fare — but I happily canceled Disney+ the last time prices went up, and I wouldn’t be surprised if a few thousand subscribers did the same just now.

With FAST services like Pluto TV, Tubi, The Roku Channel, Freevee, and many more offering a decent assortment of free content in exchange for a network television-level of ad density, it really does seem like all roads do eventually lead to cable.

Like what you just read? Subscribe to Inbox today and get it in your email every Tuesday and Thursday morning. Got feedback? Send us an email.

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. Talk to you on Tuesday.

-Daniel

title: Report: AI glasses shipments surged 263% in H1 2026 as Apple prepares to enter the market
snippet: Counterpoint Research says global AI glasses shipments surged 263% during the first half of 2026, with Meta comfortably leading the display-less segment amid growing privacy concerns. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Counterpoint Research says global AI glasses shipments surged 263% during the first half of 2026, with Meta comfortably leading the display-less segment amid growing privacy concerns. Here are the details.

While Meta’s first-generation smart glasses, launched with Ray-Ban, failed to gain much traction, its second-generation devices have been far more successful.

Earlier this year, Francesco Milleri, CEO of Ray-Ban owner EssilorLuxottica, said the two companies had sold more than 7 million AI glasses in 2025, putting a 10-million annual sales target within reach for the end of 2026.

Throughout the last year, Meta has largely had the display-less AI glasses market to itself, while most major rivals are still developing their own hardware.

Apple, for instance, is rumored to be developing its own display-less smart glasses to compete with Meta’s Ray-Bans, with a launch currently targeted for 2027. The glasses are expected to rely heavily on Siri and Apple Intelligence, with cameras, microphones, and speakers built into the frame, while a more advanced version with an AR display is reportedly still several years away.

In recent months, however, Meta’s camera-equipped smart glasses have faced increasing scrutiny, with the “perv glasses” label gaining traction as reports of non-consensual filming and harassment have drawn wider attention⁠.

That said, Counterpoint Research says Meta still accounted for 94% of global display-less AI glasses shipments in the first half of 2026, with its volumes growing 260% year over year. Xiaomi and Alibaba came in at 1% each, with other brands accounting for the remaining 4%.

North America reportedly accounted for 50% of total shipments of display-less AI glasses, with Western Europe accounting for 28%, Australia for 4.4%, followed by the Asia-Pacific region with 4%, Latin America with 3.8%, India with 3.7%, China with 3%, and the UAE with 2%.

Here’s Counterpoint on how it sees this market going forward:

“Despite near-term challenges, we expect the AI glasses market to maintain its strong growth trajectory as Meta, Google, Samsung and Apple intensify their investments and competition. The next phase of growth will be driven by agentic AI glasses offering more proactive, context-aware experiences, enabled by advancements in agent-integrated software, operating systems, voice interaction, and ultra-low-power sensing and computing technologies. These developments are expected to create new growth opportunities for component vendors in the AI glasses ecosystem. We also expect a wider range of AI glasses form factors to emerge to address privacy concerns associated with cameras, including camera-free AI audio glasses and AI glasses equipped with cameras primarily for contextual understanding rather than photo or video capture.”

Counterpoint’s report also detailed the AR & AI glasses segment, which they define as “AI glasses equipped with the necessary display(s) and optical components to enable an optical see-through experience.”

According to the report, shipments in this segment surged 449% year over year, with Rokid accounting for 41% of the market, followed by Meta at 37%, Even Realities at 11%, Alibaba at 7%, INMO at 2%, and other brands collectively accounting for the remaining 2%.

Region-wise, China accounted for 45% of total shipments in this market, followed by North America at 41% and the rest of the world at 14%.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro series goes official with ‘privacy screen,’ 8,500 mAh battery, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Xiaomi has just launched its new Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max in China with flagship specs, massive batteries, and a pair of 200MP cameras too. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi has just launched its new Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max in China with flagship specs, massive batteries, and a pair of 200MP cameras too.

With a global launch to come later, Xiaomi has unveiled its new Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Both devices run on the latest Snapdragon chips and carry over features from last year, such as the rear-facing display. 

The big new feature here is a “privacy screen,” Xiaomi’s implementation of the Privacy Display from Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra. Xiaomi immediately one-ups Samsung by putting the tech on both its top-end and compact flagship releases, while also supporting the feature more flexibly in its software. This also includes a feature that uses the front-facing camera to detect onlookers and activate the privacy screen automatically, as well as location-based triggers so it can turn on in crowded public areas without you needing to manually activate it, as The Verge points out.

The rest of the spec sheet is strong, with solid-looking displays on both devices, huge batteries, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 in both devices – the Pro Max getting the “Extreme” variant. Visually, both phones look identical, though the Pro Max gets a crazy-looking transparent edition.

	

Xiaomi 18 Pro

6.4-inch, 2436×1120 120Hz AMOLED front display

2.7-inch, 912×596 120Hz rear display

7,000 mAh battery

100W wired/27W wireless charging

200MP main camera, 200MP 3.2x telephoto, 50MP 102-degree ultrawide

Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6

12/16GB RAM, 256/512/1TB UFS 4.1 storage

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max

6.9-inch, 2624×1208 120Hz AMOLED front display

2.9-inch, 976×596 120Hz rear display

8,500 mAh battery

100W wired/27W wireless charging

200MP main camera, 200MP 3.2x telephoto, 50MP 102-degree ultrawide

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

12/16GB RAM, 256/512/1TB UFS 4.1 storage

Xiaomi’s 18 Pro series starts at 5,999CNY, just shy of $900 USD, but international pricing remains to be seen. The Xiaomi 17 launched internationally in February 2026, so we can probably expect a similar timeline this time, but Xiaomi has confirmed the Pro models will debut outside of China this time, unlike the Xiaomi 17 Pro.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro has a Privacy Display that does more than Galaxy S26 Ultra, launches this week [Video]
snippet: Xiaomi has confirmed support for the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display on the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Pro, and it apparently does a lot more than Samsung’s implementation of the feature. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi has confirmed support for the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display on the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Pro, and it apparently does a lot more than Samsung’s implementation of the feature.

The Privacy Display on Galaxy S26 Ultra is a hardware feature that can help hide the contents of your display from onlookers by physically altering how the light of the display shines outward. It’s a very clever feature which, despite some trade-offs, has been very well-received.

Now, it’s coming to a Xiaomi flagship.

In a teaser posted to Weibo, Xiaomi confirms that the Xiaomi 18 Pro will ship with a “smart privacy screen” that looks virtually identical to the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display. When activated, content is obfuscated at an angle, only allowing you as the person looking at the display straight-on to clearly see everything.

	

Similar to Samsung, Xiaomi looks to be allowing this to work in specific apps or on only certain parts of the display, like a notification, instead of being an all-or-nothing option. 

Notably, though, Xiaomi also shows the feature working on a floating app window, in split screen, and even on specific notifications on the lockscreen. While Samsung is working on improvements, Xiaomi seems to be delivering quite a bit more versatility right out of the gate.

You can see everything in action in the video below:

title: So Many New Meta Glasses: Muse AI Everywhere, and Ray-Bans Without a Camera
snippet: At Meta Connect, I tried out the AI agent, hearing enhancement and other features on all the new glasses. I was also disappointed at how little’s been done on the privacy front.
fullText:
I talked to “Henry,” a Muse agent in my AI glasses, as I stared at a box of Kind bars. Henry was trained as if it were the assistant to a 38-year-old bodybuilding marketing executive. Henry told me whether I should eat Kind bars and also helped me plan my workout schedule. 

This was me getting a preview of Muse, Meta’s AI agent that’s already on phones and Macs, but this time it was on Meta’s AI glasses. If you were concerned about AI on what many people are calling “pervert glasses” before, they’re about to get supercharged very soon.

		

			

But I also tried on a camera-free pair of Meta glasses that gave me audio assistance, meaning privacy-invading, pervy images aren’t an issue.

This was at Meta’s Connect developer conference this week, where the focus was on AI, VR and glasses and where Meta fired out a whole bunch of updates and many new designs. It was also getting a jump on the launch of Google and Samsung’s own AI glasses, which are just around the corner. 

Some of Meta’s new glasses designs come with better battery life, some with added hearing assistance, and some, made by Thai rap star and actor Lisa, come with collectible charms. But amid all of this, there was very little about fundamental changes that would address the privacy concerns and fears surrounding a wearable category that so many companies are diving into.

Every time I wear or talk about smart glasses, people increasingly give me side eye. This has been a very bad summer for global opinions on AI-enabled and camera-equipped glasses, a category in which Meta is a leader. But with Google, Samsung and a ton of others – including Apple – expected to enter the fray next year, it’s going to get crowded and weird fast. Meta’s answer to all of this: more glasses, more features, including literally getting in our faces with its new agentic AI tool, Muse.

There is a new FDA-cleared hearing enhancement mode in Meta’s glasses that I tried, which costs $149 to activate. There are new Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses with slightly better battery life, and camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses with even better battery life (up to 12 hours). 

Muse could be the biggest news of all, especially as Meta goes head-to-head against Google and Samsung’s Gemini-infused wearables. But I was also surprised that no new fitness features were announced after Meta’s push into the space with Oakley-branded visors last year, and Meta’s prescription-challenged Ray-Ban Displays, while becoming available to order in more countries, have barely changed at all.

So, let’s break it all down. I’m still trying to digest it myself.

I tried Muse on Meta’s glasses at a single demo on Meta’s campus.Scott Stein/CNET

Meta’s putting its Muse AI agent on its glasses

Muse is an agentic AI system that’s been well-received by some early reviewers and in-app downloads since it emerged just a couple of weeks ago. Its appearance on Meta’s glasses now seems inevitable, especially since the faster-responding Muse Spark AI model has given them a performance boost. 

The only chance I got to try Muse on glasses was a very quick and pretty canned demo, and the arrival timing for Muse on glasses is still unclear. Also unclear is exactly how capable Muse will truly be or how safe. The agentic AI can already tap into personal accounts of all sorts if you let it, and it can buy things for you or manage your data, but it doesn’t promise encryption or privacy. That’s why I’ve avoided connecting it to anything in my own life, and not all accounts will allow hook-ins: Amazon just blocked Muse from enabling shopping on its sites.

My Muse glasses demo showed very little of meaningful, deeper agent hooks to data I’d recognize, since it wasn’t my own being accessed. I did notice that Muse took a while to complete some actions when rescheduling workouts for the marketing manager Muse agent Henry was set up to serve. Muse worked over audio, with no sense of progress status for completing a task.

Meta is introducing some privacy updates to how its glasses handle data, promising a new Private Processing system in the future that will run on confidential virtual machines in the cloud, a system that Meta’s using now in WhatsApp and Meta AI but plans to extend to all tools for Meta glasses. It’s not here yet, though, and it doesn’t make me feel any more convinced that any of the systems can be trusted, though, and I certainly feel lots of anxiety about handing over any agentic control of my personal data to any system.

But the space is moving fast. Google Gemini can already handle a lot of agentic actions, and Samsung and Google’s glasses will be able to do them. Apple’s new Siri, meanwhile, also has increasingly agent-like actions in its connected AI and apps. And OpenAI could be introducing more wearables with direct support for its services, too. Everyone in tech seems to want something like Iron Man’s Jarvis for your face, and few actually have it. Meta’s casting its hat in the ring.

Meta’s two Ray-Ban Audio glasses models: Clubmaster (left) and Burbank (right)Scott Stein/CNET

There are camera-free Meta Ray-Ban glasses now

One way to avoid pervert glasses concerns? Not having cameras on glasses at all. I tried out the new line of camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses, which promise 12-hour battery life (a notable bump from 8 to 9 hours on Meta’s recent glasses). There are just two designs for now: Clubmaster, which is a new look, and the more familiar square Burbank.

There’s not a lot new with Ray-Ban Audio glasses. They’re Meta glasses, minus the camera. A programmable action button on top of one arm still activates Meta AI, and one arm still has a touch bar for volume control. The audio sounded as good to me as Meta’s other models, but the battery boost could be a welcome addition. So could the social comfort of not having a camera on glasses.

But they’re not cheap. At $379 to $479, they’re actually more expensive than Meta’s recently launched line of self-branded smart glasses. Oddly, Meta didn’t make a non-Ray-Ban “Meta” branded (and likely less expensive) pair of audio glasses. Not yet, at least.

Nothing’s much changed on the camera front, either. A new landscape mode for photos sounded promising at first, but it works via digital cropping, and I haven’t tried it yet.

The phone app dashboard for Hearing Enhancement, which I got to demo briefly at Meta.Scott Stein/CNET

FDA-cleared hearing enhancement costs extra

In a move that mirrors a growing trend in hearing tech, Meta’s adding an FDA-cleared hearing assistance mode to its glasses, called Hearing Enhancement, which runs a hearing test to tune the experience for people with mild to moderate hearing loss. Apple’s AirPods Pro earbuds launched a similar feature two years ago.

Unlike Apple’s feature, though, you have to pay to enable Meta’s extra. It’s either $149, with a 30-day free trial to test how it works first, or included with a Meta One subscription that’ll run on glasses soon.

I hate subscriptions, especially for health features. A one-time cost feels more bearable. But it also pushes the total price up for a pair of Meta glasses as potential hearing aids.

To simulate how they work, Meta put foam earbuds in my ears while activating the mode during a conversation I had with Ravish Mehra, Meta’s director of research science. That’s far from a true simulation of actual hearing loss, but I got some sense of how the mode enhanced treble and clarity in sounds and conversations, like a more refined version of Meta’s existing Conversation Focus mode. Hearing Enhancement works in a targeted beam-forming mode that attends to a person, or more ambiently.

Mehra told me that the mode, when running, works for about 4  hours on Meta’s recent glasses models, but longer on the Ray-Ban Audio glasses. The extra fee could have been avoided (as Apple did), but Mehra cited R&D costs as one reason for the upcharge. I’m curious how AirPods and Meta glasses would compare for someone who actually needs the hearing assistance, something I couldn’t vet. With glasses, at least there wouldn’t be a need for any buds in your ears.

Meta Adventurer glasses in the new Lisa design are coming soon.Scott Stein/CNET

Lisa is making a pair of Meta Glasses too

I actually didn’t know who Lisa was, but she’s a famous rapper, actor and social media star who’s making her own custom-branded pair of Meta glasses, in the spirit of the Kylie Jenner glasses Meta launched in June. (My colleague Faith Chihil, one of CNET’s social media producers, flipped out at the Lisa news.)

The Lisa glasses come with a collectible charm, one of 14 types. They’re also decorated with stars on the arms. Lisa fans and collectors might be excited by this. I’m not.

But Meta’s also releasing a bunch more frame designs and colors, including some new Meta Glasses looks. Meta says there are over 100 designs and colors across all types now, and it felt that way when I browsed a bunch of new frames at Meta’s campus.

A new Aviator line of Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 smart glasses.Scott Stein/CNET

Gen 3 Meta Ray-Bans have new designs, slightly better battery

There are also new third-gen Meta Ray-Bans, but they’re not nearly as notable as the second-gen ones I wore last year. The battery boost on third-gen models is just an hour more than with Gen 2 — 9  hours total at best. That matches the claims for Google and Samsung’s imminent smart glasses, which is likely no coincidence.

There are a few frame designs, mostly variations on familiar looks. One pops, though: an aviator design that I tried out without my prescription added. They’re bold, kinda interesting, and…I felt a bit sinister wearing them.

The third-gen glasses are also more expensive, ranging from $449 to $529 without a prescription. Meta’s self-branded glasses, released in June, start at $299 and have nearly identical features, except for that tiny battery bump.

This is actually a virtual version of me in Meta’s new Hologram avatar. I animated it by talking on Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.Scott Stein/CNET

Meta Ray-Ban Displays haven’t evolved much at all (except for Holograms)

Last year, Meta made a big deal with its display-enabled Ray-Bans and innovative neural band interface, a setup that seemed to push toward a future where full AR glasses lurk. 

And yet, a year later, Meta has no significant improvements for Displays. They’ll be available in more countries this year, and may be easier to buy. But they still don’t work for a larger range of prescriptions, limited to just a -4 maximum. My eyes still won’t work with them.

Meta has been opening up more app development for its glasses and rolling out more features for Displays over the last year. Still, I expected Meta might find a way to blend its neural band with a smartwatch, perhaps one of Garmin’s models, since Meta and Garmin already have a partnership. But that didn’t happen either. The prices of the glasses are also still the same.

The most interesting thing about the Displays is the addition of Holograms, a hyper-realistic video chat avatar system that I tested out at Meta’s campus and was wowed by. It scans your face with a phone app and then projects your presence to the phone screen (or glasses, or VR headset) of whoever you’re calling, to surprisingly realistic effect. It’ll only be available to a limited test group at first in beta and will work on WhatsApp, but deliver the sort of simulated video chat on glasses that has been promised by Meta for years.

Besides camera-free Meta glasses (left), the design of Meta’s new glasses and camera design (right) remains the same.Scott Stein/CNET

Sorry, no watch, new fitness modes or major privacy improvements yet

Meanwhile, I was also surprised that Meta had no fitness updates at Connect, despite introducing Oakley-branded Vanguard visors last year and Garmin-connected workout features.

The Muse agent can connect to fitness and health functions, but a lack of new dedicated fitness features leaves a gap that Google might fill quickly with possibilities for Fitbit integration on its upcoming glasses, and an interconnection between WearOS watches and its glasses to act as a mini control dashboard and even preview photos. 

Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth hinted to me last year that the neural band could evolve into a watch, but those plans haven’t yet materialized. Unlike Google and Apple’s wearables, Meta’s glasses are limited in how they connect to phones, using an app and, in the future, agentic hooks via Muse’s AI. 

And also, biggest of all, Meta’s privacy issues feel barely addressed. It’s still as easy to take a photo in public as before, and nothing’s changed with how the glasses present themselves to others: They’re easy to confuse with regular glasses (to Meta’s credit, design-wise) and still just show a small LED light when recording.

And while Meta has promises of a private compute layer in the cloud for its future features, can they be trusted, and will third-party observers get access in any way? Will any of these new agentic features misfire unpredictably, as we’ve already seen with AI agents? The answer there feels like a “when” rather than an “if.” 

But Meta won’t be alone in the pursuit of agentic AI wearables. It’s just the biggest and first in the door. There’s a lot of potential lurking in wearable AI, and lots of concerns. And Meta’s continuing to roll forward through all of it.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											I started with CNET reviewing laptops in 2009. Now I explore wearable tech, VR/AR, tablets, gaming and future/emerging trends in our changing world. Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.

fullText:
A few years back, I was at a beachside Easter egg hunt, watching my kids dash through sand dunes searching for sweet treats. My phone buzzed in my pocket; I ignored it. A moment later, it buzzed again. I pulled it out, glanced down, and saw a “motion detected” notification from my security camera. “Just my dog in the yard,” I thought, dismissing it.

As the colorful eggs piled up in the baskets, my phone kept buzzing. Reluctantly, I pulled it out again and saw several more “motion detected” alerts. I tried to load a video clip, but it just buffered endlessly.

AI-powered text descriptions paint the whole scene in a sentence. 

When I returned home, I found my four pet chickens dead, killed by my small border terrier. Looking back over the camera footage, I saw that they had pushed open their coop door, which I, in a rush to get to the Easter festivities, hadn’t properly secured.

If instead of “motion detected,” that first notification had read “small dog chasing a chicken,” I would have raced back home and maybe saved them.

Today, that type of notification is possible. With AI-generated text descriptions, a short message describing what the camera saw can arrive almost instantly, well before a video feed loads, painting the whole scene in a sentence.

Most major security camera companies now offer text descriptions, which combine traditional motion triggers with Vision Language Models, including Ring, Google Nest, Blink, Wyze, and Arlo. This month, with iOS 27, Apple finally brought the capability to its HomeKit Secure Video service with the launch of Apple Intelligence for Home.

The surprise is that Apple is charging up to three times as much as its competition for the feature. Is it worth it? And are security cameras getting better at telling us about what actually matters?

You’d think no one can get past my door without me knowing about it.

I’ve been testing Apple Intelligence for Home since it launched in beta this summer, alongside Amazon Ring’s and Google Nest’s AI camera features introduced last year. I installed several cameras for each, but for this piece, I focused mainly on video doorbells — which I set up when iOS 27 officially arrived on September 14th. I tested a Ring Wired Doorbell Pro ($249.99), Google Nest Doorbell 2K ($199.99), and for Apple, the HomeKit Secure Video-compatible Aqara Doorbell Camera G400 ($99).

I focused on how quickly each service sent the AI-powered notifications, how accurate and useful the descriptions were at telling me what happened, and how reliably it captured and notified me about activity. I also tested other AI-powered features each platform offers, including Apple’s ability to search and stitch together activity across multiple cameras, Ring’s Unusual Event that distinguished normal activity from out-of-the-ordinary events, and Google’s ability to trigger automations based on what a camera sees.

The AI features on all three platforms are a significant improvement over their basic smart alerts. It’s now easier to understand what’s happening at a glance and decide whether to react, and security cameras feel more useful and less annoying overall.

Ultimately, the real value of AI in cameras isn’t in describing what they see, but in using that knowledge to figure out what you actually need to know, and eventually what your home should do about it.

What Apple Intelligence provides, at what price

How to use Apple Intelligence for Home

2TB plan: $9.99 a month (or Apple One / $39.95 a month) for one camera

6TB plan: $29.99 a month for two cameras

12TB plan: $59.99 a month for up to five cameras

No tier supports more than five cameras.

Note: standard HomeKit Secure Video recording also requires an iCloud Plus plan, starting at $0.99 for one camera (50GB plan), $2.99 for five (200GB), and $9.99 for unlimited (2TB). All tiers that include Apple Intelligence support basic HKSV features on unlimited cameras.

Apple Intelligence is on by default for Reduce Notifications and off by default for Summarize Videos. To adjust, go to Settings in the Home app, scroll down to Apple Intelligence, toggle on Summarize Video, and select participating cameras.

With Apple Intelligence, a compatible camera connected to Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service can send you text descriptions through the Apple Home app: “A dog sat on the floor,” “a cat played in the room,” “someone delivered a package.”

It also enables natural-language video search, surfaces “noteworthy” events, stitches relevant clips together, and adds a reduce notifications feature that combines related events into a single alert that updates. This is in addition to the existing smart alerts, facial recognition, and 10 days of video storage available with HomeKit Secure Video.

Pricing is where it gets tricky. Apple Intelligence for Home is bundled into iCloud Plus: $10 a month covers one camera, $30 covers two, and $60 up to five (see sidebar). No tier supports more than five cameras.

By comparison, Google Home’s Nest cameras offer Gemini-powered text descriptions, video search, facial recognition, and a daily Home Brief digest — which summarizes the day’s activity in a short paragraph (sometimes with a fictional slant) — for $20 a month, covering unlimited cameras and 24/7 recording on wired models.

Amazon’s Ring also charges $20 a month for its AI text descriptions, video search, facial recognition, unusual events alerts, and clip recording on unlimited cameras, with 24/7 costing an extra $3 per camera on wired models. Ring has its own reduced notification option that rolls similar events from the same camera into one notification, such as “Brian is mowing the lawn.”

Apple says the least

Text descriptions are a game changer for security cameras. For me, getting an alert that says “A FedEx delivery person is walking on the lawn” rather than “person detected at front door” is the difference between getting up and going downstairs or carrying on working. But quality and accuracy vary wildly, even within a single provider.

Sometimes I get useful details, other times a few words that tell me almost nothing. Then there were the times when the descriptions were detailed, but laughably wrong: “A tennis serve simulator is rolling on the walkway,” “A gray hoverboard is driving on the pathway” — both misidentifications of a robot lawn mower.

1/3I donned a Ghostface mask to see how the various AIs would react. Nest sent the most useful alert.

In my testing, text alerts from Google and Ring provided the most context and specificity, and Apple often didn’t try, saying “someone” rather than providing any detail. For example, it would say “someone is walking in the yard,” whereas Ring and Google provided more context: a delivery person is walking in the yard, a person in uniform, someone carrying a bag, and so on.

Apple was also the briefest. For example, when my cat was on the front porch, Apple said, “A cat sat on the porch.” Ring went with “A cat is standing on the pathway outside the porch.” Google Home told me which cat: “A black and white cat walks across the porch.”

All three identified delivery trucks, correctly flagging UPS and FedEx vehicles driving past, as well as delivery people approaching the door. Apple was the only one to ID the USPS van pulling up to my mailbox, although not consistently.

Google was the most descriptive with vehicles — “a light-colored car drives by on the street” or “a white van,” “a dark-colored SUV” — Apple and Ring mostly said “a vehicle drove by,” sometimes with a type (van, car, truck).

Apple’s reduce notifications feature combines several alerts into one.

These were difficult to read and not terribly useful.

Apple’s descriptions were the hardest to digest at a glance, particularly the combined ones through reduce notifications. For example, “Someone seen. Someone carried a box” is clunky. Ring and Google merge the events more fluidly into “a person carried a box up the driveway.”

In fairness, Apple Intelligence in Home only officially launched this month, so I expect this to improve, but as things stand, Ring’s and Google’s are more useful and cost less.

Finicky facial recognition and alerts

For a doorbell camera, the real advantage of AI descriptions is knowing who’s there right away. All three offer facial recognition alongside the ability to spot a UPS driver or similar.

Ring was the most consistently accurate, identifying me every time I approached the door. Apple hedged its bets, sometimes identifying me, sometimes saying “Someone who may be Jennifer Pattison Tuohy,” and other times just “Someone.” Google got it right about half the time; the other half it thought I was my daughter’s best mate (a change from the UPS driver it pegged me as for most of last year).

Apple just wasn’t sure about me.

Ring was the most accurate; Google was mostly accurate.

Text descriptions are more useful if they show up, and quickly. But on the doorbell camera I was testing, Apple’s often didn’t. Apple Home reliably alerted me when someone pressed the doorbell, and it recorded every event, but notifications about other motion events were inconsistent.

A potential issue here is that, unlike its competition, Apple doesn’t control the whole experience. HomeKit Secure Video only works with third-party hardware — there are no Apple cameras yet. I was using the G400, Aqara’s latest wired doorbell camera.

When I first set it up, alerts arrived in Apple Home with no issues, but at some point they stopped, and no amount of troubleshooting brought them back. However, alerts kept coming through in the Aqara app. I also still got doorbell ring alerts in the Home app, and notifications from other Aqara cameras continued to work.

The Google Nest doorbell captured everything and was consistently first to notify me of an event. Ring was also fast and mostly reliable; its notifications showed up just after Google’s, though I’d occasionally get “This video is unavailable” when trying to play back footage.

Reliability is Apple’s biggest fix, plus some innovation

The good news is that recording in HomeKit Secure Video has improved significantly with iOS 27. Apple said it completely rearchitected the system, which addresses a long-standing problem with missing clips.

I’ve noticed that cameras load faster, are more stable, and no longer miss recordings. An Eve outdoor camera that was almost always offline has been stable since the upgrade, and the Aqara Camera Hub G5 outdoor camera and G350 indoor camera have also been solid. The G400 doorbell camera has been the only problem child, with missing notifications, but it records consistently.

All the other HomeKit cameras I tested reliably sent alerts; only the Aqara doorbell camera had the issue, but even when I didn’t get alerts, I could use video search to find events.

Typing “When did the USPS truck come” in the Apple Home app pulled up every instance the Aqara doorbell spotted the mail delivery. In comparison, while the Nest Cam didn’t identify the USPS truck as often, its video search results contained more specifics, including an event where the mail person dropped off an Amazon package.

Of the three, Google’s video search was the most useful, followed by Ring’s, then Apple’s, which directly correlates with the amount of detail each provides in the text descriptions.

Apple has two features Ring and Google don’t offer. The first is clip stitching, where Apple Intelligence identifies someone or something on one camera, recognizes it again on another, understands these are related, and plays the sequence as a single video in the Home app. I haven’t found a real use for this so far, but it’s been fun for tracking my dog around the house when I’m out.

The second feature is bringing events that Apple judges important to the top of the search box. In the last two weeks, it’s only highlighted the trash pickup ━ I guess my life just isn’t that noteworthy.

Here’s where Ring wins

One of the biggest problems with security cameras is filtering out the important info from the sheer volume of everything they see. Even with AI notifications turned on, I still get a stream of alerts from Apple Home and Google Home. Some are more useful than they used to be, but overload is still an issue.

These are the only alerts Ring sent from the doorbell camera over an entire weekend when I had Unusual Event enabled.

Apple’s noteworthy events is a similar concept, but it doesn’t send a specific alert instead just surfacing the clip to the top of your search page.

While Apple’s noteworthy events feature shows promise, Ring’s Unusual Event feature is the best solution I’ve seen. It learns what normal traffic looks like for each camera, then notifies you only when something isn’t normal. This summer, I cut my Ring notifications down from around 40 a day to just two or three.

Instead of getting an alert every time my cat is on my porch, I only get one when a raccoon or possum walks by. It doesn’t send alerts when my son comes home from school, but it does when he comes home at 2AM. The camera by my chicken coop no longer sends a series of notifications when someone is feeding them or collecting eggs — but it does alert me when I am out there at midnight with a flashlight to wrestle a snake.

What’s next: cameras that can act

The cats were a big fan of Google Home’s inability to tell them apart, as it meant more kibble. (This is not Smokey).

The natural progression here is automations triggered by the camera understanding what it sees. Turn on the sprinklers if there’s a raccoon in the backyard, but not if it’s just my dog. A cat at the back door broadcasts an alert through my smart speakers so someone can let them in. The trash truck rolling past without stopping sends an urgent notification to put the bins out before it comes back the other way.

This is where cameras move beyond being simply security devices to become intelligent smart-home sensors that can understand what’s happening and potentially act on it.

Google Home recently added the ability to trigger automations from camera alerts, although in my early testing, it’s not reliable enough.

I tried it with my three cats and a pet feeder using Google’s new Pet Memory feature. But instead of only dispensing food for one specific cat as I asked, it triggered every time it saw a cat. At least the cats were happy.

The problem is accuracy. When AI can’t reliably identify the subject, the automations can’t respond reliably. So, my earlier example of Apple accurately recognizing the USPS van half the time would mean any automation I set up to alert me the mail is here would only work half the time.

Today, Apple doesn’t have this capability, but if the rumors that the company is developing its own video doorbell and security camera are true, I would expect to see a feature like this come to Apple Home.

The privacy tradeoff

The smarter cameras become, the more they need to know about your home. For a system to understand what’s normal, it needs to learn who lives there, when they come and go, which pets are around, and which vehicles belong. This raises very real concerns around privacy and surveillance.

Ring has faced particular scrutiny over its cloud-based architecture and partnerships with law enforcement. Where Google and Apple can start with local processing, Ring processes all footage in the cloud by default.

There’s real benefit in a system knowing everything about my home — I’d just prefer to be the only one who knows it.

Last month, Ring announced an overhaul to that model, introducing a new default encryption system called TAKE. This rotates encryption keys for cloud-stored video and deletes Ring’s copy after 24 hours. Among other privacy protections, including no admin access, Ring says this means it can no longer hand over decrypted footage to the police. However, it can still be compelled to provide encrypted files.

With Apple’s standard HomeKit Secure Video, your home hub processes footage locally and encrypts it end-to-end before sending it to the cloud for storage. But adding Apple Intelligence changes that: Video summaries are now processed in the cloud using Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC), where they are unencrypted for processing.

According to Apple, PCC writes the captions, sends them back, and then “permanently deletes the data from PCC.” Apple support docs also state that there is no admin access, and nothing identifies who the footage belongs to.

Google takes a similar approach to Apple, but without end-to-end encryption; footage is encrypted in transit and at rest. Gemini for Home-enabled Nest cameras can use some on-device processing, but the heavy work is done in the Gemini cloud, in line with Google Home’s privacy practices.

A big question for me is whether all this intelligence has to live on someone else’s computers. There’s real benefit in a system knowing everything about my home — I’d just prefer to be the only one who knows it. For privacy, security, and potentially speed, local AI processing and storage feels like the right answer. Manufacturers including Anker Eufy, Reolink, Ubiquiti UniFi, and UGreen already have or have announced products that do this.

With a new Apple TV, HomePod, and a possible smart display all rumored to be imminent, Apple’s next generation of hardware might shift more processing back into the house — which could mean paying less every month for the privilege.

When Ghostface is at my door, I want Apple Home to tell me.

Is Apple Intelligence worth it?

Based on my testing of the beta and the initial full release, Apple Intelligence in Home has brought substantial improvements, finally putting HomeKit Secure Video in contention with Ring and Google.

Whether it’s worth the price depends on how many cameras you own. If you have one — say, a video doorbell — Apple Intelligence is a reasonable deal at $10 a month if you also need 2TB of iCloud storage. You get competent descriptions, better video search, and Apple’s privacy position. Even with multiple cameras, you can get some benefit by enabling it on just one.

Next let’s make them better at telling us what actually matters.

However, if you want AI capabilities across your home, including clip stitching, the math gets bad fast. At five cameras, you’re paying $60 a month for Apple to tell you “a cat sat on the porch” or “a vehicle drove by.” The competition gives you more detailed descriptions on as many cameras as you own for $20 a month.

Today, you’re paying an Apple premium for less. But this is Apple’s first move, and I expect it to improve. AI has unlocked genuine utility here, making security cameras better at telling us what’s happening; next, let’s make them better at telling us what actually matters.

A few years ago, a “motion detected” alert wasn’t enough to tell me that my chickens were in trouble. Today, AI can tell me it’s a dog chasing a chicken. The next step is for it to understand that this is something I need to know right now and make sure I get that information quickly enough to act. Eventually, an intelligent home might actually be able to do something about it, too.

That’s the smart home I want. But we’re not there yet.

title: Lightspeed targets $250M for new India fund, focusing on early-stage AI
snippet: The venture firm is aligning its India fundraising cycle with its global funds for the first time, as it shifts to a shorter investment period.
fullText:
Lightspeed is sharpening its India strategy around AI, targeting $250 million for a new early-stage fund as the venture firm bets the technology will drive the next wave of startups in one of the world’s largest markets.

The Silicon Valley venture firm is already a major investor in AI companies including Anthropic, xAI, and Databricks. In India, it has backed Sarvam AI, one of the country’s leading large language model developers and a startup selected by the Indian government to help develop sovereign AI models.

The new fund, Lightspeed India Partners V, will be half the size of its $500 million predecessor, raised in 2022, and has already secured commitments for 80% of its $250 million target, according to a letter sent to investors on Thursday and seen by TechCrunch.

In late April, Lightspeed disclosed the new fund in a U.S. regulatory filing, though the filing did not specify its target size. Indian media had previously reported that the firm was looking to raise between $300 million and $350 million for the vehicle.

Lightspeed plans to begin investing from the new fund within two months and has designed it around an investment period of roughly two and a half years, per the letter. Until then, it will continue making its final investments from the existing fund.

A Lightspeed spokesperson declined to comment.

Starting with the new fund, Lightspeed is also moving its India funds onto the same fundraising cycle as its global funds for the first time, per the investor letter. The change brings a regional business it established nearly two decades ago more closely in line with the rest of the firm.

The move follows a similar shift by rival firm Accel, which in August raised its latest $550 million India fund alongside new U.S. and Europe funds and a global growth vehicle as part of a coordinated $3.5 billion fundraising effort. It was the first time Accel had raised all four funds simultaneously.

The $250 million fund is sized to match how quickly Lightspeed is currently investing and its shorter investment period, according to the letter. Lightspeed suggested to investors that the smaller size lets it focus on individual deals rather than fund size, and raise its next fund sooner.

The new fund also marks a sharper focus on AI for Lightspeed’s early-stage investment strategy in the region. The investment thesis outlined in the letter anticipates AI creating more value in India than the internet did, with the fund seeking out AI companies across India and Southeast Asia.

India has yet to produce a major frontier AI model developer on the global stage and has attracted far less investment in AI than the U.S. and China. Investors, nonetheless, increasingly see an opportunity for India in the application layer, drawing on the country’s large pool of software developers and its decades-long history as a hub for software and technology services.

The new $250 million India vehicle is a fraction of the capital available across Lightspeed’s global platform. The firm, which manages more than $65 billion in assets globally, raised $9 billion across several new funds last December, the largest fundraising haul in its history. The total included a $980 million early-stage venture fund.

Lightspeed’s dedicated India and Southeast Asia funds represent only part of the capital the firm has put to work in the region. Those funds have deployed roughly $900 million, while Lightspeed’s global funds have invested another $1.6 billion to support companies from the regional portfolio, according to the investor letter.

The decision to dedicate its newest regional fund entirely to AI also marks a sharper thematic focus for Lightspeed in a market where it has historically invested across sectors. Its India portfolio spans businesses including quick commerce, consumer internet, software, and household services.

Lightspeed’s bets in India have included companies such as quick-commerce startup Zepto, audio platform Pocket FM, house-help startup Snabbit, rooftop solar startup SolarSquare, and a range of enterprise software businesses.

The same team that led Lightspeed’s previous four India funds will manage the new fund, per the letter.

title: Meta’s New AI Device Is This Tamagotchi-Like Muse Charm Keychain
snippet: Meta says the keychain will be ready to ship by the holiday season, like some kind of bizarre AI stocking stuffer.
fullText:
If you were overwhelmed by all the new Meta AI smart glasses at its annual Connect event on Wednesday, you’re not alone. CEO Mark Zuckerberg introduced many new glasses, including the reimagined Meta VR glasses that make the Quest 3 and Vision Pro look very old and bulky. But the keynote brought us one more AI device: Meet the Muse Charm.

This keychain looks like you took the face of an Apple Watch and tied a short phone strap to it. It’s a small, round device with a fingerprint sensor for you to activate it without needing a phone or laptop. The reason for it? To talk to your AI agent, Muse, whenever you want.

		

			

Muse is Meta’s AI agent, an autonomous bot that can assist you with tasks. Unlike chatbots, agents can take action and complete tasks independently. You can use Muse to send messages on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, for example.

The Muse Charm keychain isn’t available yet, but Zuckerberg said in the keynote that it will be ready by December — just in time for the holidays, if your loved ones are into that AI stocking-stuffer thing. You can sign up for email updates on the device here.

Building Muse into a physical device

Muse has been relatively popular since its early September launch, with reports saying the agent’s app has been downloaded more than half a million times. This week’s reports of a serious zero-day cybersecurity vulnerability — now patched — haven’t seemed to dampen folks’ enthusiasm for Muse.

That is likely because agentic AI is largely seen as the future of AI. But it isn’t without risk. Privacy and security are huge concerns. Earlier this summer, AI agents from Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic escaped their digital testing environments and hacked real websites, including the popular AI platform Hugging Face and a system run by the Australian government. These incidents of so-called “rogue agents” — although they typically stemmed from poorly designed testing protocols — have prompted a lot of concern inside and outside of the AI industry, drawing the attention of governments around the world that are still struggling to create rules around AI.

Zuckerberg, for his part, has been clear that he doesn’t think a coordinated industry slowdown will be necessary. Every lab should be able to police itself, he wrote on X, citing the months Meta spent developing the tech behind Muse. But during those months, Meta was largely seen by the AI industry and investors as “falling behind in the AI race.” All the AI labs, including Meta, have significant financial incentives to develop the best AI quickly, even if that means safety falls to the wayside.

And safety will be key to the success of any AI device, including the Muse Charm. Meta, ironically, has already proven that. Its AI-enabled smart glasses drew widespread public backlash this summer after it was reported that Meta was considering adding facial recognition technology to the glasses. That built on mounting fears people had of glasses-wearers recording them with the camera in the glasses, without their consent, leading to Meta smart glasses being nicknamed “pervert glasses.”

Meta denied the facial recognition report despite the evidence and told CNET that privacy is important. But Meta still hasn’t provided many details on how it will protect wearers and bystanders. At Connect this year, Zuckerberg and the company left many of these questions still unanswered, as CNET’s Scott Stein reported.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Discord Introduces Alternative Age Verification Tools After Pushback
snippet: Teenage users have options, but some appear safer than others. We pick the best options.
fullText:
After Discord users pushed back on ID requirements for age verification, the social platform announced in a blog post on Tuesday that it would implement age verification for teens — but not in the way people expected.

“Discord is introducing a new approach to age assurance, strengthening teen safety without requiring everyone to prove their age,” the company said in an email to CNET. “More than 90% of users won’t be asked to confirm their age. Most will either be placed into an age group automatically or will be able to continue using Discord without confirming their age unless they want to access age-restricted content, spaces, or settings.”

For those who do need to verify, Discord focuses on measuring “age signals” for teens rather than actual IDs, and it tells users it will not receive any direct data about them except their age signal results. The platform will work with a variety of vendors who will examine different types of data to assess a person’s age. Discord says those vendors won’t use any of this data for ad targeting or AI model training.

			

More from CNET

This follows a Discord-related data breach in 2025, which exposed 70,000 government ID photos of users, among with other information, on a vendor website.

The good news is that young Discord users can now choose how to verify their age, including options that don’t show their faces or IDs. Some of Discord’s options look fairly privacy-friendly, such as the ability to use documentation already in Google Wallet or the Apple App Store to verify age. If you’ve been using Apple’s store long enough, you may not have to send any further documentation at all. They can also use a site called AgeKey to create a reusable age credential. This allows teens to verify their age across multiple platforms without sharing their personal data directly with Discord.

Some troubling choices

However, some of Discord’s verification options raise serious privacy concerns.

“While estimating age based on user behavior is less invasive than requiring users to upload photos, credit card information or a state-issued ID, age-gating the internet creates dangerous new forms of surveillance, censorship, and exclusion,” Electronic Frontier Foundation senior counsel David Greene told CNET.

Discord includes a facial age-estimation option that requires a video selfie. Although the site says all facial analysis happens locally on the device, this use of AI still gives us pause. Experts point to ongoing accuracy challenges and inherent data risks, raising concerns over how corporate policies and algorithmic parameters might evolve in the future.

We’re also not fans of the credit-card check option, which not only costs money but sends credit card details to a third party, which may increase financial security risks.

Inaccurate age estimates can always happen, and they complicate the process. While Discord notes that users can initially switch to alternative confirmation methods, manual review serves as the fallback if those options fail. However, this manual route is a last resort and requires a human representative to personally verify both a government ID and a photograph.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: OpenAI upgrading ChatGPT and Codex with two more GPT-6 models
snippet: Earlier this month, OpenAI released the first GPT-6 model with Astra. Now GPT-6 is expanding with new GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. more…
fullText:
Earlier this month, OpenAI released the first GPT-6 model with Astra. Now GPT-6 is expanding with new GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models.

GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are now available

Per the ChatGPT desktop app release notes, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna will use fewer tokens to run than GPT-5.6 versions of the same class model.

GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are rolling out to Codex and ChatGPT Work at lower token prices than their GPT-5.6 predecessors. Use Sol for complex coding and agentic workflows, and Luna for focused, high-volume tasks.

Both models are rolling out to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access Luna in the desktop app. Availability depends on rollout and workspace settings; Enterprise administrators must enable the new models. In ChatGPT, the models are available in Work and Codex, but not Chat.

Note the absence of a GPT-6 Terra model. It’s expected that OpenAI is dropping the medium model in favor of just three: Terra (small), Sol (large), and Astra (extra large).

GPT-6 Sol and Luna are out. Not only are they a very significant improvement across the board, but also in writing and general "you know when you try it" quality. 

We are also permanently reducing the API price by 50% making both of them viable for a ton of new usecases and… https://t.co/vbyUhVlKH3

— Tibo (@thsottiaux) September 22, 2026

Here’s the official announcement from OpenAI:

While the most demanding and important projects still call for Astra’s full depth, work happens at different scales, rhythms, and budgets.

That’s why we’re expanding the GPT‑6 universe with GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna. GPT‑6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence—these models help distribute the benefits of that intelligence by advancing the frontier on cost efficiency. We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The company describes its two newest models as more capable than the GPT-5.6 versions as well as more affordable than Astra (and the GPT-5.6 versions they replace). For instance, the GPT-6 versions of Sol and Luna are 50% cheaper than the GPT-5.6 versions.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing. Together, these improvements make advanced AI practical for more everyday tasks and applications at scale.

In terms of coding, this is what OpenAI says about its new models:

This year, coding agents have begun tackling tasks with more complexity, scope, and duration than ever before. At OpenAI, our internal usage has grown exponentially. Valued at API prices, daily token usage has exceeded $600 for the median researcher and $7,000 for researchers at the 90th percentile (Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI⁠). As coding agents take on longer and more demanding tasks, the cost of sustained use matters more. GPT‑6 Sol and Luna combine strong coding performance with lower API prices, giving developers more room to iterate and teams the confidence to be more ambitious about what they ask Codex to take on.

ChatGPT also excels at Computer Use, and these new models continue that push:

While GPT‑6 Astra remains the world’s best model for computer use, GPT‑6 Sol and Luna offer more cost-efficient performance than their predecessors. On OSWorld 2.0 offline, GPT‑6 Sol at xhigh effort achieves a similar score to Claude Opus 5 at medium effort—60.5% versus 60.3%—at approximately 80% lower cost per task. GPT‑6 Luna (max) is able to exceed GPT‑5.6 Sol (medium) at one tenth of its cost.

In terms of availability, OpenAI says both new models will be rolling out throughout the day.

GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access GPT‑6 Luna in the desktop app. 

You can learn much more about the new models here.

Please welcome GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna to the GPT-6 universe.

title: Databricks buys Row Zero and is scouting for more startups to acquire
snippet: Databricks has bought cloud spreadsheet startup Row Zero, adding yet another acquisition to its 2026 shopping spree.
fullText:
Databricks announced on Thursday that it has acquired an early-stage spreadsheet startup called Row Zero.

The story goes that Databricks’ finance team fell in love with Row Zero because it was a cloud tool that could scale beyond 1 million live spreadsheet rows. They were combining Row Zero with Databricks’ homegrown AI agent called Genie. With Genie, Databricks users can use natural-language prompts to ask complicated business questions of their data stored in Databricks systems, such as analyzing profit margins or the status of sales prospects.

When the executive team asked the finance team about this cloud tool they were using, a light bulb went off. 

“Spreadsheets are one such interface that every business analyst loves. So it makes a lot of sense to intermarry Business Intelligence (BI), Agents, and Spreadsheets!” Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi posted on X about how the acquisition went down.

So an enterprise’s secure data lives in Databricks’ cloud storage, and AI agents and humans interact with it through the spreadsheet format and formulas they know well, rather than using and learning some other business intelligence software. By integrating Row Zero with Databricks, the data can be manipulated in a spreadsheet form but remain secure, rather than transferred to an insecure spreadsheet that is shared around.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Row Zero, founded by former AWS and Tableau engineers, raised $10 million in May 2025, at an estimated $40 million valuation at the time, according to PitchBook.

Databricks, which closed another $5 billion in funding in August and hit $7 billion in annualized revenue run rate, has been busy shopping in 2026 and is eager to keep doing so. “We intend to do many more acquisitions like this in the future,” Ghodsi told TechCrunch.

In March, Databricks bought two startups, Quotient AI, which does evaluation and reinforcement learning for AI agents, and very early-stage interactive notebook SiftD.ai. In June, the company bought AI security operations center startup Panther, previously valued at $1.4 billion in 2021. Last month, it bought Electric, makers of a small, lite Postgres database known as PGlite, useful for agents running locally on devices.
