title: Apple vs. Adobe: How does iOS 27’s AI photo editing compare to Photoshop?
snippet: I’ve been using Photoshop’s generative AI features to remove unwanted objects and extend photos since Adobe introduced them in 2023. They’ve been hit or miss for me, but they’re certainly a lot faster than the old-fashioned approach of masking, cloning, and manually painting things out. But with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved its Clean Up tool and introduced the new Extend tool, and I was curious to see how Apple’s offerings compare with Adobe’s. So, with the help of a friend, I put both to the test using a variety of photos to see how they stack up. more…
fullText:
I’ve been using Photoshop’s generative AI features to remove unwanted objects and extend photos since Adobe introduced them in 2023. They’ve been hit or miss for me, but they’re certainly a lot faster than the old-fashioned approach of masking, cloning, and manually painting things out. But with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved its Clean Up tool and introduced the new Extend tool, and I was curious to see how Apple’s offerings compare with Adobe’s. So, with the help of a friend, I put both to the test using a variety of photos to see how they stack up.

For this article, my friend Jürg was kind enough to provide several photos from his travels throughout Switzerland and Europe. He takes much better photos than I ever could, and takes pictures of more exciting subjects than my corner of Ohio has to offer. You can see more of his photography on Instagram. I narrowed the selection down to six photos: three to test object removal and three to test image extension.

All photos were shot on an iPhone 17 Pro Max and edited on an iPhone 18 Pro Max running iOS 27.0. The Clean Up tool in iOS 27 has three options: Auto, Fast, and High Quality. I left the setting on Auto for all three tests.

Photoshop tests were done on a MacBook Pro running Adobe Photoshop 27.10.0 using the “Firefly Fill & Expand” model. I selected the objects using either the Object Selection Tool or Lasso Tool, then chose Generative Fill and left the prompt box blank.

For the Extend tool, I used whatever extension Photos selected by default. The Extend tool in Photos limits how far you can expand the edges of an image, while Photoshop doesn’t have the same restriction. To keep the comparison as consistent as possible, I used the result from Apple’s Photos as my reference, and had Photoshop create something in a similar size.

I made every effort to keep the HDR appearance as consistent as possible between the photos edited in Photos on iOS 27 and those edited in Photoshop, but there was some minor variation.

Making things disappear

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

First up is the removal of this red chair in front of the yellow door. This was the first photo I tested with the new Clean Up tool, and I have to say, it left quite a positive impression. The result looks very believable, and the only real mistake I noticed is that the rivet behind the chair’s left armrest was also removed instead of being correctly reconstructed. It’s not something I’m convinced most people would notice, though, and it would be an easy fix to clone back in with Photoshop. I was particularly impressed by how the shadow beneath the chair was replaced with a texture that matches the surrounding scene while also maintaining the existing lighting.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop doesn’t do as good a job as Apple’s Clean Up tool here. The chair’s shadow remains and looks more like an oil stain. The door’s rivets are misaligned, and one is obviously missing. The replacement texture also contains significantly more visual artifacts. Overall, it isn’t nearly as clean or realistic as what Clean Up produced.

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

I was really impressed with Clean Up’s results here. Not only did it remove the plate with bread, but it also added a nice reflection of the mug and jars. Notice it even got the handle of the spoon right in the reflection. A nice detail. Clean Up also completely removed the plate’s shadow from the napkin. I thought removing a red plate from a red table of the same color might prove more of a challenge for Clean Up, but nope! If I had one nitpick, it’s that Clean Up left the crumbs from the plate, though removing them would be very easy to do by running Clean Up again over that area.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop removed the plate with bread well enough, but again, it had issues with leaving behind an out-of-place shadow. The napkin looks dirty or wet here, but at least Photoshop didn’t leave behind as many pesky crumbs.

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

This photo proved to be a much bigger challenge for Clean Up. After attempting to remove the man on the right, Clean Up left behind a garbled mess with plenty of obvious artifacts. The leaves are too chunky. It struggled in a similar way on the left side of the image, where the woman with white hair was standing behind the white flowers. Clean Up also left behind a “ghost” of the dog’s head, though it arguably blends in with the stone wall and is much more noticeable in this side-by-side comparison.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop had no issues removing the woman on the left behind the white flowers or the man on the right behind the leaves, realistically filling in both areas in the process. The end result is a very convincing photo that looks like nobody was ever there. Photoshop also avoided leaving behind any phantom shadows this time.

Adding to the picture

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

I thought this photograph of these old, winding steps would make for a good test because I didn’t think it would be immediately obvious to either AI what it was looking at, and I was curious to see how each would interpret the scene. Or even what it would do with it. It looks like iOS 27’s Extend tool interpreted the photo as something more like a ceiling fan, rounding off the ends of the stairs as though they were blades. Photoshop, on the other hand, simply extended the stairs outward and did a surprisingly good job of matching the wood grain.

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Extend does an excellent job living up to its name here. It extends the scene really well and creates a very convincing final image. Notice the windows are believably repeated and the bridge on the right side of the photo, while arguably too smooth, still manages to look fairly convincing.

Now look at Photoshop’s attempt. Actually, Photoshop, did you even make an attempt? This is a complete failure by just about every measure. Pure, obvious AI slop. The windows and roofline in the upper-left corner of the photo look terrible. The bridge on the right doesn’t have anything resembling the realistic arch Apple created, and for some reason, Photoshop decided the waterfall should randomly change direction rather than continue along the existing river line.

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Extend again manages to create a convincing image that, while not perfect, is significantly better than what Photoshop produced. Extend creates a believable table with some books or magazines, and the flowers in the vase look much more realistic than those generated by Photoshop. The decorative ornamentation above the left door also matches the real ones in the photo surprisingly well. There is some strangeness on the right side of the photo, where Extend has added a radiator, a random power cord, and a table for some reason.

Perhaps the biggest difference between Extend and Photoshop is at the ceiling. Extend has recreated more of the wood from the opposite wall, while Photoshop has tried to turn it into something more like a structural beam.

Photoshop, meanwhile, can’t seem to generate an image without the telltale signs of AI slop. Its table has too many legs and appears to simply “break off” before blending into the floor. The ornamentation above the door is less convincing, missing one of the “swirls” and doesn’t have the textured paint found on the real ornamentation in the photo.

I wouldn’t say either is perfect, but when it comes to realism, I think Apple’s solution edges out Adobe’s.

The good, the bad, and the AI slop

It’s worth mentioning that Photoshop requires a subscription to use, but none of the features I tested consume generative AI credits. Adobe does give users the option to choose other AI models that may require credits, but I didn’t use those models in my tests. Apple, too, has made it clear that “usage limits may apply” to some Apple Intelligence features and may charge for expanded access in the future. 

It’s clear that Apple has made significant improvements to the Clean Up tool over previous versions of iOS. I’ve tried it before and always found it underwhelming, but now it’s genuinely good. The new Extend tool is impressive as well, and I found it significantly better than Adobe’s offering in my tests. Adobe gives you unlimited refinements and the ability to adjust results with prompts, but I question the value of those benefits if additional generations and prompts simply churn out more obvious AI slop. Apple may be more limiting in this regard, but its initial results are much better to begin with.

Of course, results will vary depending on the photograph, the complexity of the scene, and what you’re asking the tools to do. These were simply the results I got from the photos I tested.

How about you: Have you had a chance to try out Apple’s new Clean Up and Extend tools? If so, what do you think?

title: A Patent Filed by Microsoft Would Let Games Use AI to Rewrite Themselves
snippet: The new technology would consider how players explore the game and then rewrite the game to fit these interests.
fullText:
Most narratively driven computer games don’t change much once they’re released to the public. But what if AI could change a game based on how a player interacts with it? A patent filed by Microsoft in June might allow future Xbox games to do just that. 

The patent outlines a system that would allow generative AI to intelligently change the game based on what players do. In modern games, changes are usually dictated by dialog branches, which are the game’s different pathways of choices and responses, and player decisions, resulting in unique endings or character interactions. Some games handle change very well, but there’s always a limit. 

This new system would go beyond that, taking into account how players explore the game world, what they interact with and the characters they meet regularly. The generative AI would then rewrite or rework the game to favor those interactions, giving the player more of what they enjoy. Microsoft even outlines a system in which players’ facial expressions and reactions would be measured to further tune the experience.

			

More from CNET

“Players have the potential to become co-creators of the game as a result of their exploration of and interaction with the game,” Microsoft says in the patent filing. “The game may allow for very different gameplay per player and session.”

For example, if a player spends a lot of time in a specific area of the game, generative AI would create new quests, lore and in-game assets, such as monsters or NPCs, to give players more to do in that area. Similarly, Microsoft says that unengaging content may be removed to further prune the experience. This new content is then observed by the AI, which can decide whether to incorporate it into the game’s main narrative.

All of this would be done on the fly and be user-specific. The game would essentially adapt to what it thinks the player wants and create a wholly unique experience, separate from other gamers.

Could this be a fun idea?

A diagram showing that the generative AI would be controllable by the game designer.Microsoft

The use of generative AI in games has elicited mixed reactions. Gamers tend to shy away from games that use it, but Baldur’s Gate 3 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — both of which have won game of the year awards and are very highly rated by both reviewers and players — used generative AI to some extent. It’s tough to estimate how well a game would be received if it could automatically rewrite itself at the whims of its players. 

Such games would still require developers and writers, so this may not be an example of replacing humans. The AI needs a game world, rules, stories and existing characters to learn how to create more of them. So while the key phrase in Microsoft’s patent is generative AI, it’s actually more reminiscent of an existing game development tool: procedural generation. 

You’re most likely familiar with procedural generation in Minecraft, where each new map is procedurally generated using a “seed” code consisting of numbers and text. That seed is fed into the game’s procedural generation algorithm to determine where mountains, caves, resources and biomes appear as the map is built. Each seed generates an entirely different map. 

No Man’s Sky is another example, with each new solar system and planet being the work of procedural generation. Some smaller modern games have even taken it a step further. Titles like RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress, and Wildermyth use procedural generation in character creation, world-building and storytelling. 

Procedural generation is generally preemptive, creating these parts of the game before the player can interact with them. Microsoft’s idea would theoretically generate content only after the player interacts with it, making it reactive rather than preemptive. 

That would make it more like Pandemic Legacy. This story-based version of the board game requires players to permanently alter the game board and player cards as they play through the story, resulting in a one-of-a-kind version of the game once players complete it. 

Don’t expect to see games using this concept any time soon. The patent remains pending, and it could be years before the patent application is approved. Additionally, Microsoft has declined to comment on whether any current Xbox titles in development utilize this technology, suggesting a lengthy timeline before the system is seen in active operation.

title: PrismML brings its tiny LLMs to Qualcomm-powered smart glasses
snippet: Prism's larger goal is open-weight AI that runs on devices and makes better use of the computing power they already have.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:00 PM PDT · September 24, 2026

Image Credits:PrismML

		

							

											
									

					

	

The AI Lab PrismML — founded by Caltech researchers and advised by UC Berkeley’s Ion Stoica — has created a version of its tiny language models for smart glasses running on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

On Wednesday, at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit, the chipmaker showcased PrismML’s 1-bit Bonsai LLM, which can be run locally on AI smart glasses built on the Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 Platform.

As TechCrunch previously reported, PrismML’s claim to fame is that it shrinks larger models substantially (in this case, by 4x), while retaining almost all of their performance on standard benchmarks. The smart glasses version is a 2-billion-parameter model tuned for vision and language, so wearers can ask what they’re looking at in real time.

Prism’s larger goal is open-weight AI that runs on devices and makes better use of the computing power they already have. The startup pitches this as an alternative to depending on the privacy promises of proprietary AI labs and their insatiable need for more compute. 

Releasing a model for Qualcomm’s chip is a step toward that vision. But no smart glasses running PrismML have been announced yet.

title: OpenAI says Apple Intelligence users showed little interest in ChatGPT integration
snippet: As reported by The Financial Times, new court filings show that OpenAI was disappointed by the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, which it says “dramatically underperformed” after launching in 2024. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As reported by The Financial Times, new court filings show that OpenAI was disappointed by the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, which it says “dramatically underperformed” after launching in 2024. Here are the details.

OpenAI asks court to rule before trial

In August 2025, Elon Musk said that X, now part of SpaceXAI, would sue Apple and OpenAI over alleged collusion to shut out competitors in the AI space, stemming from OpenAI’s deal with Apple to make ChatGPT part of Apple Intelligence and Siri.

When the lawsuit was filed, it actually went beyond Musk’s original public complaint about App Store rankings. X and SpaceXAI also accused Apple of trying to stifle the development of “super apps,” including X’s effort to turn itself into an “everything app.”

In the weeks and months that followed, all companies involved filed briefs, accusations, and defenses with the court. Apple and OpenAI have argued, among other things, that their deal was not exclusive as the complaint alleged, while court filings have also revealed new details about how the partnership worked behind the scenes.

One of those details surfaced today in a filing from OpenAI. As first reported by The Financial Times, OpenAI “said it was disappointed by how little interest Apple generated from iPhone users after the two companies struck a deal in 2024 for ChatGPT to power ‘Apple Intelligence’.”

From the report:

When the 2024 deal was agreed, OpenAI expected a “halo effect” from promotion and brand association with Apple, as well as more subscriptions coming from Apple Intelligence users, Wednesday’s court document says.

But a month after the ChatGPT integration launched, it “appeared to be off to a slow start” and OpenAI was cutting its forecasts for how many weekly active users it expected to attract, it said. By the summer of 2025, “it was clear that Apple’s integration of ChatGPT was dramatically underperforming”.

The report notes that today’s filing contains multiple redacted conversations, but the unredacted portions show that OpenAI executives were concerned Apple could “want to move faster” to secure another AI partner.

When Apple Intelligence was first announced in 2024, Craig Federighi said in an interview that Apple ultimately wanted users to be able to choose between different AI models, specifically pointing to Google Gemini as a potential future integration.

That specific partnership never materialized, but Apple has since turned to Google’s Gemini models to help power the new Siri AI, while Xcode has expanded to support coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI.

	

Back to today’s filing, The Financial Times notes that it also points to the way Apple implemented ChatGPT as one possible reason for the slow adoption, as the integration was turned off by default.

Finally, as noted by Reuters, OpenAI is also arguing that recent securities disclosures from SpaceX undermine SpaceXAI’s claims that the Apple partnership harmed competition. In its filing, OpenAI said SpaceX’s IPO registration statement was “replete with disclosures diametrically opposed” to the competitive harm alleged in the lawsuit.

For these reasons, OpenAI is asking Judge Mark Pittman to rule in its favor before trial on SpaceXAI’s antitrust claims. The case is currently set to go to trial in January.

title: Insta360 conquered 360 cameras — now it’s eyeing glasses
snippet: It's right there in the name: "Insta360" makes 360-degree cameras, ones that film every angle simultaneously so you can shoot first and frame later. fullText:
It’s right there in the name: “Insta360” makes 360-degree cameras, ones that film every angle simultaneously so you can shoot first and frame later. It didn’t invent the idea, but Insta360 has become so synonymous with 360 cameras that it dominates the category with 73 percent of worldwide marketshare. It’s preparing to ship so many cameras, it just spent $298 million — more than GoPro’s entire valuation — on memory chips alone.

But as Insta360 sells its 10 millionth camera and opens its first flagship US store in New York City’s Times Square, it’s thinking bigger than two hemispherical lenses on a stick. It’s looking to challenge Canon, Sony, Nikon, and Fujifilm by becoming a “top imaging camera company” or “even a tech company,” cofounder Max Richter tells me — and it’s experimentally building its own mirrorless cameras and smart glasses to get there.

Insta360, also known as Shadow Stone or Arashi Vision in its native China, isn’t targeting Meta’s AI glasses or DSLR-wielding professional photographers just yet. Nor is it trying to replace the smartphone camera in your pocket.

“We don’t try to fight against the rise of the smartphone in photography and content creation,” says Richter. “We see that there’s an opportunity between smartphone users and professional cameras — a growing trend that people want to express themselves,” he adds.

He tells me that if Insta360 were to sell a pair of smart glasses, “we wouldn’t necessarily compete with companies on smart intelligent features.” It’d be about helping people conveniently capture high-quality images, not about an AI assistant on your face. And while that doesn’t sidestep the “pervert glasses” problem, there might be room for Insta360 to go about it differently, with headgear that’s obviously a camera instead of covertly spying.

Though Insta360’s smart glasses ambitions haven’t been widely reported — I could only find one brief mention — founder JK Liu previously confirmed that two mirrorless cameras are already in development. One will have a shape that “you have never thought of before,” Liu told MyNavi News in August. (Liu reportedly became a billionaire when Insta360 went public last year.)

“When you think about mirrorless, for us it would really go into making it more convenient and making a camera that is really suited for a new generation of content creators, not necessarily what’s already out there on the market,” Richter tells The Verge.

If Insta360 does expand into those camera categories, they’ll just be the tip of the spear. The company has already been pushing into many other categories dominated by its Chinese rival DJI, including DJI-challenging drones, gimbals and gimbaled baby steadycams, and modular action cameras.

While Insta360 might be the 360-camera market leader with 73 percent share, it’s a distant number 2 in other categories that DJI serves. IDC estimates that Insta360 has 20 percent of the worldwide handheld smart camera market compared to DJI’s 73 percent overall. Still, Insta360 is making significant headway: In Q2 2026, it had 43 percent of the detachable action camera market, 17 percent of non-detachable GoPro style action cameras, and its brand-new Luna Ultra already has 6 percent marketshare in gimbaled cameras.

GoPro itself, meanwhile, is a distant number 3 in IDC data, with just 3 percent of the smart camera market in Q2 2026, after shipments fell by half to just 200,000 cameras in the quarter.

It’s not unthinkable that Insta360 could help challenge traditional cameras. The traditional market leader, Canon, shipped 4.5 million digital cameras last year according to Nikkei data. DJI shipped 4.3 million cameras last quarter alone, according to IDC.

Insta360’s founders have explained that their grand vision is to become the robot cameraman for the world — not necessarily an actual humanoid robot, but rather an expectation that these devices can do more and more of the capture and motion and editing themselves, automatically understanding your intent using built-in AI tech.

The company’s latest Insta360 X6 is another small step in this direction: It comes with an onboard AI model and enough processing to automatically create a highlight reel from your footage while the camera is plugged in and charging, and it’s got a 2.0 version of a previous “InstaFrame” feature that can track and frame the person you select and automatically produce a video.

Insta360’s also launching a new feature for the X6 that can create 3D Gaussian splats with one tap in the company’s smartphone app, for free. It takes an hour or two for cloud servers to process the video, and users will only get four free splats per month, says Insta360 spokesperson Caroline Chen, but early results look neat.

It’s not at all clear whether the United States will embrace Insta360 the way Insta360 has embraced the US. While Apple, Best Buy, and Costco all stock the company’s products, that could change if the US government decides to enact a foreign camera ban — or if it simply decides that Insta360 is a drone company, like DJI, and pushes back on its cameras, too.

Insta360 already distanced itself from its drone brand Antigravity in the lead-up to the US drone ban, which will theoretically prevent Antigravity from shipping any future drones into the United States. Its first drone beat the ban by weeks.

As for Insta360, “We remain on the ground,” Richter tells me. “When it comes to drones, it’s not something that Insta360 is working on,” he says, suggesting I speak to Antigravity CEO Michael Shabun instead.

Richter says he’s “quite confident” that he can continue to bring cameras to people all around the world, and that Insta360 will fully comply with any local laws, but admits “there are certain things that are out of our control.”

I ask: Would Insta360 consider hedging against future risk by manufacturing some products in the US? If the company was required to, perhaps — but there’s no current plan to do so. “We would potentially look into it, but it’s not in our plan or roadmap at this moment.” He says the US is a key market, and Insta360 plans to be there for the long haul.

title: Google Photos ‘Clueless’-inspired virtual closet is now available on Android and iOS
snippet: The AI-powered feature builds a virtual wardrobe from your photos, and is now broadly available after first rolling out to Android users in June.
fullText:
Google’s new AI-powered feature that turns photos of your outfits into a virtual closet — one seemingly inspired by Cher’s iconic virtual wardrobe app featured in the movie “Clueless” — is now available to everyone in the U.S., Brazil, and India, on both iOS and Android devices.

The company announced the feature earlier this year with plans to begin the rollout in the summer. Android users gained access first, starting in June, and now the virtual closet is available to all Android and iOS users in the supported markets.

Image Credits:Google

The idea of a digital closet in “Clueless” was meant to highlight Cher’s privileged life, where she had so many outfits that she needed a digital system to help her choose what to wear and keep everything organized. Now, you don’t have to be a rich Beverly Hills teenager to take advantage of such technology. 

Instead, Google uses AI technology to create a copy of your wardrobe, based on the items you wore in your photos. From the app, you can also filter items by category — like tops, bottoms, jewelry, and more — then mix and match them to create different outfits.

Google says the feature is designed to assist the user, and the data about how you dress or what you wear is not being shared with third parties, like retailers. 

Image Credits:Google

The broader rollout of the virtual closet feature arrives alongside a handful of other Google Photos updates, including a way to select, brighten, and share photos using a single prompt in Gemini Spark, an upgraded markup tool, and more Remix templates that use AI to transform your photos. (The Gemini Spark feature requires a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription in the U.S.)

With Markup, you’ll be able to use a redacting pen to blur sensitive information like license plates, access precise thickness sliders for custom sketches, and pick from different fonts when adding text to photos.

Image Credits:Google

For Android users, there are also new photo filters, called “Moods,” that let you give your images different looks, like 35mm film, 2000s digicam, and more.

title: The camera is my favorite part of smart glasses, but it just feels wrong now
snippet: Smart glasses are such a logical, futuristic step in mobile tech, and it’s one we’re on the cusp of being able to embrace. Yet, there’s a huge hurdle to overcome. fullText:
Smart glasses are such a logical, futuristic step in mobile tech, and it’s one we’re on the cusp of being able to embrace. Yet, there’s a huge hurdle to overcome. For as useful and enjoyable as it is, the camera on smart glasses has become a massive problem, and it’s basically ruined existing smart glasses for me personally.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

There are a few core use cases for smart glasses. The most futuristic is a mixed-reality experience where a display layers information on top of what you’re seeing around you. But that’s also the hardest to accomplish with today’s tech. So, with that in mind, audio-based glasses have been more popular.

Open-ear audio and always-ready access make these glasses very useful, but the real selling point for many has been the camera. Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses are the catalyst in all of this. Meta will go on and on about AI features, but a huge part of the appeal here is having a camera at the ready with point-of-view footage. That’s what sold me on it, and my pair has captured some really fun memories in my favorite hobby. 

	

Yet, I’ve barely touched those glasses over the past year, nor had I really gotten around to testing any others I’ve been offered. For example, the L’atitude 52°N Berlin glasses were originally pitched around having a better camera than Meta and, while I’m not a huge fan of the styling, the camera is at least decent – I wouldn’t say better with focus and direct sunlight being clear issues, but I do like that it can capture in landscape.

But, for as much fun as these cameras can be, it just feels wrong now.

The social stigma around cameras on smart glasses has been ruined by the misuse of these cameras. That was, sadly, somewhat inevitable. Any new piece of technology has the potential to be misused, but the subtle nature of these cameras turns simple misuse into making people downright uncomfortable. And, honestly, rightfully so! I initially had trouble understanding the issues many were taking with a camera on glasses, but example after example has shown just how many people are willing to misuse this tech.

Arguably, the bigger problem comes down to how it’s all been handled.

With Meta Ray-Bans, two problems became clear.

Firstly, there was the simple fact that Meta was at the helm. The company’s long history of handling private data, rightfully, did not mix well with a camera on your face. While Meta tried to convince users otherwise, leaks of human moderators viewing uncensored private recordings, combined with rumblings of Meta’s plans for facial recognition and always-on recording, simply evaporated any goodwill or trust that might have been left.

Secondly, there’s the amount of time it took for Meta to address the misuse. Stories have run rampant for the better part of two years now around back-alley deals to disable the privacy LED on Ray-Ban glasses, and it took until July of this year for Meta to implement a fix. An even more obvious loophole is only being patched now.

And now we’re approaching the debut of the first Android XR glasses from Samsung and Google – with every style having a camera. They’re facing a massive uphill battle as the “perv glasses” stigma is widely known and loud – a previous issue of our “Inbox” newsletter discussed this. Samsung has said that it has protections immediately in place around camera tampering, but not everyone is going to know that.

Basically what this boils down to is – thanks Meta, you’ve ruined this for everyone else.

The smart glasses market is going to have a rough time getting around all of this. The Ray-Bans debacle has done some serious damage that every other brand is going to have to work around. That is, assuming they want a camera in the first place. There are plenty of smart glasses that deliver useful functionality without a camera. Even Realities springs to mind as a clear example of this. Yet, when I was testing out those glasses, I constantly found myself missing the utility of an on-board camera (and a speaker, for that matter) for simply capturing the world around me, or wanting to use it with AI features. As overbearing as Meta has been with them, using the camera for various types of interactions such as scanning & translating menus, getting descriptions of real-world objects, and more, are very handy. 

It’s going to take years to get all of this tech to its ideal state no matter what, but I hope that the camera stigma eventually calms down.

iOS 27 is packed with a wide array of new features for iPhone, including in Apple Maps. Here are the two tentpole iOS 27 features for Apple Maps, plus some miscellaneous improvements.

Apple Maps in iOS 27 gets upgraded Flyover feature and Local Lists, plus other improvements

Apple Maps doesn’t look drastically different when you open it in iOS 27. But Apple has a variety of big and small improvements in its latest update.

One tentpole feature is an upgraded Flyover experience. Per Apple:

Apple Maps brings an enhanced Flyover experience, which combines aerial imagery with AI to enable users to view imagery in stunning detail for select cities around the world like never before. Whether scouting a location before a trip or simply exploring a city from a new perspective, the enhanced experience gives users a sharper and more lifelike glimpse into destinations across the globe.

Apple also highlights a new Local Lists feature that’s available in the US:

With Local Lists, Apple Maps users in the U.S. can find the perfect spot for meeting friends, dining, and more. Using intelligent insights from what’s trending, Maps surfaces locally relevant collections of places — from trending restaurants to great spots to take kids — so it’s easy for users to find what they are looking for. All insights are derived with privacy in mind and never tied to individual users.

Beyond these two tentpole changes, iOS 27 also has a variety of other improvements:

More Suggested Places: The new Suggested Places feature that arrived in iOS 26.5 now lets you swipe horizontally through many more suggestions, so it’s not limited to just two placed

Offline Maps update improvements: Apple doesn’t say what the exact improvements are

title: Microsoft launches 12-inch Surface Pro with Snapdragon X2 Plus & 5G, 13-inch Surface Laptop too
snippet: Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149. more…
fullText:
Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149.

The Surface Laptop and Surface Pro both picked up their Snapdragon X2 upgrades back in June, but that left the smaller models waiting on refreshes. As a part of Snapdragon Summit, Microsoft is confirming that those will arrive on October 13.

Surface Pro 12-inch is getting a Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, a 25% brighter display, and a battery that’s “30% more efficient.” There’s an optional 5G model coming too, which Microsoft says was “one of the most requested additions.” All models now include either 16GB or 24GB of RAM, removing the 8GB option on last year’s model, with either 256GB or 512GB of storage. 

It’s mostly the same tablet otherwise, just now with a starting price of $1,149. That’s $300 more than the base model sold for, and that’s after a major price hike across the whole lineup back in April. Even directly comparing the 16/256GB model, it’s still a $100 price hike. 

	

The formula is similar on Surface Laptop 13-inch, with this latest generation getting Snapdragon X2 Plus, ditching its 8GB model, and starting at $1,199 – $50 up from the last generation. Again, there are upgrades including a brigher display, but it’s nearly identical to last year’s model outside of the chipset bump.

Microsoft is also launching a new Surface Mouse which has haptic feedback and a customizable Copilot button. It costs $79.99 and will also be available on October 13. Both come with a new “Microsoft Ink Canvas” app.

title: Microsoft Brings Snapdragon X2 to Smallest Surface Pro and Laptop Lines
snippet: The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop get brought up to speed with Qualcomm’s latest processors. And there’s a new Surface Mouse with haptics.
fullText:
I’m the first born in my family, so I haven’t experienced this feeling directly, but my younger brother tells me it wasn’t all that fun when I would get a gift that he was too little to receive along with his big brother (like the time I got my first bike for my 6th birthday while he was still circling our cul-de-sac on a Big Wheel). On Wednesday, Microsoft granted upgrades to its littlest Surface models, which lets them two-wheel around the neighborhood with the bigger models.

The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop have each been upgraded to Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 series processors, bringing them in line with the larger 13-inch Surface Pro and 13.8- and 15-inch Surface Laptops that received the Snapdragon X2 jolt a few months ago. 

The second-generation Qualcomm processors offer a tick up in application performance and battery life, a larger leap in graphics performance and a giant jump in local AI capabilities, according to Microsoft. My tests with other laptops based on Snapdragon X2 series processors support Microsoft’s estimates.

			

More from CNET

Along with the two new Surface models, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Mouse that offers haptic feedback. Let’s have a look at the two Surface updates and new mouse.

12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition)

The new 12-inch Surface Pro is based on a Snapdragon X2 Plus processor and available in business black.Katie Collins/CNET

The second-gen 12-inch Surface Pro trots out the same design as the inaugural model, but inside it has moved to a six-core Snapdragon X Plus X2P-42-100. You are actually giving up two cores from the previous Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 but getting a more advanced X2-45 integrated GPU and neural processing unit. The NPU is designed for the integer math required for AI tasks, and the Snapdragon X2’s NPU is capable of 80 trillion operations per second. That’s nearly double the 45 TOPS of the NPU of the first-gen Snapdragon X Plus.

The 12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition) also ups the memory, giving you the choice of 16GB or 24GB of RAM. That’s an increase from the previous 8GB and 16GB options. Storage remains the same and rather uninspired: 256GB or 512GB.

The display also stays the same: a 12-inch PixelSense touch LCD with a 3:2 aspect ratio, a resolution of 2,196×1,464 pixels and 90Hz refresh rate. The only difference is it’s 25% brighter, pushing the max brightness from 400 to 500 nits.

And there’s a new color option, but it might not excite you. In addition to platinum and violet, the new 12-inch Surface Pro comes in black. The bluish-gray ocean color has been discontinued.

The new 12-inch Surface Pro comes preinstalled with Microsoft Ink Canvas, a new AI-powered app for sketching, annotating, generating images and summarizing text directly on the screen with the Slim Pen. 

The 12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition) will be available on Oct. 13, starting at $1,150. As with all Surface Pro pricing, the starting price is misleading because Microsoft charges extra for accessories, including the keyboard. Microsoft hasn’t divulged accessory pricing, but the keyboard for the first-gen 12-inch Surface Pro, which is very much needed, adds $150 to the bill. Still, it’s nice that the entry-level model starts at 16GB of RAM, saving you from having to spend extra to move up from the meager 8GB.

13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition)

The 13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition) looks no different than the first edition, but it offers newer Qualcomm processors, more RAM and a brighter display.Katie Collins/CNET

The 13-inch Surface Laptop has two big brothers in the 13.8-inch Surface Laptop and 15-inch model. They have each offered Snapdragon X2 series processors since May or June, and now the smallest Surface Laptop gets its Snapdragon X2 upgrade. It offers the same configuration options as the new 12-inch Surface Pro:

Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 CPU

16GB or 24GB RAM

256GB or 512GB SSD

There’s no change to the display other than the same bump in brightness as the second-gen 12-inch Surface Pro got. It’s a 13-inch PixelSense touch LCD with a 3:2 aspect ratio, a pixel resolution of 1,920×1,280 and a 60Hz refresh rate, but it is now rated for 500 nits of brightness. It also comes in the same three colors as the new 12-inch Surface Pro: platinum, violet and black.

Microsoft says you can expect up to 22.5 hours of battery life from the second-gen 13-inch Surface Laptop. That would actually be slightly shorter if our tests bear that out. The previous 13-inch Surface Laptop lasted more than 24 hours in testing.

The 13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition) will be available on Oct. 13 starting at $1,199.

Surface Mouse (2nd Edition)

The new Surface Mouse has haptics to provide physical, tactile feedback.Katie Collins/CNET

If you’re more of a mouser than a touchpad user, Microsoft has a new mouse it’s hoping you’ll pick up with your next Surface purchase. The most interesting part about the second-generation Surface Mouse is the inclusion of haptics that offer tactile feedback across its entire surface. These pulses can confirm clicks, drags, alignment and other actions in apps including PowerPoint, Concepts, Affinity by Canva and Filmora.

The Surface Mouse also adds a customizable action button that sits in front of the scroll wheel. The Bluetooth 6.0 mouse will be available in black and platinum for $80. Like the new Surface computers, the Surface Mouse (2nd Edition) will start shipping on Oct. 13.

title: Meta launches audio-only glasses and Gen 3 Ray-Ban with slimmer designs
snippet: Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release. more…
fullText:
Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release.

Despite public backlash in recent months, smart glasses continue to explode in popularity and, as it stands, Meta is by far the biggest player in the game. Today’s event further saw the company digging in on its smart glasses success with three new releases.

The self-branded Meta Glasses lineup is adding new styles that start at just $249. A new pair of Meta Adventurer glasses will be available with a black frame and grey lenses and a plug-in case. They’re available starting October 23. 

Next in line is a pair of audio-only glasses, Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Starting at $349 in October, these glasses ditch the camera and, in turn, also deliver a much slimmer form factor. They weigh 43g and run for 12 hours on a single charge (48 hours in the case). Meta says the new hardware features “professional-adjustable temple tips, adjustable or swappable nose pads, and overextension hinges.” 

	

Styles include “Clubmaster” and “Burbank” in a variety of frame and lens styles.

Beyond that, Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is available today starting at $449. Meta says to expect longer battery life – 9 hours, an hour longer than Gen 2 – and the same camera capabilities, including 3K video recording. The hardware is slimmer and adds professional-adjustable temple tips. 

Meta is also launching this latest generation in way more styles, with 27 combinations across “Aviator,” “Wayfarer,” and cateye “Zena” frame styles.

You can order Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) now through Meta’s store.

Finally, Meta is also upgrading its Display glasses with hands-free navigation, “Hologram” personas for video calls, new apps, notification mirroring from your phone, and Threads integration. Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are also expanding to the UK, Canada, France, Italy, and Germany, and you can finally order them online in the US, still priced at $799.

title: Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Sol & Luna both launch today with lower costs
snippet: Anthropic and OpenAI are both launching new model updates today, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol & Luna both being announced within roughly an hour of each other. more…
fullText:
Anthropic and OpenAI are both launching new model updates today, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol & Luna both being announced within roughly an hour of each other.

Claude Opus 5.5 was up to bat first today, so we’ll start there. 

Anthropic explains that its latest model update performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on “most work” while cutting costs to run by around 40% compared to Opus 5 – which was already around half the price of Fable 5. 

Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.

Despite the lower compute costs, Anthropic says that Opus 5.5 is more powerful, beating out Fable 5.1 in every metric and beating OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra in virtually every category measured as well including metrics such as agentic coding, knowledge work, and more. 

	

Claude Opus 5.5 is available now on “all platforms,” Anthropic says.

And that’s not all. OpenAI, roughly an hour after Claude’s announcement, launched its GPT-6 Sol & Luna models, also focused on costs.

Like Opus 5.5, OpenAI says that GPT-6 Sol and Luna are both much more affordable to run compared to their GPT-5.6 counterparts. Specifically, they’re both about 50% less expensive when measuring input and output per 1 million tokens in API use. 

Both models are marginally more powerful than their predecessors, but well behind that of Astra, which remains the overall most powerful model OpenAI offers. Luna prioritizes cost over capability, while Sol strikes a balance between the two by offering more horsepower than Luna but at a more affordable cost compared to Astra.

We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing.

OpenAI says Sol and Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, while Luna is available in the desktop app for Free and Go users. Neither model is available in Chat just yet.

title: YouTube Music adding corner access to ‘Ask Music’ with Gemini
snippet: As part of Made on YouTube 2026, a handful of updates to YouTube Music that are coming later this year were previewed. more…
fullText:
As part of Made on YouTube 2026, a handful of updates to YouTube Music that are coming later this year were previewed.

After moving search to the bottom bar earlier this year, YouTube Music is placing the Gemini spark icon in the top-right corner of the mobile app to let you access Ask Music. This more consistent entry point — compared to the Home feed card — slides up a sheet with the chat experience. 

The prompt box is at the bottom of the screen with voice input available, while suggested queries include Create a mix, Discover artists, and Find podcasts. 

Ask Music will also be surfaced throughout YouTube Music when relevant, like when you’re editing a playlist or creating a mix. The conversational tool is also adding more agentic features this year that let you “customize your queue or dive deeper into artist lore.”

	

These updates are coming later this year for global YouTube Premium and Music Premium subscribers.

The other YouTube Music update today is a “Your Podcast Lineup” feature that acts as a “personalized AI-audio guide.” It gives you a “weekly spoken preview of recommended shows” that includes why you might like them, as well as suggested episodes. 

This “completely eyes-optional and hands-free” experience leverages audio gen AI capabilities. Testing will start later this year for subscribers worldwide.

title: Black Workers Allege Systemic Racism at Tesla as Landmark California Trial Begins
snippet: State regulators presented evidence of unaddressed discrimination, wage disparities and hostile conditions on the EV maker’s Fremont assembly line.
fullText:
Tesla is facing a major civil rights lawsuit due to years of alleged rampant racist behavior against dozens of Black employees at its flagship Fremont assembly factory in California.

During opening statements on Monday, California Civil Rights Department attorney Brett Watson presented evidence of severe workplace harassment at Tesla, as reported by The Guardian. Photos and court documents revealed swastikas carved into factory surfaces, widespread use of the N-word, images of Confederate flags and other white supremacist symbols across the Fremont plant.

Black employees reported receiving harassing messages, such as: “Go back to Africa,” and “You want to hang from a tree?”

			

More from CNET

The allegations extend beyond harassment, as several Black workers say Elon Musk’s company subjected them to unequal pay and were given inferior job assignments and fewer opportunities for career advancement than other employees. Complaints of unchecked systemic racism at Tesla’s Fremont plant date back to 2012. The current lawsuit was filed 10 years later, in 2022.

This isn’t the first time Tesla has been involved in a legal battle over racial discrimination. Also in 2022, a former Tesla worker at the Fremont plant, Owen Diaz, was awarded over $3 million in damages for similar racial discrimination accusations.

Tesla has denied any wrongdoing, calling the lawsuit “misguided” and suggesting the company is the real victim.

Tesla’s lead attorney, Tyree Jones, countered the state’s claims during opening arguments by repeatedly uttering the racial slur to illustrate his defense. Jones argued that in the context of the factory floor, the N-word was frequently used as a casual greeting among Black workers rather than a derogatory insult.

Because this is a bench trial, no jury will be present throughout the case. Judge Peter Borkon will determine whether Tesla violated California’s civil rights laws. If the state wins, it’s very possible Borkon could force Tesla to overhaul its labor policies and HR practices.

Given that this is one of Tesla’s most prominent factories, the judge’s ruling could have ripple effects throughout Silicon Valley, impacting workplace equity policies, while also serving as a test of the state’s strict antidiscrimination laws. The trial is expected to conclude in late October.

Tesla and the California Civil Rights Department didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment.

title: These Lightweight Audio Memory-Recording Glasses Might Be Meta’s Next Step (and Apple’s)
snippet: Vonder is making camera-free smart glasses that can differentiate between personal voice memos and conversations. I tried on some of the frames ahead of their November launch.
fullText:
The multiple pairs of smart glasses prototypes I’m trying on are attractive, familiar and lightweight. They look normal, fit my face well and have no cameras. All they have on board is audio and microphone support. These Vonder smart glasses are all about listening to you as much as to others. And they can tell the difference.

Meta announced its own camera-free audio glasses this week, but Vonder, a company founded by execs from display glasses maker Viture, along with Guillaume Hamon, the chief brand officer, goes further. I met with Hamon and David Jiang, Viture’s CEO and co-founder, in New York a few weeks ago to learn about their new $299 to $399 glasses, which fit a wide range of eye prescriptions but also require a monthly paid AI subscription. 

Viture’s frames look totally normal, are lightweight, and lack cameras.Scott Stein/CNET

Bone conduction inside

Viture’s tethered wearables are more like wearable monitors in glasses form with augmented-reality bells and whistles. Vonder has no displays and leans on extended battery life and a unique approach to audio technology, using bone conduction in the glasses to help with privacy to filter personal voice memos versus recording external voices in a room.

			

More from CNET

The onboard array of microphones can listen in on conversations and summarize them using AI, which then appears in a phone app or a web app. But the glasses don’t keep any audio recordings. Apple is doing something similar on its Apple Watches and iPhones later this year via Siri Recap. Meta, meanwhile, hasn’t gotten into the memory-recording audio space yet.

I wore Vonder’s glasses. They look good.Scott Stein/CNET

I found the bone conduction microphones in the glasses’ arms to be the most interesting feature, which can listen to your own voice even at a whisper. I hadn’t seen that idea before in the glasses I’ve worn. According to Jiang and Hamon, Vonder’s glasses can either record just your own voice for memos and personal notes or a conversation with others. The bone conduction microphones help differentiate between your voice and whoever you’re speaking to.

In conversation modes where the glasses are recording others, a small side LED light turns on after you press a recording button on the glasses’ arm. In personal modes, there’s no light.

Vonder’s memory graph becomes a mind map of related memories that’s cloud stored. I saw a demo on a laptop in the web app.Scott Stein/CNET

A memory assistant, for a monthly subscription

“The idea of Vonder is fashion-forward glasses that allow you to basically reduce your cognitive load and rely on Vonder as a second memory, almost, so you can stay in the flow of your life, your conversations and rely on Vonder to keep track of what matters,” Hamon tells me.

These glasses aren’t designed as phone replacements. “It’s utopic, I think, at this current stage, to ask people to ditch the phone,” Jiang says. Jiang’s other company, Viture, also uses glasses (display-enabled ones) as phone accessories, not self-contained face computers.

Vonder’s phone app and its discrete recording and microphone controls.Scott Stein/CNET

It’s also utopian – some would say dystopian – to imagine AI platforms as true memory extensions. That was how I tried to live for a month with a pendant called Looki, and it didn’t go well. I don’t know how Vonder’s Personal Memory Graph, its cloud and phone app-based AI system that pulls from OpenAI, Gemini and Claude models, will actually work in practice. Vonder’s AI service won’t directly log into those other AI services; it’ll draw from their AI models instead, similar to how AI glasses services like Rokid’s work.

Vonder’s AI services can also proactively summarize and brief, like it did for my name.Scott Stein/CNET

Vonder’s memory-mapping platform aims to be a safe place to store all your conversations and personal memos, creating a searchable mind map. Seeing an early preview of the software in a web browser, I was skeptical. Every company wants to be our collective memory now: How do we trust collecting those memories, though? Vonder’s pitch is also a subscription one: The required AI service is priced in tiers based on how much it’s used, from $5 to $30 a month. I don’t like the idea of subscription memories, not at all.

There are lots of good looking Vonder glasses styles I saw.Scott Stein/CNET

No cameras here

I do like how small Vonder’s glasses frames are, though, and how they’re styled. At 30 grams, they feel exactly like regular glasses and have flexible arms for a comfortable temple fit. They’re notably lighter than Meta’s smart glasses, which hover around 50 grams. They’re also lighter than the small Even Realities G2 glasses I wore earlier this year.

And Vonder’s leaning completely on audio at a time when the rest of the smart glasses industry may be seeing a similar pivot. With the ongoing backlash against smart glasses cameras, privacy features will be what Meta’s new glasses, and Google and Samsung’s, will be judged against. Meta’s already promising more private computing in the year ahead. How will Vonder measure up? And, with Meta now promising better battery life on its Ray-Ban Audio glasses, could audio-recording memory modes like these be on deck next? Or Apple, for that matter?

Vonder says its glasses will last over 16 hours on a single charge, even when recording continuously. They truly could be used all day. Apple’s promising all-day battery life in its upcoming Siri Recap recording mode, too. To do this, Vonder’s using a chipset also found in earbuds instead of a higher-end Qualcomm glasses-focused processor, making the glasses more power-efficient.

I won’t know more till I try a pair, but Vonder’s frames are the nicest-looking I’ve seen. Will the AI services be worth it, too? I expect a lot out of any device promising to extend my memory. I’m very protective about my memories, too, so we’ll see.

Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.

title: Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Opus 5.5 model, details here
snippet: Anthropic has released its latest AI model with Claude Opus 5.5. The new version arrives about two months after the previous Opus model upgrade, matching Anthropic’s previous upgrade cadence. more…
fullText:
Anthropic has released its latest AI model with Claude Opus 5.5. The new version arrives about two months after the previous Opus model upgrade, matching Anthropic’s previous upgrade cadence.

Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5

Anthropic currently offers a few AI models under the Claude umbrella. 

The three main models are Haiku (smallest and cheapest), Sonnet (medium size and price), and Opus (largest and most expensive of the three).

There’s also Fable/Mythos, which is even more capable and costly, which represents Anthropic’s highest tier.

Opus 5.5 is here! 🎉  It's honestly such a nice model to work with. 

Feels like Fable, but ~30% faster and ~40% cheaper per task than Opus 5. Go try it out! pic.twitter.com/zwo83sbgez

— Lydia Hallie ✨ (@lydiahallie) September 22, 2026

Today’s release upgrades Claude’s Opus model from version 5 to version 5.5.

“Opus 5.5 is our first model since we called for pacing the frontier,” Anthropic says. “As with previous models, it was tested by external evaluators before release, including METR and Frontier Design. On our most comprehensive alignment test, it achieves the strongest score to date.”

Here’s what Anthropic says about Opus 5.5 performance:

Opus 5.5 is a major step up from Opus 5. It’s the new leading model, and early testers saw large jumps in performance on their most complex work. One tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in less than a day—work that would have taken an engineering team weeks. It’s good at finding and fixing inefficiencies in software: when we asked it to cut load times across every page of a web app, Opus 5.5 succeeded 39 of 40 times, while Opus 5 made smaller improvements that also altered the app’s behavior. A different tester had several Claude models build a game from a single prompt; Opus 5.5 scored higher than any other model on the strength of its graphics and polish.

When it comes to coding specifically, here’s what Anthropic says:

Opus 5.5 is particularly good at long and sprawling jobs like codebase-wide migrations and audits. An early tester used it to audit and fix a 200,000-line codebase in under three hours, where Opus 5 took over 20 hours and used 2.5x as many tokens. In an internal test, we asked Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 to translate HAProxy, widely used software that balances web traffic loads across servers, from C into Rust. Both rewrites passed nearly all of HAProxy’s own regression tests, but Opus 5.5 finished in 9.5 hours compared to 12 for Fable 5.1, and cost 51% less.

Opus 5.5 delivers frontier results on agentic coding at a fraction of the cost. At its default effort level on FrontierCode, it beats GPT-6 Astra at roughly 20% of the cost per task. On Terminal Bench 4.0, it matches Astra for about 40% of the cost, while on CursorBench it beats GPT-5.6 Sol by 11 points for about a third of the cost.

Additionally, pricing has been adjusted for Opus 5.5 compared to Opus 5:

Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.

In addition to the price drop, we’re increasing five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, and Team plans. We’re also providing subscription users a rate limit reset, which you can now save and use whenever you choose.

The new Claude Opus 5.5 model is now available. Looking ahead, Anthropic says both Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 models will arrive “in the coming weeks, with many of the same improvements to performance, efficiency, and safety.”

You can learn much more about the new Claude Opus 5.5 model here.

Introducing Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in our new Claude 5.5 family.

It performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 for most tasks, and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5. pic.twitter.com/Q9C2VKQ79f

— Claude (@claudeai) September 22, 2026

title: Oracle sends force majeure notice on its New Mexico Stargate data center
snippet: The notice would allow Oracle to delay payments should the facility miss its 2028 target to come online.
fullText:
Oracle has sent a force majeure notice to the developer of Project Jupiter, a Stargate data center campus in New Mexico, Bloomberg first reported Thursday.

Force majeure clauses, common in energy and commodities contracts, excuse a party from contractual obligations when events outside its control get in the way. Oracle is not seeking to exit as the campus’s main tenant, according to Bloomberg’s sources. Instead, the notice would allow the company to delay payments should the facility miss its 2028 target to come online. 

The notice also comes as AI data center construction faces growing scrutiny nationally, and as developers take on steep costs to build capacity for customers like OpenAI.

Oracle maintains that it does not expect a delay. “Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule,” Oracle said in a statement to CNBC. “We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward.”

Blue Owl Capital, whose unit received the notice, said in its own statement to CNBC that “this notice does not change the financial commitments to this multi-year project.”

Neither Oracle nor Blue Owl immediately responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

Still, the notice follows a string of setbacks at the site, many of them tied to its energy supply. The campus, designed to handle 2.45 gigawatts, is meant to run on gas-powered fuel cells from Bloom Energy, which makes a reliable gas supply central to its timeline.

An Energy Transfer pipeline intended to deliver gas to the site has also been delayed nearly six months, to February 1, 2027, after regulators repeatedly denied permits for the line. In August, Bloomberg reported that the pipeline’s route had been changed following those rejections. A separate air-quality permit for the fuel cell system that would power the campus is also pending. The state’s environment department faces a November 23 deadline to decide.

Project Jupiter is one of the flagship sites of Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative Oracle, OpenAI, and SoftBank announced with President Donald Trump early in his second term. The campus has drawn opposition from residents and environmental groups and has become a political flashpoint ahead of the midterm elections. Oracle has responded with a public outreach campaign in the state aimed at winning over the project’s critics, according to Bloomberg.

title: iOS 27 adds an all-new app to your iPhone’s Home Screen
snippet: Apple released iOS 27 to everyone last week, including a ton of new Siri and Apple Intelligence features. One of the biggest changes here is the addition of an all-new Siri app. This marks the first time that Siri has been pre-installed as a standalone app for iPhone users … more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27 to everyone last week, including a ton of new Siri and Apple Intelligence features. One of the biggest changes here is the addition of an all-new Siri app. This marks the first time that Siri has been pre-installed as a standalone app for iPhone users …

The Siri app in iOS 27

After you update to iOS 27, you’ll see the new Siri icon appear on your iPhone’s Home Screen. This app is also coming to the Mac with macOS 27, Vision Pro with visionOS 27, iPad with iPadOS 27, and Apple Watch with watchOS 27.

The Siri app in iOS 27 lets you revisit all your conversations with Siri and easily start new ones. The Siri app syncs with iCloud, so you can continue conversations across all of your Apple devices. It features a chat-style interface with a stream of your previous conversations. You can also upload photos and files to the Siri app for analysis.

The Siri app ties into the new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities introduced in iOS 27. This includes access to broad world knowledge, personal context of everything on your iPhone, and much more. Siri AI can also recognize what’s on your screen and answer questions about it.

With access to that personal context, Siri AI can reference things like your messages, emails, photos, and more to answer your specific questions. 

Siri app compatibility in iOS 27

The Siri app, however, won’t be coming to all iPhone models. It will be available on devices that support Apple Intelligence, which covers the iPhone 15 Pro and newer:

iPhone 15 Pro

iPhone 15 Pro Max

iPhone 16

iPhone 16 Plus

iPhone 17

Wrap up

Apple has recently added several new iPhone apps by default, including Image Playground as part of iOS 18.2 in December 2024. Last year’s iOS 26 update added the new Preview and Games apps for iPhone users.

snippet: After teasing its new Copilot "super app" last month, Microsoft is officially unveiling it today. The redesigned Copilot app bundles three AI capabilities into a single interface of chat, coding, and agents. As part of the launch, Microsoft is also rebranding Scout, the AI personal assistant it unveiled at Build earlier this year, as Autopilot. This new Copilot app will have three tabs for Home, Code, and Autopilot, with Home combining Copilot Chat and Cowork together. fullText:
After teasing its new Copilot “super app” last month, Microsoft is officially unveiling it today. The redesigned Copilot app bundles three AI capabilities into a single interface of chat, coding, and agents. As part of the launch, Microsoft is also rebranding Scout, the AI personal assistant it unveiled at Build earlier this year, as Autopilot.

This new Copilot app will have three tabs for Home, Code, and Autopilot, with Home combining Copilot Chat and Cowork together. It’s the default landing experience for Copilot users, and Microsoft is also planning to include a Today feature inside it that works as a personalized dashboard for important emails, meeting requests, Teams threads, and more.

“Home is where you get your bearings, keeping you grounded and moving forward: review recent activity, get suggestions on what Copilot can help with, and pick up work right where you left off,” explains Jared Spataro, chief marketing officer of AI at work at Microsoft.

The Code tab is the surprise addition to this so-called “super app,” and not one you’d typically associate with an app designed for knowledge workers. It will let anyone create an app, tracker, dashboard, or automation and share the results with colleagues as cloud-hosted internal apps. “Powered by the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot, Code runs in a sandboxed environment and can be hosted securely within your tenant,” says Spataro.

Autopilot is a new addition to the Copilot experience, and one that Spataro describes as a “digital teammate.” Previously called Scout and available initially as a desktop app, Autopilot is the cloud equivalent that enables a personal AI assistant to keep running while you’re asleep. Like many other AI agents, Autopilot has its own cloud computer instance that can be tasked to do things like watch Teams channels, run recurring work tasks, or handle follow-ups.

The real difference against some other AI agents is that Microsoft has made Autopilot enterprise grade, appealing to businesses that rely on its Office and identity management suites. “Autopilot lives in your tenant with its own identity, memory, computer, and workspace, and it’s built on Microsoft IQ so it understands how your organization actually works,” says Spataro. “It shows up where people already work — Teams, Outlook, chats, channels, and documents — so you can @mention it like a colleague, with permissions, audit, and governance behind it.”

All of this focus on enterprise security and control is a big part of Microsoft trying to sell businesses on Copilot once again. The difference this time around is that how much a business pays for Copilot will depend on what their employees are doing. Microsoft is using usage-based billing for the Cowork, Code, and Autopilot parts of this new Copilot app, so any long-running agentic capabilities or usage of models like Astra and Fable will be billed based on usage.

The regular Copilot license, known as a user subscription license, will give you Copilot in Chat, and in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams. Microsoft is using an auto model picker to match the model for each task, but IT admins will need to use Microsoft’s new FinOps for AI to manage AI spend and ensure any agentic usage doesn’t get out of control.

With this new Copilot app it feels like Microsoft has finally settled on a formula for its AI assistant. The company has redesigned Copilot plenty of times since its introduction as a chatbot inside Bing, and this latest three-tab design builds on the combination of its two separate consumer and commercial Copilot apps last month. That’s a long-overdue change, alongside some big AI leadership shapeups that helped finally appoint a single Copilot boss for the first time.

The new Home and Code tabs will start rolling out to Microsoft’s Frontier program for early access AI features “in the coming weeks,” and Autopilot will go into private preview later this month. Code will also be in preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.

It’s fair to say that Copilot has failed in the consumer space compared to Claude or ChatGPT, but Microsoft’s core commercial customers are slowly showing interest. This new Copilot app isn’t really designed to compete with things like Muse, and Microsoft is now calling it “the AI built for work.” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also calls Copilot a new operating system. “We’re building Copilot as a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task,” says Nadella in a post on X.

Microsoft is even comparing its new Copilot to how influential Office was on productivity. “Just as Office defined work for the PC era, the new Copilot is built to define it for the AI era,” says Spataro.

That might well be Microsoft’s goal, but there’s a lot more competition in this AI era than there ever was in the PC era. Microsoft has certainly fallen behind the likes of Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and now Meta, and it’ll be interesting to see if “the AI built for work” is enough to help it catch up.

Update, September 25th: Article updated with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s comments.

title: Apple has three products launching soon that we’ve waited a long time for
snippet: Apple had a big September, but it’s set to keep momentum going in October with several rumored product unveilings soon that we’ve waited a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple had a big September, but it’s set to keep momentum going in October with several rumored product unveilings soon that we’ve waited a long time for.

#1: MacBook Pro / Ultra redesign with touchscreen

The Mac is a long-time touchscreen holdout, but that’s finally set to change with a new MacBook Pro (or MacBook Ultra) product expected to launch in October.

Apple’s next-gen MacBook Pro will introduce a brand new industrial design—the first such overhaul in five years. And in addition to touch support, it will boast an OLED display, Dynamic Island, and possibly a C2 cellular modem option.

It’s been a long time since the MacBook Pro got a new look. But far longer since touchscreens became the norm, and Apple decided to forego them on the Mac. I’m excited to see how touch might enhance the experience of the Mac moving forward.

#2: New Apple TV 4K

There’s never been a longer wait for new Apple TV hardware than the current drought of updates. Apple’s latest model, the third-gen Apple TV 4K, was introduced in 2022.

Rumors indicate we’ll finally get a new Apple TV 4K in October, headlined by a powerful A19 or A19 Pro chip and Siri AI support.

This summer Apple raised prices on most of its products, including the Apple TV. That means the four-year-old Apple TV 4K now costs $199—far more than the $129 price it launched at. Here’s hoping the new Apple TV doesn’t go any higher.

#3: ‘HomePad’

Rumors of a HomePod with a display have been around for nearly as long as the HomePod’s existence. But they ramped up in 2024 when Mark Gurman offered an in-depth report on what’s commonly called the ‘HomePad.’

	

HomePad is a smart display with built-in speaker that will reportedly spearhead Apple’s renewed push into home products. It will have a new OS that resembles parts of iOS, tvOS, and watchOS, including a StandBy-like mode.

Siri AI is expected to be central to the product, which will also feature a camera, customizable widgets, and built-in Apple apps like Photos, Notes, Music, Calendar, and more.

title: Motorola Signature 27 confirmed to support GrapheneOS
snippet: It’s confirmed: The mysterious Motorola phone getting support for the privacy-focused GrapheneOS will be the Motorola Signature 27 that was announced earlier this week. more…
fullText:
It’s confirmed: The mysterious Motorola phone getting support for the privacy-focused GrapheneOS will be the Motorola Signature 27 that was announced earlier this week.

GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused take on Android that’s grown popular in recent years, has so far only been available on Pixel devices. That’s for a number of reasons relating back to how Google handles the software and the security components in Pixel (and Tensor) hardware.

But, now, GrapheneOS is officially stepping beyond Pixel and into a device that will come pre-loaded with its version of Android. It was announced that this would be a Motorola device, but which device was left a mystery as all existing Motorola devices were not compatible with the platform.

Unsurprisingly, though, the first GrapheneOS device from Motorola will be the Motorola Signature 27. GrapheneOS confirmed the news on Twitter/X, though other details are still minimal. It’s apparently still planned that devices will be sold with GrapheneOS pre-installed. The Signature 27 was announced earlier this week and its use of the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset is likely a major part of the reason it will be able to run GrapheneOS properly.

	

An exact release date for the Motorola Signature 27 has yet to be confirmed, and it’s unclear if GrapheneOS will be available right away either. It’s already known that future versions of Razr flip and Razr Fold will also support the privacy-focused OS.

title: Microsoft puts Brad Smith in charge of communications
snippet: Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith. | Image: Getty Images Microsoft is moving its communications group out of marketing and into its Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization. The surprise change will see Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith oversee communications, while the company searches for a replacement for Frank Shaw, chief communications officer, who is departing later this year.
