fullText:
Microsoft is moving its communications group out of marketing and into its Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization. The surprise change will see Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith oversee communications, while the company searches for a replacement for Frank Shaw, chief communications officer, who is departing later this year.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella thanked Shaw “for everything he has done for Microsoft” in an internal memo announcing the communications changes. Shaw announced earlier this month that he’s leaving Microsoft after nearly three decades supporting the company’s communications.

Brent Colburn, VP of global public affairs, has been appointed as interim communications leader to help navigate what Nadella calls “a media environment that is increasingly fragmented and noisier than ever.” Nadella also says he’s “excited about the opportunity to help our engineers, sellers, partners, and others closest to our products and customers become an even bigger part of how we tell our story.”

As GeekWire points out, that sounds a lot like how AI startups work, with researchers leading the demos and blogs at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft has been chasing Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI to “become one of the top four labs in the world,” according to Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. In an interview with The Verge earlier this year, Suleyman said he wants Microsoft “to build the very best frontier models in the world.”

Brad Smith, who’s taking over communications from chief marketing officer Takeshi Numoto, is often the public face of Microsoft’s policy and corporate communications. Smith travels the world meeting with governments, regulators, and Microsoft’s customers. It’s still not clear who will take over permanently from Shaw later this year, but Microsoft is looking at both internal and external candidates.

Here’s Satya Nadella’s memo:

Communications has never been more important to Microsoft. The company is changing, our industry is changing, and the world around us is changing. And in a media environment that is increasingly fragmented and noisier than ever, we need to continue to be grounded in our mission, earn trust each day, and find new ways to connect directly with all of our constituencies.

I first want to thank Frank for everything he has done for Microsoft. He has made tremendous contributions to the company and to our communications function over the last 17+ years. And he’s been a great source of counsel to our leadership team and to me personally, across the company’s biggest moments.

As Frank prepares to embark on his next chapter, Takeshi, Brad, and I have been discussing the evolution of comms at the company. I have asked Brad to lead the communications function going forward. Few leaders embody Microsoft’s voice as authentically as Brad. He brings a deep understanding of our business, a strong connection to our stakeholders, and a rare ability to communicate complex ideas with clarity, conviction, and trust.

During this transition, Brent Colburn will continue reporting to Brad and will now act as our interim communications leader. The comms leadership team will report to Brent, and Frank will continue to advise Brad and Brent on the transition.

In many ways, the people closest to the work have the best opportunity to shape how Microsoft is understood. We need to give people across the company the tools and support to do it well. And I’m excited about the opportunity to help our engineers, sellers, partners, and others closest to our products and customers become an even bigger part of how we tell our story, all connected by a shared strategy and set of principles. All of you have a critical role to play in making that possible.

We have an exciting fall ahead, with a number of important moments and events coming up and great marketing behind them. It is a real opportunity to bring together our product story, our marketing, and our communications in new ways.

We will learn, we will experiment, and we will evolve. There is a fundamentally new way to think about communications, and this team will be central to building it.

Thank you for everything you do for Microsoft, and for the role you each play in telling our story.

Satya

title: Opera’s free built-in VPN can now turn on automatically when using public Wi-Fi
snippet: Opera announced today that its free, built-in VPN for desktop can now automatically activate when users connect to public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Opera announced today that its free, built-in VPN for desktop can now automatically activate when users connect to public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Here are the details.

Opt-in feature rolls out today in the US and France

Since 2016, the Opera browser has offered a free, built-in VPN. The company says this builds on its core belief that “making basic online privacy accessible to everyone.”

In recent years, VPNs have gone from being a relatively niche privacy tool to something much more mainstream. Still, according to data from We Are Social’s Digital 2026 Mid-Year Global Update Report, only 23% of internet users aged 16 and older use a VPN for at least some of their online activities.

That is a problem, particularly for users who rely on public Wi-Fi for work or while traveling.

Today, Opera announced that users in the US and France can opt to have its built-in VPN turn on automatically whenever they connect to a public or unsecured Wi-Fi network.

Here’s Opera:

Public Wi-Fi networks are notoriously vulnerable to snooping and data interception. Opera’s browser VPN now removes manual friction by automatically activating when detecting public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Users can study, work, manage finances, or browse without having to remember to turn on protection manually. To respect user agency, the feature remains strictly opt-in and can be easily toggled within settings. This functionality is rolling out today to Opera users in the US and France.

Opera notes that its “free VPN operates under strict GDPR laws,” adding that it “has been independently audited by Deloitte.” The company also stresses that the VPN is part of a broader set of built-in privacy tools, alongside Opera’s native Ad Blocker and Tracker Blocker.

title: I Wore Meta’s New $1,299 VR Glasses: A Tiny Quest, or Vision Pro to Go?
snippet: Meta’s not done with VR. Its sleek and expensive glasses-like VR device doesn’t need controllers, plays Quest games and is aiming to be your personal cinema too.
fullText:
I could see the whole room in front of me in surprisingly crisp color video detail, while looking at a grid of apps in front of me. Selecting an app with my eyes and a pinch of my fingers, I launched a 3D Billie Eilish concert video. Then I watched an immersive NBA game that stretched all around me. Was I on the Apple Vision Pro? No, I was wearing a pair of Meta VR Glasses, Meta’s $1,299 reimagining of its VR ecosystem coming next spring that feels like one part Apple, one part Meta Quest and one part AR glasses that haven’t been built yet.

Despite releasing waves of smart glasses over the last few years and ditching games studios, software initiatives and fitness apps, including Supernatural earlier this year, Meta’s not done with VR. But the Meta VR Glasses are a very different proposition than the Quest: in price, in design, in portability and in ambition. They’re not AR glasses, like Meta’s Orion prototype I tried two years ago. But they are a VR headset in glasses form, and share a lot in common with the Orion.

I felt echoes of other products as I slipped Meta’s new visor-like pair of VR glasses over my head. An Apple Vision Pro that’s been put onto folding glasses. No: a Meta Quest Pro shrunken down. Or, the Xreal Aura I tried earlier this year. The Meta VR Glasses – yes, that’s their real name – feel like they’re straddling gadget categories. And they’re pushing a price Meta hasn’t tried for in years.

Meta unveiled the VR Glasses on Wednesday at its Connect developer conference, along with camera-free Meta Ray-Bans and an FDA-cleared hearing enhancement feature and plans to install its Muse AI agent across its lineup of smart glasses.

Meta VR Glasses, when folded, are seriously compact. Scott Stein/CNET

Ultraportable VR

The best point of comparison for the Meta VR Glasses might be the now-discontinued Quest Pro, from their small size to their vivid displays and eye- and hand-tracking controls. But they’re also oddly evolutionary, like many other recent VR/AR products I’ve tried.

The magnesium frame glasses-like visor looks minimal compared to any other VR headset, but I’ve seen this form before. I wore another “VR glasses” device called the URXR One back in June. 

Meta’s VR Glasses wired to the processor puck. They work as a team.Scott Stein/CNET

I felt like I was wearing a smaller, like a sliced-off front end of an Apple Vision Pro, bonded to a pair of glasses’ arms. The curved front visor is studded with cameras and sensors that can sense movement in front of and well below my field of view: I could gently pinch my fingers while resting them on the table, the sort of lazy interactions I can do on the Vision Pro. Volume buttons and another control button are embedded in the arms.

The processor puck is where the one USB-C passthrough port is located, and devices that input through it can stream that device into the VR environment, something I didn’t get to try. The puck comes with 128GB of storage, but also has a MicroSD card slot for expandable storage, which requires higher-speed cards. Still, it’s a first for Meta’s VR headsets.

The color passthrough video quality, which makes virtual experiences look projected into the room like augmented reality, was a big notch up from the Quest 3. It felt close to where Samsung and Apple are with their more expensive headsets.

Meta scanned my eyeglasses to provide prescription lens inserts that matched my vision. The inserts fit into the clear pancake lenses in the visor, which were covered in a soft mesh much like the inside of the Vision Pro headset. The Meta VR glasses fit well on my face, too, and they’re far lighter than wearing a Quest 3. They’re 100 grams, which is heavy for glasses but very, very light for a VR headset. They come in two different sizes, but I’m not sure which one I tried.

The lenses in Meta VR Glasses are small, but the viewing experience is impressive.Scott Stein/CNET

My hands-on time with the Meta VR Glasses

I controlled everything with my hands and eyes, because the Meta VR Glasses don’t come with any controllers at all. They’ll work with Meta Quest controllers, and new controllers will be sold separately, but the whole device is designed to work controller-free. Meta’s promising a series of new optimized games for the headset that will be eye and hand-tracking controlled, too.

I played one of them: a new version of Meta’s classic VR-lightsaber fitness game Beat Saber called Beat Saber Flux, which is arriving next year to time with the glasses. Flux has no sabers at all, actually. Instead, the game tracked my hands as I formed energy fields to punch and slice through oncoming waves of targets. It reminded me more of rhythm games like Synth Riders and Supernatural, but also was a good demo of the headset’s hand tracking chops.

Meta’s VR Glasses wowed me with their size.Scott Stein/CNET

I also tried casting multiple virtual monitors in front of me from a wirelessly connected laptop, something you can already do on the Quest and headsets like the Vision Pro and Samsung’s Galaxy XR. But it’s the smaller size of the Meta VR Glasses that makes this achievement seem particularly impressive. 

I typed on a virtual keyboard projected directly onto the table in front of me, a trick Quest headsets can already do but which looked more impressive on Meta’s VR Glasses, particularly since the keyboard really looked as though it had been projected onto the table. It was properly positioned over my hands with realistic occlusion effects. But I don’t know how well it would work beyond my rapid hunt and pecking.

Another look at the glasses and their processor puck.Celso Bugatti/CNET

Navigating Meta’s hand and eye tracking interfaces felt fine, and again, very Apple Vision-esque. But also like Meta’s neural band hand gestures for its Ray-Ban Display glasses. Taps and thumb-swipes on my closed fist handled scrolling around, but I found that pinch-and-pull gestures in the air worked for scrolling too. It wasn’t always that easy to make out on-screen indicators of where my eyes were looking, though: Sometimes icons got a little bigger or wiggled, but not always.

Meta promises a 3-hour battery life with the included processor puck, which can fast recharge at 45W. It runs off a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset, the same one that’s in Xreal’s upcoming processor puck-tethered, VR-like pair of Android XR glasses, Xreal Aura.

Meta’s VR Glasses are small but they pack impressive micro OLED displays inside.Scott Stein/CNET

A clear display upgrade

In a half-hour demo session at Meta’s Connect developer conference, I watched a series of movie clips and videos meant to show off the quality of the headset as a portable cinema. The twin micro OLED displays with a combined effective 5K resolution felt as vivid as that of a Vision Pro, to my memory, but with a smaller 84-degree field of view. They’re 2,412×2,288 pixels per eye.

Watching a few movies on the Meta VR Glasses looked better than anything I’ve seen on Quest headsets, and clearly offers a step-up to approach the good-enough-for-home-cinema feel I get in the Vision Pro.

Beat Saber Flux is a hand tracking-focused game update for Meta VR Glasses (and coming to Quest too). Meta

Meta’s promising lots of streaming video app support. I viewed a series of brief Disney interactive environments for some of its streaming movies, which tried to give me a taste of something more immersive than what’s already on the Vision Pro and Quest’s Disney Plus app. As I watched Avengers: Infinity War, my room was engulfed by parts of the stellar forge Nidavellir while a scene between Thor and Peter Dinklage’s dwarf king Eitri played on a big virtual movie screen. At one point, Groot also popped out in 3D beyond the screen’s dimensions.

The displays and spatial audio are Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision capable, and Meta’s touting that the headset is certified for Imax film viewing in the proper aspect ratio. Meta’s launching its own movie store with these VR glasses, and it’ll also be available on Quest headsets.

In a sense, the Meta VR Glasses almost remind me of smaller micro OLED-equipped display glasses like the ones made by Viture and Xreal. They especially resemble Xreal’s upcoming Aura glasses, which I’ve tried several times and run Google’s Android XR operating system and connect to a processing puck. Aura’s field of view is even smaller at 70 degrees, but it’s more like a pair of display glasses that are remarkably VR-like. Meta’s headset feels like a VR headset that’s remarkably glasses-like. The two sort of meet in the middle.

This is how my early version of Hologram looks on a phone screen. It’s even more impressive in VR.Scott Stein/CNET

Holograms for chat, at last

A demo I tried in a separate session showed me something Meta’s been promising for years: realistic 3D avatars for video chat, much like what Apple already has in its Vision Pro Personas. Meta showed me early prototypes of its “Codec Avatar” vision for hyper-real avatar embodiment back in 2022 at its research labs, but the new Holograms feel like a slice of that, aimed at working on both VR Glasses, Quest headsets, and even Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays in its smaller 2D screen.

I was actually blown away by my Holograms demo, because what I saw didn’t look like uncannily real people: they looked exactly like real people, as if appearing in a video chat in front of me. A quick head scan and recording of my voice and expressions (mostly with smiling or positive emotions expressed) on a phone app led to a 3D scan of myself that then appeared inside VR Glasses when I made a WhatsApp call to a Meta team member. I couldn’t see myself, but I did see them appear in front of me, first as a 3D torso in a window, then opening out to stand in the room with me, legs and all, when I tapped an icon in my chat window.

It looked like a volumetric video capture of someone, not an artificial scan. And while Holograms currently animate body movement using AI to interpret voice tone, they’ll eventually have body tracking using the VR Glasses’ downward-facing cameras, which track both face and body movements. It seemed like they were in the room, right by a table in front of me…but turning in a ghostly manner to keep facing me no matter which way I turned.

Holograms are going to launch alongside Meta VR Glasses, but also get tested as a Met Ray-Ban Display feature in beta later this year for WhatsApp calling. The technology leans heavily on cloud compute, using stable diffusion versus Gaussian splatting like Apple’s Personas uses. I’ve never seen a more realistic deepfaked version of myself before.

The Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses (left) next to Meta VR Glasses (right). They’re getting closer in size than ever.Scott Stein/CNET

The start of a new phase for VR and AR?

My time with the Meta VR Glasses impressed me, especially compared to other recent VR devices and display glasses I’ve tried, and I immediately thought about what it would be like to travel with them. But their unusual design and higher price, clearly aimed at making a premium experience for movie-watching, immersive HD video and wearable displays, is a risk. It’s a play that Meta hasn’t made since the Quest Pro was released back in 2022.

Would I use the Meta VR Glasses for work? Maybe. I like that they can also connect directly to a laptop, phone or any other UBS-C device with video out to turn them into a portable display, but Xreal Aura will do that too. I also like that they’ll run all the Quest apps I already use, but Meta’s still facing an uphill battle over all the Android and iOS apps Google and Apple’s XR devices can tap into. 

How long will it be until Meta’s VR and glasses lines converge?Scott Stein/CNET

I feel more comfortable with Meta as a wear-sometimes device maker in the VR space. I’m much less happy with Meta as a broker of some sort of always-on glasses-based personal assistant (which is where all the AI glasses are headed). But, clearly, those categories are merging, slowly. The VR Glasses feel like an early herald of the attempted merge.

Which raises my final question: Are the Meta VR Glasses a premium upgrade for Quest owners, a portable upsell or a pitch to reach people who’ve never tried VR or AR before? I definitely found them more wearable than any Quest headset, with no pressure on my face and a more casual comfort. 

I kept thinking about Valve’s recently released Steam Frame, a headset that costs a similar amount but has a more traditional but modular VR headset design. Valve’s Frame wants to push Steam into new forms. Meta’s VR Glasses are aiming to push the Quest library into new forms, too. And then there are Xreal’s similar Aura glasses coming this fall, and even Snap Specs, which are full augmented reality glasses with clear lenses but have no processor puck tether at all.

They all want to come with me on a trip. Which would I actually take? Or afford? Meta VR Glasses aren’t even on sale until next spring, but I’m already wondering if they’ll be something I’d pick over alternatives, or whether Meta’s VR glasses flex is more of a stepping stone to AR glasses the company can’t quite make happen yet. But I want another go in them, for sure. And I’d love to travel with them next year.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											I started with CNET reviewing laptops in 2009. Now I explore wearable tech, VR/AR, tablets, gaming and future/emerging trends in our changing world. Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.

snippet: Remember the Tesla Semi? The long-gestating, heavy-duty truck first introduced in concept form in 2017 is finally in volume production as of April 2026 - nearly a decade after its initial introduction. On Thursday evening, the company held yet another event for the Semi to demonstrate to customers and investors that the long wait was finally over. fullText:
Remember the Tesla Semi? The long-gestating, heavy-duty truck first introduced in concept form in 2017 is finally in volume production as of April 2026 — nearly a decade after its initial introduction. On Thursday evening, the company held yet another event for the Semi to demonstrate to customers and investors that the long wait was finally over.

The event was held at Tesla’s new Semi factory next to Gigafactory Nevada, where the company says it can build 50,000 trucks a year, or 1,000 per week. The purpose was to announce a raft of new (and old) customers for the Semi, including PepsiCo, US Foods, DHL, WattEV, ABF, Einride, IMC, and OK Produce. (Most of these names were leaked ahead of the event by a YouTuber flying a drone over the company’s facility in Sparks, Nevada.) First deliveries of the truck started this week.

1/9

But there were still a lot of missing details that could have helped explain why the wait was so long, and where the Semi goes from here. Tesla didn’t reveal order numbers, nor did it update the price of the Semi — which is rumored to be $290,000 for the long range version. In short, like many Tesla events these days, this one was lacking in some key updates.

The trucks were supposed to go into production in 2019 but were delayed for a variety of reasons, including the covid pandemic and a global parts shortage. Tesla delivered a handful of trucks to PepsiCo in 2022, but those units were essentially built by hand on a pilot line.

Back in 2017, the company advertised a starting price of $150,000 for the 300-mile version and $180,000 for the 500-mile one. Tesla never officially updated those prices until today, but Electrek reported earlier this year that Tesla was quoting customers $290,000 for the 500-mile range version.

Tesla spent the last three years refining the Semi’s design, shaving nearly 1,000 lbs off the weight, and building out a dedicated factory next to its Gigafactory in Sparks. The company revealed the final production design in February 2026, confirming two trims: a Standard Range truck with 325 miles at full 82,000-lb gross combination weight, and a Long Range version with 500 miles of range. In April, Tesla announced that the first Semi had rolled off the line at the new facility, kicking off volume production of the long-delayed truck.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk wasn’t at the event — he was in Washington, DC, attending a state dinner with President Trump and Chinese President Xi — but in a prerecorded message, he praised the Semi as “the funnest truck to drive.”

“This is really going to be a revolutionary truck,” Musk said, “that is capable of carrying the heaviest loads over very long distances. With ease of recharge, Megacharger that’s capable of a megawatt of power. This is really going to be a phenomenal truck.”

Battery and engineering

Much of the event was devoted to the hardware and engineering that went into the truck. Tesla’s director of Semi Truck Engineering Dan Priestley emphasized that the 500 mile figure comes from fully loaded trucks rather than tests with a diminishing payload. Tesla vice president of Engineering Lars Moravy said a Semi carrying a lighter load of around 60,000 pounds could potentially reach about 600 miles. The lower-range truck will have lower mass and be suited to a variety of applications, giving the company multiple Semi configurations rather than relying solely on the long-range version.

Tesla claims the Semi, with its lower energy cost and far fewer parts to maintain, is cheaper to run than diesel. That’s not hard to believe with diesel prices having hit historic record highs, soaring past $6.50 a gallon in the US — nearly double what it cost a year ago. Tesla says the fully loaded truck now consumes about 1,700 Wh/mile, compared with an original target of 2,000 Wh/mile. The efficiency gains allow Tesla to use a smaller, lighter, and cheaper battery while retaining the same range.

The Semi is using Tesla’s in-house 4680 battery cells, replacing the purchased 2170 cells used in previous test versions. Tesla says the change, combined with vehicle-efficiency improvements, produces a lower-mass, lower-kWh battery without sacrificing range.

Much of the event was devoted to the hardware and engineering that went into the truck

The company has also substantially redesigned the powertrain and drive axle since the Semi’s initial reveal. The truck gets a new steel-caged rotor instead of the earlier carbon-fiber-sleeved rotor, a bar-wound stator shared with Cybertruck, and a redesigned drive axle that is about 80 kilograms lighter. Tesla also eliminated the three separate oils used in the original drive axle, leaving no oil in the hub and one common oil for the motor and gearbox, which Moravy says should last more than 250,000 miles.

The hydraulic steering has been replaced by redundant electric power steering that Tesla says provides much greater precision and response. Meanwhile, the truck’s increased wheel cut gives it nearly the turning radius of a Model Y. Tesla specifically designed the system to make tight urban and loading-dock maneuvers easier, Priestley said.

The Semi also shares parts with the newly road-worthy Cybercab, using the same indirect thermal system, including pumps, compressors, and heat exchangers, as the autonomous vehicle. Tesla says the system eliminates long refrigerant lines running to the front of the vehicle and can move heat between the cabin, battery, and drive unit to improve efficiency.

1/8

Charging and uptime

Over the past year, Tesla has been building up a customer list for the Semi, including PepsiCo, DHL, ABF Freight, and others. Autonomous trucking startup Einride announced a 500-truck order in August, while IMC Logistics said it would buy 50 Semis for California drayage earlier this week. And on Monday, Tesla was selected by “a coalition of the world’s largest cargo-owning shippers” to supply 2,500 trucks for zero-emission freight shipping in California.

Now the challenge will be meeting this demand by getting trucks to customers — and quickly. Some of these freight operators have been waiting for years for Tesla to deliver its promised electric trucks, and any more delay will just further damage the company’s reputation.

“This is really going to be a revolutionary truck.”

— Elon Musk

Charging will be another challenge, as the Semi requires higher power levels in order to fill its enormous 822 kWh battery pack. Tesla has begun to build out its Megacharger system that can deliver up to 1.2 Megawatts of power per stall. Tesla says it will have more than 30 Semi charging stations representing over 200 megawatt-capable posts by the end of the year, while also supporting customer-installed overnight charging. During the event, Priestley and Moravy kept checking in on a Semi charging at one of the new Megawatt chargers, demonstrating a 3-60 percent charge in about 30 minutes.

Tesla is positioning the Semi as an integrated fleet product, not just an electric truck. The company says its existing fleet has demonstrated more than 98 percent uptime, compared to an average 90–95 percent for diesel-powered class 8 trucks across the industry. Tesla is also building out a dedicated Semi service, mobile service, remote diagnostics, and OTA updates around the truck.

The executives demonstrated a number of innovations they said would make for a better driving experience, including driver profiles that follow drivers from truck to truck and range estimates dynamically accounting for changing payloads.

While Tesla didn’t reveal order numbers or starting prices, Musk did say that the “waiting list is significant” and encouraged people to place orders. The company repeatedly emphasized how the Semi is able to achieve a lower total cost of ownership versus diesel, including lower energy costs, reduced maintenance, and less exposure to diesel-price volatility.

“You know, volatility in the oil market and the diesel market goes up and down,” Moravy said. “But typically, we’ve seen in the history of the last 20 years, electricity is pretty flat. And wouldn’t it be great to have a flat cost in your shipping rates?”

Images by Tesla

title: New iPad mini coming soon with these major changes
snippet: Apple is about to release a new iPad mini. This will mark the first update to the device in two years, and it’s expected to be a big one. Here’s everything we know so far about the new iPad mini coming as soon as next month. more…
fullText:
Apple is about to release a new iPad mini. This will mark the first update to the device in two years, and it’s expected to be a big one. Here’s everything we know so far about the new iPad mini coming as soon as next month.

OLED display

By far the biggest change to the new iPad mini will be to the display. According to multiple sources, the iPad mini 8 will feature an OLED display.

This will be a dramatic improvement to the iPad mini’s current LCD panel. For users, the move to OLED means deeper blacks, richer colors, and better contrast. The iPhone X was the first iPhone to use an OLED display in 2017, while the OLED iPad Pro debuted in 2024.

One lingering question, though, is whether the new iPad mini will use a ProMotion display for refresh rates of up to 120Hz. According to a sketchy rumor last week, the new iPad mini won’t offer ProMotion support and will instead be limited to 60Hz.

This hasn’t been corroborated by any other sources, though, so I’m holding out hope this leak is incorrect.

New chip

The current iPad mini, released in October 2024, is powered by Apple’s A17 Pro chip. The new iPad mini will likely feature the A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip. This will offer a solid boost in performance, and could enable support for the most advanced Siri AI features in iOS 27.

Better water resistance

According to Bloomberg, Apple has tested a “redesigned casing” for the iPad mini that is water-resistant like the iPhone.

Whether or not this water-resistant casing pans out remains to be seen. However, it would make the iPad mini far more durable. It’d be especially notable for people who use it as an e-reader, as one of the top features of dedicated e-readers like the Kindle is water resistance.

New speaker technology

The iPad mini 8 might also be Apple’s first device with a revamped vibration-based speaker system. This vibration-based speaker system would let Apple remove speaker holes, aiding its work to make the device water-resistant.

In contrast, the iPhone has speaker holes, but Apple uses gaskets and adhesives to make the device water-resistant.

New iPad mini release date

According to the latest reporting from Bloomberg, Apple is aiming to release the OLED iPad mini as early as this October. It’s allegedly the “biggest overhaul to the iPad mini in half a decade.”

There’s no word on how much the new iPad mini will cost. Apple increased the price of the current iPad mini in July from $499 to $599 (currently discounted to $569 on Amazon). Whether the new iPad mini with OLED is even more expensive remains to be seen.

What do you think of Apple’s rumored plans for the iPad mini? Are you tempted by the OLED display? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Google rolling out blood pressure & insulin resistance, more on Pixel Watch 3, 4, 5
snippet: As previewed during last month’s Pixel Watch 5 launch, Google is now starting to roll out blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality metrics. more…
fullText:
As previewed during last month’s Pixel Watch 5 launch, Google is now starting to roll out blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality metrics.

Health Guardian is Google’s overarching brand for the Pixel Watch’s suite of “proactive health and safety tools.” It includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is available in Europe on the Pixel Watch 4 and 5.

The blood pressure trends feature works by passively measuring your pulse and motion patterns over the course of a month. It’s intended to let you detect “persistent higher cardiovascular trends early.” This works without a cuff or manual calibration, and was trained using billions of minutes of raw heart and movement data. You need “at least 5 consecutive days in a week” of data.

Insulin resistance trends analyze multi-week physiological data to track shifts in metabolic health without requiring a blood draw. Insulin resistance impacts how your body absorbs energy from food, with Google needing a minimum of 7 days of data in a month. The feature uses Google’s largest sensor foundational model. It was pre-trained using over 1 trillion minutes of data from 5 million opted-in users.

	

Both sets of trend insights will appear in the Google Health app on the first day of each month.

Meanwhile, sleep breathing quality metrics will track overnight breathing changes. In the morning, you’ll see how much time was spent optimally breathing, while a monthly report identifies longer-term patterns.

Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 users will be able to set up these three features in the Google Health app starting this week. Access is free on those three devices, with the first trend reports coming in early October.

If you’re a Google Health Premium subscriber, these three features are also coming to the Fitbit Air “later this year.”

title: Motorola Signature 27 is a proper flagship with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Alongside Qualcomm’s latest announcements, Motorola has officially shown off the Motorola Signature 27, a true flagship offering that’s set to launch before the end of this year. more…
fullText:
Alongside Qualcomm’s latest announcements, Motorola has officially shown off the Motorola Signature 27, a true flagship offering that’s set to launch before the end of this year.

Building on the Motorola Signature, a pseudo-flagship that launched earlier this year, the Signature 27 adopts a new naming scheme (based on the coming year), a wild-looking design, and a proper flagship spec sheet.

While its predecessor was based on Qualcomm’s step-down Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, the Motorola Signature 27 uses the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, a new chip that’s just as powerful as its mouthful of a name. It’s a big deal on Motorola’s part, as the brand hasn’t used any flagship chipsets in quite a while. The Motorola Razr Ultra (2025) used the Snapdragon 8 Elite, but its successor didn’t upgrade, and other devices in the company’s lineup, including the $1,900 Razr Fold, haven’t gone beyond the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5.

Qualcomm announces the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

Motorola says to expect stronger on-device AI features with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, as well as “responsive” gaming, faster download speeds over various networks, and improvements to the camera, too. There’s an “ArcticMesh” cooling system that combines a 40% larger vapor chamber with liquid metal, copper mesh, and “diamond-infused thermal gel.”

	

Motorola Signature 27 is promised 7 years of Android OS and security updates and has quite the look with its quad-camera setup on the back. That includes a 50MP Sony LYTIA 910 main sensor and 200MP periscope telephoto lens. The other two haven’t been confirmed just yet. The design itself brings back some Droid Razr vibes from over a decade ago. 

Signature 27 will come in “Coal Smoke” with a “Tactical Weave” finish, or “Capulet Green” with a “brushed textile-inspired finish.”

A firm release date hasn’t been announced, nor has Motorola spilled the beans on exact launch markets. The company says it will debut “worldwide” in 2026, and also confirmed a launch in North America in the “coming months.”

9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: The Memoket Gem is an 11g AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch in a co-wear band. Press once to capture a conversation, and Gem connects it to what you discussed weeks ago — surfacing the earlier thread with a source link. From $179, shipping now.

Right before all of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo craziness, I was lucky enough to attend my first IFA in Berlin. For those unaware, IFA is the CES of Europe. There are thousands of brands and companies, ranging from tiny start-ups to giant juggernauts. They all have one goal: to show off what they have been creating to the 100,000s of visitors that attend. 

I saw everything from flying cars to mini robots to 200-inch transparent displays, and while all of those products are awesome for a quick demo and to show off, I was not there for them. I wanted to see the tech that is actually about to come out, not the tech that maybe one day will see the light of day. So here are my favorite products from IFA, with a bit of an Apple twist, of course!

Lexar Muse

I have been, and still am, a huge Lexar SSD user. They make reliable, fast, and compact SSDs that I use in my workflow daily. I currently use their SL500 and their magnetic SSD with my iPhone 18 Pro Max. They are versatile and work in my Apple ecosystem because they have the speed to support that ProRes Raw footage. But their newest announcement, the Lexar Muse, blew me away. I am a huge fan of thin tech, so when I saw that this SSD is just 3.8mm at its thickest point, I was all over this. 

Just 3.8mm at its thickest point, tapering to 1mm at the edges

Up to 1,050 MB/s read and 1,000 MB/s write

512GB and 1TB

Proprietary PogoPin connection with a SnapLink Magnetic Cable

Supports direct external Apple ProRes 4K recording at up to 120 fps on compatible iPhones

The main thing I was curious about was how you can fit a USB-C port on such a small device. The answer is: you can’t. So what they created was a pogo pin connection. You just slap the SSD to the rear of your iPhone with the Magsafe accessory, and it comes with a USB-C to pogo pin cable. It’s sized perfectly to be long enough to not be in the way and reach the back of the Lexar Muse. I thought this was a genius use case. 

As of now, given how thin it is and the current storage crisis, Lexar will be offering these in 512 MB and 1 TB sizes, with higher capacities in the future. It is set to release in October of 2026!

Belkin LilyPad

Now this one is more of a guilty pleasure than anything else. I recently took my 5-year-old to her first movie theater experience, and we went to see the new Toy Story 5. If you have yet to see it, the main villain in the movie is an iPad-like tablet called LilyPad that eventually turns good and becomes an ally of all the main characters. So when I saw the actual LilyPad character at the Belkin booth, I had to stop by. Turns out that this is part of a much bigger collaboration that brings all the characters to a bunch of Apple-friendly accessories. But the show stopper here is the LilyPad case because it turns your iPad into that character. 

Officially licensed Disney Pixar Toy Story 5 Lilypad character design

Compatbile with iPad 10th generation (10.9-inch) and iPad 11th generation (11-inch A16)

Shock-absorbing EVA foam construction with rounded edges and 4-foot drop protection

Integrated handle with an easy-grip texture designed for smaller hands

Built-in kickstand

Exclusive and licensed Lilypad wallpapers included

But as I mentioned, this is an entire collection. Belkin has also made a Toy Story iPhone case, a MagSafe power bank, and a larger power bank that resembles one of the toys from the movie. I think these were tastefully done, as they still provide plenty of functionality and look fun for any Toy Story fan. All of these products are available today and range from $35 to $55, with the LilyPad being $49. 

Wokyis i5 Docking Station

I am a huge fan of Wokyis products. They have found a way to bring a nostalgic look and feel to products that bring modern functionality. I recently reviewed their G5 and G7 docks for the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. But those are built to physically be attached to the Mac. So what Wokyis did was bring all that function and nostalgia to a standalone dock that works with any computer. You get all the pro-level ports you needed and a display as well!

Built-in 5-inch HD IPS display with a 1280 × 720 resolution

Four dedicated shortcut keys and a rotary control knob for frequently used functions

Built-in M.2 NVMe SSD enclosure for additional storage

Four USB-A ports, one USB-C data port, SD and microSD 4.0 card readers, HDMI input, and a 3.5mm headphone jack with up to 10Gbps speeds

Supports up to 65W pass-through charging for compatible laptops

As I mentioned, I love products with a bit of character. I want my accessories to be conversation starters, making people wonder and say, “What is that?” That is exactly what Wokyis products do, and the i5 Docking Station is no different. It brings some awesome personality at a time when most docks are completely sterile. 

The i5 Docking Station is available on Amazon today for $153. If you need a new docking station that adds a bit of fun and tactility without sacrificing function, this is a good one to grab.

iPhone cases 

You can just imagine the thousands, if not millions, of different iPhone case brands that were at IFA. From every shape, material, size, and function, there is a case for any type of person. The thing about cases is that they are completely subjective. There is no real good or bad, or right or wrong. You either like it or you don’t. But there are two cases I wanted to highlight because they are different from some of the others I have seen. 

First is the Xtrem Inno cases. I reviewed their first gen last year and loved it because I had never seen another case do this. The Xtrem Inno case has a Color E ink display that allows you to change what it shows on the rear of the case to anything you want. 

Circular, customizable rear display with four-color reproduction and a resolution of 212 PPI

The display requires no separate charging and retains its image without continuously consuming power

Supports MagSafe wireless charging and magnetic accessories

On the surface, it looks like a nicely designed case, but when you pair it with their app, you can send an image via NFC to the case. It’s so cool how it all works. The amazing thing is that since it uses NFC and E-ink, that means no batteries, Bluetooth, or wired connections are needed. The phone uses a tiny bit of power to send the image via NFC, and since it’s E-ink, once it’s on, it stays on without persistent power.

The case is available today on Amazon for $75 and comes in a ton of new colors. If you need a fun new case, this is the way to go. 

Moft Movas Coffee Edition

Last year, Moft introduced a new ultra-thin case for the iPhone 17 lineup. The base itself was great for anyone who wanted a super-slim, minimal case. They ended up bringing it back for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, but the interesting part is the material they went with, more than anything else. At a time when sustainability is high on the agenda, Moft decided to use a new coffee-based bio-leather for this case, and it’s awesome. The best part is that it gives off a bit of a coffee aroma. So this is the case for all my coffee lovers out there! Outside of that, you get all the trimmings you want out of a rthin case.

Built-in magnets for MagSafe

Weighs just 28g and is ultra-thin

Reinforced TPU corners provide basic drop protection, while the open-sided frame design preserves the natural feel of the iPhone

Available in a Coffee Brown and Sapphire Blue color combination

Again, the innovation here is the choice of material. I had never heard of or seen this choice of using coffee grounds to create a sort of bio-leather. They are also using this material for their famous moft wallet stand. They are all available on Amazon today for $49. 

Final thoughts

Again, there was a ton, and I mean a ton of things that came from IFA that I am excited about. I was able to see things like ultra-fast supercars, the Xiaomi iPhone Duo clone before it was announced, and so much more. But these were just a few of the things that caught my eye and made sense to me in our Apple-focused world.

title: MacWhisper update brings real-time meeting transcripts, improved speaker recognition, more
snippet: My transcription tool of choice on the Mac, MacWhisper, got another major update today with real-time meeting transcripts, significantly improved speaker recognition, tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, and a new transcription model. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
My transcription tool of choice on the Mac, MacWhisper, got another major update today with real-time meeting transcripts, significantly improved speaker recognition, tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, and a new transcription model. Here are the details.

MacWhisper gets deeper Apple Intelligence integration

I’ve written in the past about how much I rely on MacWhisper, particularly as part of my podcast production workflow.

MacWhisper was one of the first AI-powered transcription tools for the Mac. Since indie developer Jordi Bruin launched it in 2023, it has been on a relentless streak of improvements and expanded support for new models, services, and workflows.

That has included everything from automatic meeting recording and speaker recognition to watched folders, system-wide dictation, local and cloud AI models, and integrations with services such as Notion, Zapier, Obsidian, and n8n.

Today, MacWhisper was updated to version 15.2, introducing an improved speaker recognition powered by NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Diarization model, which was announced just hours ago.

It supports up to 8 speakers and can also be used during live meetings in the new realtime meeting view!

Which brings us to another major addition in today’s update: real-time meeting transcriptions.

This feature had been sitting near the top of MacWhisper’s public roadmap for a while, and it is now here, allowing users to follow, refer back to, copy, or transfer a live transcript as the meeting unfolds.

You can keep the window above your other apps to follow along, and your recording and transcript are saved when the meeting ends.

When it comes to the actual transcription models, MacWhisper 15.2 adds Alibaba’s QWEN3-ASR transcription model with support for 22 languages, in addition to a tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, Siri, Spotlight, and Shortcuts on macOS 27.

Now, users running macOS (including in the EU) can search for transcripts system-wide, open them with Siri, pull their text into Shortcuts, and refer to the transcript currently on screen in Siri or Apple Intelligence requests.

Finally, MacWhisper 15.2 adds folders and subfolders for organizing transcripts and meetings, with support for dragging existing transcriptions into them from the sidebar.

title: iOS 27.2: New features, release date, more
snippet: Apple has kicked off beta testing of iOS 27.2, and the update brings several notable changes and new features. Here’s everything you need to know about iOS 27.2, which will likely be released to iPhone users as soon as next month. more…
fullText:
Apple has kicked off beta testing of iOS 27.2, and the update brings several notable changes and new features. Here’s everything you need to know about iOS 27.2, which will likely be released to iPhone users as soon as next month.

Why iOS 27.2 and not iOS 27.1?

Apple released iOS 27 on September 14, bringing a ton of new iPhone features, including Siri AI. iOS 27.2 entered beta testing just two days later on September 16.

What happened to iOS 27.1?

Apple previously confirmed that iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1 when it’s released on October 23. This means iOS 27.1 includes many references to the iPhone Duo in its code, which Apple wants to keep under wraps until the device ships. iOS 27.1 will therefore be exclusive to the iPhone Duo.

The software paths for iPhone Duo and other iPhone models will then converge, either with an iOS 27.2.x software update or perhaps with iOS 27.3.

So, things will be awkward for a little bit, but everything will eventually return to normal.

iOS 27.2 new features

Redesigned Health app

At the iPhone 18 Pro event, Apple showcased an all-new version of the Health app that it said would be coming later this year. That new app has entered beta testing as part of iOS 27.2.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

The new Health app likely won’t be released with iOS 27.2 next month. Instead, this is Apple kicking off beta testing of the new app before ultimately releasing it to everyone later this year.

Read more: iOS 27.2 introduces Apple Health app overhaul, here’s what’s new

Profiles in the TV app

The Apple TV app in iOS 27.2 adds support for profiles for the first time. This feature has been available on tvOS for several years, but this is the first time it has come to iPhone.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

More Siri AI languages

Siri AI is the big new feature in iOS 27, and iOS 27.2 expands the feature to even more users. The update adds Siri AI support for the following languages:

French

Japanese

Korean

Portuguese

Spanish

Dual Capture mode for Group FaceTime

In iOS 27, Apple added a new Dual Capture feature for FaceTime that lets you have your front and rear cameras active at the same time. The person on the other end of the call will see you as well as whatever you’re looking at. iOS 27.2 expands this feature to Group FaceTime calls for the first time.

Dual Capture requires an iPhone 17 or later, and everyone on the call needs to be running iOS 27.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Odds and ends

In Apple Podcasts, the “Up Next” queue has been renamed to “New Episodes.” The “Continue Playing” section is directly below New Episodes. Episode lists also now use color-matched backgrounds based on the podcast art.

In the Music app, some of the red icons and accents have been changed to black.

iOS 27’s Call Context feature, which surfaces information right on your screen when calling a business, has been expanded to include anniversaries.

There are small changes to the alarms interface in the Clock app, such as smaller text for the AM and PM labels.

Hints at more features to come

Finally, iOS 27.2 code hints at a handful of other new features that could come soon to iPhone users. This includes live countdowns for new album releases in Apple Music, third-party app support for Describe a Shortcut, and new themes for CarPlay Ultra. iOS 27.2 also shows Apple is continuing its work on an anti-snatching feature for iPhone.

These features aren’t live in iOS 27.2 just yet, but the code suggests they are in active development inside Apple.

iOS 27.2 release date

iOS 27.2 is expected to be released to iPhone users sometime in October. Apple promised that Siri AI would come to new languages in October, and iOS 27.2 adds those new languages, so the update needs to be released before November for Apple to hit that promise.

Wrap up

Are you running the iOS 27.2 beta? Have you found any useful new features? What do you think of the new Health app? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Review: Beats 360 are the closest Apple headphones to AirPods Max, with one caveat
snippet: The highly anticipated Beats 360 are now available for purchase. After being teased prior to the World Cup, Apple’s latest pair of Beats headphones are now on the market. I got an early hands-on with them, and they’re quite an interesting product offering that I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using – though they have one key flaw: no wired connectivity, which will bother some more than others. more…
fullText:
The highly anticipated Beats 360 are now available for purchase. After being teased prior to the World Cup, Apple’s latest pair of Beats headphones are now on the market. I got an early hands-on with them, and they’re quite an interesting product offering that I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using – though they have one key flaw: no wired connectivity, which will bother some more than others.

Product overview

First things first, the Beats 360 come in at $349.99. At that price, they’re leaning towards the high end of the market, though they still fall well below the AirPods Max at $549. Alongside this launch, the existing Beats Studio Pro are being permanently reduced to a new price of $299.99. Of course, you can find them much cheaper at retailers: they currently run $169.95 on Amazon.

If you’ve been following Beats launches, you’ll know that they sometimes use Apple H1 or H2 chips, and sometimes they use custom Beats silicon. The Beats 360 do use Beats silicon, however there’s one key upgrade here: they now finally support automatic device switching with your Apple Account, Hey Siri support, as well as proper Find My integration. If you’re an Apple fan who’s been eyeing Beats as a more affordable version of AirPods Max, the Beats 360 are closer than ever to providing a true Apple experience. I was certainly pleased when I learned this.

There is one loss compared to most high-end headphones: there’s no automatic pausing when you take them off your head. You learn to live with it, though it takes some time to get used to.

Compared to Beats Studio Pro, the Beats 360 get 12dB louder, and offer 1.75x more active noise cancellation. They also support Adaptive EQ in iOS 27, and are the first Beats headphones to be IPX4 sweat and water resistant. Both offer spatial audio with dynamic head tracking, and the Beats 360 last around 8 hours longer than Beats Studio Pro with ANC turned on.

Beats 360 come in four colors: Cloud, Sky, Black, and Pink. I’ve personally been trying out the Sky’s, but they’re all pretty elegant colors.

Customization

The headlining feature of Beats 360 is their customizable design. You can easily swap out the ear cushions and head cushion for different color options. The ear cushions also have two variants, UltraPlush and Performance Knit. The former will be more comfortable for everyday wear, whereas the latter is better for working out.

Each set of cushions is available for $49.99, though there’s a launch promo while supplies last where you can pick them up for just $9.99. This is an incredible promo for those who want to customize their headphones based on their outfit, or to match their mood. I’d personally take advantage of it.

Customization is really the name of the game with Beats 360. With the four base color options, as well as eight additional cushion options, there are 32 total ways you can mix up your Beats 360. If you mix headband cushions from the earcups, there are up to 256 different options.

You can truly make these headphones yours – which is quite fun. Another advantage to this is the fact that when your ear cushions wear down, you can easily swap them out instead of calling the headphones a loss.

Plethora of Beats 360 color combos
My personal Beats 360 color combo

9to5Mac’s Take

The Beats 360 are good headphones for most Apple enthusiasts. If you’re looking to switch away from your AirPods Max to something lighter and more comfortable, I’d say these fit those criteria pretty well, though you’re taking a hit on sound quality. I’d also highly recommend picking up an UltraPlush cushion kit, as I personally find the fabric ones a bit uncomfortable for casual use. With the launch promo for cushion kits, there isn’t much reason not to.

As someone who primarily used AirPods Pro 3 prior to testing out the Beats 360, I’ve actually found myself to much prefer the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is solid, transparency didn’t disappoint, and the fact that they fold down flat didn’t make them too much of a hurdle to fit in my everyday backpack. Of course, earbuds will simply be more convenient for many scenarios, but I found myself missing these headphones when I was away from home (as I couldn’t wear them outdoors during review), which I’ve never really thought for any pair of over-ears in the past.

Frankly, the only major complaint I have with the Beats 360 is that they don’t support wired connectivity. There’s no headphone jack, and USB-C seemingly doesn’t support it either. This is a little bit of an inconvenience if you’re looking to use them in an environment that doesn’t play super nicely with Bluetooth, such as an airplane or with a game console.

Regardless of that, I truly adore what Beats has done with the customizable design. These have been some of my favorite headphones I’ve tested out, even compared to AirPods Max, which I could never get comfortable with because of their weight. Beats 360 have no comfort issues whatsoever, so long as I use the UltraPlush cushions.

Pricing & availability

Beats 360 are launching at $349.99, with deliveries and in-store availability beginning September 24th. You can order them on Amazon and at Apple.com.

The limited-time $9.99 cushion kit promo is available in the US, Canada, the UK, France, China, Australia, and South Korea. It’s valid through October 31st, while supplies last.

title: iPhone users running iOS 27 can no longer downgrade to iOS 26
snippet: Apple today stopped signing iOS 26.6.2, which means iPhone users can no longer downgrade to non-iOS 27 system versions. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Apple today stopped signing iOS 26.6.2, which means iPhone users can no longer downgrade to non-iOS 27 system versions. Here’s why.

Apple no longer signing iOS 26.6.2 installs

When a user tries to install a version of iOS on their iPhone, part of the process involves checking with Apple’s servers to make sure that version is still authorized for installation. This is what’s referred to as signing, and it works for both upgrading or downgrading to any iOS version.

Because iOS updates often patch known security vulnerabilities, Apple keeps a rather short list of signed iOS versions. This prevents users from installing or downgrading to older versions that may contain flaws that could be exploited by attackers.

Today, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple stopped signing iOS 26.6.2. This means that users running iOS 27 can no longer downgrade to iOS 26.6.2, essentially closing the window on official downgrades to iOS 26.

Apple is no longer signing iOS 26.6.2, this means you can't downgrade to iOS 26 anymore from iOS 27

— Aaron (@aaronp613) September 21, 2026

It is worth noting that although Apple released iOS 26.7 last week, the company currently doesn’t officially offer a restore image for it, unlike iPadOS 26.7.

In practice, this means that iPhone users who are still running an earlier version of iOS 26 can install iOS 26.7 as an over-the-air update, but those already on iOS 27 cannot officially use it to downgrade.

title: Meta’s Muse Charm looks like a Tamagotchi, but it’s tapping into a much newer trend
snippet: Meta’s new AI gadget may look like a Tamagotchi, but its dangling form factor taps into a much broader Gen Z trend around bag charms, retro tech, and turning gadgets into fashion accessories.
fullText:
Is Meta’s just-announced Muse Charm a playful device that will make AI more approachable to everyday consumers, or will it be yet another flop in a long list of AI hardware gadgets that didn’t take off, like the Ai Pin, Rabbit, or Friend pendant? Reactions, so far, have been mixed. What the Charm is, however, is on-trend.

Like it or not, the form factor could potentially appeal to Gen Z consumers who, in this post-Labubu era, have already been into various dangling items from keychains and bags. It’s all part of a broader kitschy, retro-inspired shift in their approach to fashion and technology.

Already, Gen Z has created a market for things that dangle, with everything from lip glosses to hand sanitizers to sunblocks to fragrances and more turned into bag charms, primarily targeted at women.

Hailey Bieber’s viral Rhode lip case, which stuck the lip gloss onto a phone case, had a big influence on this idea that beauty products could also be fashion accessories, as did its other beauty-focused bag charms. (The brand saw $212 million in annual net sales from a lineup of roughly 10 products, Vogue noted last year, as the company announced its billion-dollar exit to Elf Beauty.)

Then there was the Labubu craze, which saw sales of the so-ugly-it’s-cute fuzzy monster bag charm explode, growing Pop Mart’s (the Chinese retailer behind the product) revenue to $1.8 billion in 2024, a 7x jump from 2019. While demand for the Labubu itself has since faded, the concept of the decorative bag charm has not. One analyst firm estimates the global bag charm market will grow to over $1 billion by 2030.

Image Credits:LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA / Contributor / Getty Images

Today, bag charms can be characters, bedazzled beauty products, or other whimsical designs or objects, like Coach’s coveted cherry charms, a Gen Z favorite. They’ve proven popular because they’re a means of expressing your personality, just as humans have done for ages through their fashion choices, makeup, and jewelry.

Similarly, Meta’s Muse is a customizable character; you design your own avatar, which makes the AI agent a reflection of you, too. 

And, as many have pointed out, Muse Charm’s form factor recalls a Tamagotchi, the pocket-sized digital virtual pet that became a major toy fad in the late 90s and again in the mid-2000s. 

However, the Tamagotchi is not the most current reference. It seems the Muse Charm is actually a twist on what some young people are already doing with their Apple Watch. Often meant as a way to repurpose an older device, the concept of the Apple Watch keychain or charm has been growing in popularity, fueled by TikTok videos showing different ways to use the watch when not on your wrist.

On retailers like Amazon and Walmart, and marketplaces like eBay and Etsy, there are thousands of Apple Watch keychains, straps, pendants, lanyards, clips, and bag charm cases now available in nearly every style you can think of. As you might expect, these keychain watches are often being adopted by younger women as a fashion accessory first, rather than a piece of technology.

This all then intersects with the broader retro-tech trend, which has seen older tech like digital cameras, flip phones, iPods, CDs, cassette tapes, home phones, and wired earbuds making a quiet comeback. 

This vibe shift in tech comes as young people describe the addictive, algorithm-driven feeds and “soulness” nature of technology as making them feel more disconnected, which has also fed into this trend of wanting tech they can touch and feel. (One startup, Clicks, is even bringing back the physical phone keyboard in a BlackBerry-inspired device, for instance.)

For Gen Z, these physical objects help them feel more connected with the technology they’re using and offer a sense of control over a world where technology has become so deeply integrated into our lives that it no longer feels like a choice to use it. 

Young women, again, have been at the forefront of this trend, with some even crafting their own portable, mini computers, “cyberdecks,” which they fit inside clamshell purses or custom cases, and bedazzle with jewels, flowers, stickers, pearls, and other items to make them feel more personal.

Image Credits:CC / Bimbo Tech (opens in a new window)

That brings us back to the Muse Charm. While it’s clearly designed with the tech-as-fashion-accessory trend in mind, that doesn’t mean it will be a hit. 

Meta has abused consumer trust over the years to such an extent that it may never fully recover.  

Image Credits:Meta

To name just a few examples: The tech giant had to settle with the FTC over charges that it deceived consumers by making users’ private information public without their consent, and has been penalized by the FTC for numerous privacy-related violations. In 2023, the FTC charged Meta with violating a privacy order that was filed after the 2019 settlement. It’s also been repeatedly hauled before Congress over its harms to minors, has lost or settled multiple lawsuits over the same topics, and has seen various whistleblowers outing its abuses.

These careless privacy practices could ultimately see Meta lose the battle to be the consumer AI of choice… unless, of course, consumers decide that the “devil you know” is better than the one you don’t. (Especially when the latter are those warning AI could put an end to the human race.)

Meta’s end game, after all, is highly-targeted, highly-personalized ads. If that’s the privacy tradeoff in gaining access to free AI — Meta said it will monetize Muse by taking a small fee from transactions — consumers could be willing to take the risk.

Is Meta’s just-announced Muse Charm a playful device that will make AI more approachable to everyday consumers, or will it be yet another flop in a long list of AI hardware gadgets that didn’t take off, like the Ai Pin, Rabbit, or Friend pendant? Reactions, so far, have been mixed. What the Charm is, however, is on-trend.

Like it or not, the form factor could potentially appeal to Gen Z consumers who, in this post-Labubu era, have already been into various dangling items from keychains and bags. It’s all part of a broader kitschy, retro-inspired shift in their approach to fashion and technology.

title: North Korean hackers suspected in $351M crypto theft, the largest so far this year
snippet: The $351 million theft from crypto exchange Bitget is the latest in a string of high-profile hacks targeting the crypto sector.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

6:24 AM PDT · September 25, 2026

Image Credits:Samuil Levich / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

North Korean hackers are suspected of stealing more than $351 million from the servers of cryptocurrency exchange Bitget during a cyberattack on Thursday.

The cyberattack is the latest in an ongoing spate of high profile hacks targeting the crypto sector. It’s also the largest known heist of digital currency this year, eclipsing a $340 million hack in September that saw the hacker returning all but $47 million of the stolen funds.

In a series of posts on X on Thursday and Friday, Bitget said the breach involved the unauthorized transfer of crypto from its hot wallets, which are connected to the internet and designed to be used for active trading. Bitget has since suspended crypto withdrawals on its network. The company said it has $464 million in its user protection fund, which should cover the costs of the theft.

Bitget chief executive Gracy Chen said the breach and heist was “highly consistent with known patterns of North Korean hacker organizations.” Such collectives have been linked to crypto thefts and have been suspected of targeting open-source software to mass-hack victims with the aim of funding the country’s nuclear weapons program.

According to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, North Korea is behind around three-quarters of all crypto thefts during 2026 to date.

Chen did not say when Bitget’s withdrawals would open again.

title: What do you actually use a laptop for, and would Googlebook be able to do it? [Poll]
snippet: Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced. more…
fullText:
Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced.

Our initial coverage of Googlebook is live, with Abner, Jordan, and Damien all walking away with a good first impression of Google’s efforts.

Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]

Yet, I’m unconvinced thus far. I’ve yet to get my hands on a Googlebook and, as someone sitting mostly in the same boat as you, our readers, I’m yet to be sold on this new platform. I simply don’t understand why it exists, even more so why Google seems to think it will succeed.

Google’s entire pitch around why you should buy a Googlebook more or less boils down to smartphone integration – specifically Android integration. Googlebook takes existing tools from ChromeOS and supercharges them, giving you the ability to mirror apps, sync files, and do a whole lot more between your Android phone and your laptop. And it does sound pretty good! As someone who currently juggles a MacBook with various Android phones, there are integrations I wish existed; instant hotspot and proper Quick Share support (AirDrop works, but tends to be wildly slow) are at the top of that list. 

	

Googlebook is delivering the MacBook + iPhone experience, just for Android users. That’s the pitch.

Where it falls flat for me is in the apparent functionality. At its core, Googlebook is Android, just with a desktop experience built on top. The core stuff is there – desktop-class Chrome browser, customizable desktop, keyboard shorts, the lot. But the app ecosystem is built around Android apps, web apps, and Linux apps. The same core as ChromeOS, just with a different priority and with better performance on the Android app side, as Abner and Damien both noticed.

That’s where I’m struggling to get on board.

There’s plenty you can do on a Googlebook, sure, just like there was plenty you could do on a Chromebook. But you’re still making a trade-off. Google pointed out that around 70% of things people do on a laptop are done through their browser (Chrome, of course). And, yeah, I’d say that’s about how much I do in the browser on my Windows desktop or my MacBook. That other 30%, though, is the “make or break” that eventually broke me on ChromeOS. For me, it largely came down to Adobe’s apps which, as it stands, still aren’t replicated on Googlebook. On Google’s own website, the company touts a Googlebook’s ability to use Photoshop and Lightroom, but that’s just with the mobile apps – not the full-featured apps you can use on you know, most other laptops. 

Google knows people use these apps; otherwise, it wouldn’t take up a place on this site in the first place – the same goes for games, where Google advertises tons of popular titles like Forza Horizon, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, and more, with only two of the games shown running natively and the rest delivered via GeForce Now.

The market has pretty clearly spoken in this regard. Chromebooks are out. There are remarkably few consumer-focused Chromebooks on the market today and, especially on the high end, it seems like hardly anyone is buying them – Google itself gave up on first-party Chromebooks over five years ago. 

To me at least, the reasoning seems obvious. When Chromebooks hit their stride, the market was full of compromises everywhere. There was no one perfect answer. But that’s changed in recent years. Apple’s M-series chips ushered in a new era for the MacBook which, in turn, influenced some major improvements across Windows laptops. Fast forward to today and there’s no lack of powerful, battery-efficient, thin & light laptop options and, despite “RAMageddon” ruining the price side of things, there’s been a huge push for more affordable machines in the wave of MacBook Neo and its clones – and those are very popular too. Giving up access to a full collection of full-featured apps for a lightweight operating system that gets roughly the same battery life for roughly the same price is a no-brainer, which means that Chromebooks are relegated to a niche. In enterprise/schools, for more affordable machines, for low-end hardware, ChromeOS still makes a lot of sense, but it’s a tough sell basically anywhere else, so you might be able to see why I’m so confused by Googlebook.

Googlebook’s pitch, again, isn’t bad, but does it make sense in today’s market? Who’s buying a laptop that’s inherently (and inarguably) restricted in what it can do, especially at a time when laptops are wildly inflated in price in the first place due to component shortages? 

This is the part where I turn the floor over to you.

Do you think Googlebook has stuck the landing? Has Google’s pitch resonated with you? 

	

Even more so, what are you using a laptop for in the first place? That’s perhaps the most important question around this. As mentioned, I’m personally using my laptop mostly in Chrome, with non-Chrome apps including the likes of Photoshop/Lightroom/Premiere, Spotify, Slack, and a handful of assorted other tools. There are a few of those I can replace – Spotify’s tablet interface should be a treat on a laptop, though I think Slack will be awful given how the Android app lacks any semblance of big-screen optimizations (on Android, as they’re immediately giving Apple something better), so maybe the Linux app will be better.

That’s just me. There are infinite ways people use their laptop. So, looking at what you do today, do you think a Googlebook can do it all? Vote in the poll below, then leave a comment.

title: Microsoft is killing off the ‘Copilot Plus PC’ brand
snippet: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella introducing the company’s Copilot Plus PC initiative. | Image: Allison Johnson Remember when Microsoft wanted everyone to know that "Copilot Plus PCs" were the ones to get, because those were the PCs that that'd have enough built-in AI muscle to get things done? Two and a half years later, Microsoft and Qualcomm seem to be admitting the brand is already dead. fullText:
Sean Hollister

 

is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Remember when Microsoft wanted everyone to know that “Copilot Plus PCs” were the ones to get, because those were the PCs that that’d have enough built-in AI muscle to get things done? Two and a half years later, Microsoft and Qualcomm seem to be admitting the brand is already dead.

Windows Central’s Zac Bowden reports that even though the new 12-inch Microsoft Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop technically meet the system requirements for a Copilot Plus PC, Microsoft is not calling them by that name anymore. “These are not called Copilot Plus PCs,” Microsoft Surface CVP Brett Ostrom told the publication.

Kedar Kondap, Qualcomm’s SVP of compute and gaming, seemed to agree that the brand’s time is done, telling Bowden that computers that offer the same experiences will “probably” not use that branding anymore.

It’s not surprising to me that Microsoft and its partners would back away. Back in 2024, smart minds pointed out that (almost) every PC would soon contain the basic levels of AI hardware that the brand was supposed to reflect. The flagship feature of Copilot Plus PCs, Microsoft’s Recall feature, wasn’t well received, and Microsoft took flak for constantly annoying Windows users with AI upsells, not to mention the dedicated Copilot keyboard key that you can now finally remap.

Besides, Microsoft’s flagship hardware is now about to have Nvidia chips instead, which will supposedly kick off a new era of personal AI in Windows. On October 7th, when Microsoft hosts a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” I’m guessing it will have a shiny new brand to replace “Copilot Plus PC.”

title: Qualcomm’s new ‘Elite’ sound chip might finally deliver the Wi-Fi earbud dream
snippet: What if your wireless earbuds - or audio glasses - could stream high-quality lossless audio that doesn't cut out when you leave your phone on the bedside charger or buried in the couch? Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 is its first to integrate "micro-power Wi-Fi 6E" right into the chip, so they can connect directly to your home Wi-Fi network, and from there to the cloud. If that sounds like a familiar promise, it's probably because Qualcomm promised something similar back in 2023 with the "S7 Pro sound platform" and its Expanded Personal Area Network (XPAN) tech, saying that Wi-Fi earbuds can do what Bluetooth alone cannot. Name … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Sean Hollister

 

is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

What if your wireless earbuds — or audio glasses — could stream high-quality lossless audio that doesn’t cut out when you leave your phone on the bedside charger or buried in the couch? Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 is its first to integrate “micro-power Wi-Fi 6E” right into the chip, so they can connect directly to your home Wi-Fi network, and from there to the cloud.

If that sounds like a familiar promise, it’s probably because Qualcomm promised something similar back in 2023 with the “S7 Pro sound platform” and its Expanded Personal Area Network (XPAN) tech, saying that Wi-Fi earbuds can do what Bluetooth alone cannot. Namely, 24-bit 96kHz lossless audio that can’t fit into Bluetooth’s meager bandwidth.

But that old 7-series platform required a separate Wi-Fi chip to give you Wi-Fi earbuds, and it seems that wasn’t a winning formula for getting makers of incredibly tiny devices to adopt the tech! In fact, we’ve only ever heard of one: Xiaomi’s 2025 Buds 5 Pro, which didn’t get a global release.

Image: Qualcomm

Now that Wi-Fi no longer requires an extra chip, perhaps the idea can take off. Qualcomm says the Elite is also 30 percent smaller, consumes up to 40 percent less power, and has twice the AI processing capabilities of the previous gen chip, all of which should be music to device makers’ ears.

So far, Qualcomm says it’s working with HP on one specific unnamed product, is “working closely with Bose,” and is “pioneering a new category of intelligent hearables” (read: earbuds with built-in cameras) with Cleer.
