snippet: Apple announced this week that creators will soon be able to offer video through Apple Podcasts Subscriptions, “including subscriber-exclusive episodes, ad-free video, early access, and bonus content.” Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple announced this week that creators will soon be able to offer video through Apple Podcasts Subscriptions, “including subscriber-exclusive episodes, ad-free video, early access, and bonus content.” Here are the details.

Apple Podcasts Subscriptions to get support for video

Back in 2021, Apple announced Apple Podcasts Subscriptions. This service lets creators offer paid subscriptions to their shows in exchange for perks such as ad-free listening, bonus episodes, early access, and subscriber-only content.

Since then, creators have been able to offer paid subscriptions through Apple Podcasts to listeners in more than 170 countries and regions.

With the podcast market increasingly shifting toward video, Apple has been expanding the format across its platform.

Earlier this year, Apple introduced a new HLS-based video podcast experience that lets users seamlessly switch between watching and listening, view episodes full-screen, download videos for offline viewing, and more.

More recently, with iOS 27 and its other software updates, Apple expanded video support in Apple Podcasts with features including read-along transcripts, chapters, media links, and playback on Mac and Apple TV.

Now, Apple has announced that video is coming to Apple Podcasts Subscriptions as well.

This means creators will be able to offer subscriber-exclusive video episodes, ad-free video, early access, and bonus video content through the same subscription system currently used for premium audio.

From Apple’s announcement:

Since Apple Podcasts Subscriptions launched, creators have built direct-to-listener businesses around premium audio. Adding video opens new opportunities for you to connect with your audiences and grow your business.

A new way to grow your business: Apple Podcasts Subscriptions already help creators build direct-to-listener businesses around premium audio. With the introduction of video, you have new ways to connect with audiences and expand your business directly on Apple Podcasts.

Streamlined delivery: Deliver both audio and video seamlessly without maintaining separate offerings or workflows.

A familiar Apple experience: Audiences can discover and enjoy premium video across Apple devices and the web, wherever and however they choose to tune in.

Apple says it is currently working with hosting providers to make this integration seamless and will share more details “in the coming months.”

title: Google Maps update shows traffic lights and stop signs at your next turn on Android Auto, more
snippet: Google Maps is rolling out a new update on Android Auto that makes it easier to know what to expect at your next turn, with a visual indicator to show upcoming traffic lights or stop signs. more…
fullText:
Google Maps is rolling out a new update on Android Auto that makes it easier to know what to expect at your next turn, with a visual indicator to show upcoming traffic lights or stop signs.

It’s been around six years since Google Maps started showing traffic lights and stop signs along your route, but a new tweak gives these more relevance to your actual route. Where Maps previously showed these as fixed parts of the map, there’s a new pop-up that shows what to expect at upcoming intersections.

Alongside the floating name of the street at your next turn, Google Maps on Android Auto now also highlights whether you’ll see a traffic light or a stop sign at that intersection. We first observed this behavior earlier this week, and it’s been showing consistently in the time since. It’s also showing on the phone directly, which means iPhone users seeing the update will likely also see this on CarPlay.

It’s a subtle tweak, but it’s also a very glanceable way to give drivers a better idea of what to expect at a coming intersection, which could be invaluable if you’re driving around an unfamiliar area.

	

Like many visual updates, this is likely a server-side update for Google Maps. Let us know in the comments below if you’re seeing this update.

fullText:
Apple Watch Ultra includes a few more ways to customize your watch face than Series models. These include Ultra-only faces, colors and fonts, and a bezel-type complication. Apple Watch Ultra 4 goes even further, adding a new option in the bezel configuration category.

Readiness is a new bezel option on Apple Watch Ultra 4

Both Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduce the new Readiness app. This uses data like fitness activity, vitals, and sleep score to present you with a Readiness score.

Overnight vitals include heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and recovery HRV. Daytime vitals include heart rate and recovery HRV. 

Apple Watch Ultra 4 faces that support displaying bezel information add Readiness as a new watch face configuration. Bezel options now include:

None

Seconds

Depth

Elevation

Training

Readiness

The Readiness bezel option puts your numerical score and description at the bottom of the watch face.

Four bars wrap the edge of the watch face, showing the different readiness score categories, while a dot indicates where your score fits within that category.

Watch faces like Modular Ultra and the new Siri Modular face support displaying the bezel configuration.

If you’re looking for a way to focus on your readiness score, the new bezel configuration is a great way to keep track of the number.

Since readiness can change throughout the day, it may be worth having front-and-center for a lot of users.

Square has announced a new integration with Apple Business that should make Apple Maps better for both businesses and users. Here are the details.

Square integration lets businesses easily keep Apple Maps listings up to date with accurate info

Have you ever been frustrated to learn that an Apple Maps business listing has outdated info? Maybe the listed hours are inaccurate, or it has an error in the address, phone number, and so on.

Square’s new integration with Apple Business should help. From the announcement:

Square today announced a new integration with Apple that enables Square sellers to connect their locations to Apple Business from their Square Dashboard, so they can seamlessly manage and synchronize key business location information that appears on Apple Maps. Rather than managing multiple channels separately, sellers can now maintain their Apple presence alongside the rest of their business in Square. The integration makes it easier for sellers to ensure Apple users see up-to-date and accurate information across Apple Maps, Siri AI, Apple Wallet and other Apple apps.

Per Square, this integration provides several key benefits to business owners. It lets them:

Manage their brand and add a logo across connected locations, allowing them to enhance and extend their brand presence to Apple Maps place cards, directly from Square Dashboard.

Automatically sync key business details for each connected location, such as hours, address, and phone number, so this information stays up-to-date and accurate across Apple Maps, Siri AI, Apple Wallet, and other Apple apps and services without manual updates.

Turn discovery into engagement across connected locations with action links such as Menu, Order, Pickup, Delivery, Book, or Schedule Appointment, so customers can take action directly from an Apple Maps place card.

The partnership sounds like a clear win for businesses, since so many already rely on Square. But it should result in a better Apple Maps experience for users over time too.

title: iOS 27.2 reveals new features coming to Apple Music, CarPlay, more
snippet: iOS 27.2 beta 2 arrived today, and so far seems to have minimal user-facing changes. But code for iOS 27.2’s beta releases points to new features in the works for Apple Music, CarPlay Ultra, and more. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 beta 2 arrived today, and so far seems to have minimal user-facing changes. But code for iOS 27.2’s beta releases points to new features in the works for Apple Music, CarPlay Ultra, and more.

Whenever Apple releases new beta software, we tend to discover changes in two ways: through user-facing features active in the software, as well as underlying code changes that point to forthcoming changes.

With iOS 27.2, there were a variety of new features available for testing from day one, like the all-new Health app, user profiles in Apple TV, Siri AI expansions, and more.

But users skilled at examining the underlying code found even more changes in the works. 

For example, X user pdfu discovered that Apple Music will soon add live countdowns for new album releases.

Another discovery by pdfu in iOS 27.2 beta code involves the Shortcuts app.

Shortcuts’ new ‘Describe a Shortcut’ feature looks like it will soon gain support for including actions from third-party apps.

Describe a Shortcut could soon support actions from third-party developers.

Currently, the feature only supports Apple-developed actions. With a new feature flag in iOS 27.2 and macOS 27.2, the model can now choose actions from third-party apps.

To enable:

sudo mkdir -p… pic.twitter.com/sR6OJMwADy

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 17, 2026

Another noteworthy reveal from iOS 27.2 code involves CarPlay Ultra.

Aaron Perris discovered that code references a ‘Drive Mode Theme’ that changes things like gauge style and color, and even syncs ambient lighting in the vehicle.

iOS 27.2 beta 1 includes text that describes a "Drive Mode Theme" meant for CarPlay Ultra

"This will reset all customizations made to this theme, including gauge style, color, and wallpaper, to defaults."

"Ambient lighting will automatically sync with the color of your current… pic.twitter.com/7g2E5BeCB4

— Aaron (@aaronp613) September 17, 2026

CarPlay Ultra is still limited to only Aston Martin vehicles. But perhaps the addition of new theming features means Apple is about to expand support to another automaker.

We previously reported that iOS 27.2 will add a feature to more thoroughly wipe the data of your iPhone. Today’s beta 2 has more descriptive language on this addition—now called “Extended Erase”—as discovered by Aaron Perris.

Finally, Perris found evidence that Apple may be preparing a demo mode for users of its forthcoming ‘HomePad’ smart home device.

Which of iOS 27.2’s new and upcoming features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more
snippet: Following the May preview, Google today fully announced Googlebooks ahead of the consumer launch in October. more…
fullText:
Following the May preview, Google today fully announced Googlebooks ahead of the consumer launch in October.

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Software

Google’s main pitch is that Googlebooks should be the laptop of choice for those with Android phones:

Today, we often switch between starting tasks on our phones and finishing them on our laptops. To make that experience better for Android users, we teamed up with the best laptop makers in the industry to deliver top-tier hardware alongside Google’s software experience that connects effortlessly with your phone.

Following phones and watches, Material 3 Expressive is coming to desktops. Quick Settings and notifications, which are nearly identical in design to what you’d find on Pixel, can be found in the top-right corner, while you have the time and date at the left. The bottom dock is center-aligned with the ‘G’ opening your app drawer. 

	

Upon signing in to a Googlebook, your Android phone’s settings, saved passwords, Wi-Fi, and messages will appear. Cross-device continuity includes Android 17’s “Continue On” capability and Cast My Apps if you don’t want to install the Android application on your laptop.

Additionally, Google touts a first-class Files app that can show what documents and photos are available on your phone. One good use of on-device AI is automatically generating file descriptions that aid search.

Gemini Intelligence is led by Magic Pointer and the wiggle gesture to bring up Gemini and enter a prompt, like adding dates to your Calendar. There’s also Rambler, like on the Pixel 11 series, to dictate a stream of consciousness, while Create My Widget is billed as letting you “customize your desktop by describing what you need in plain language.”

You get a “desktop-class” Chrome browser with support for extensions, the Gemini side panel, vertical tabs, and more. Most features found on Mac and Windows are available here.

The application story is a combination of Android and the web, with Google noting how 70% of time spent on laptops is in a browser. The company ultimately thinks it is up to developers to choose whether an Android app or the web is better for their application. There is a growing number of desktop-class Android apps, and the Play Store will highlight them with a new badge. 

On the gaming front, 20,000 mobile and PC titles will run on Googlebooks. They are optimized for keyboard, mouse, and touchscreen, with Google’s existing Play Games Level Up program resulting in monthly title launches. For everything else, Google offers a year of Nvidia GeForce Now.

For developers, Google very notably created an Antigravity app for Googlebooks that offers a native UI and interacts with the Linux environment. You can also install the Linux version of Antigravity if you wish, along with Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. For Android app development, Antigravity allows you to deploy directly to the Googlebook.

Under the hood, Google is integrating the multi-window performance and full browser capabilities of ChromeOS with a native Android stack that offers power and battery efficiency.

On the security front, Google touts the same security architecture as ChromeOS. There’s a Google Titan security chip and on-device malware detection. Additionally, a Level 5 security-certified hypervisor powered by pKVM isolation allows for the isolated Linux environment with full terminal access. This lets you “safely run any Linux developer tools, pull code repositories, access networks and the ports, or execute autonomous agents.”

Googlebooks get 10 years of automatic updates with quarterly feature drops similar to Pixel.

Hardware

On the hardware front, there are five flagship Googlebooks at launch, with Google mandating several key specs across the lineup. All devices are powered by Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with NPUs (40+ TOPS). As such, Googlebook OS is optimized for ARM and x86, with MediaTek-powered devices coming in the future.

There’s a baseline of 16 GB of RAM with 32 GB variants available. All have a touchscreen with up to 2.8K LCD or OLED. Devices have up to six speakers with Dolby Atmos surround sound and “studio-quality, background noise-canceling” microphones.

Googlebooks are made from “premium materials” like aluminum, magnesium, or carbon fiber.

There are also backlit keyboards and large glass trackpads with haptic feedback and support for gestures. Google touts up to 14 hours of video playback and 16 hours of web browsing.

Finally, all devices have a Glowbar on the cover that lights up in the Google colors when you open and close the lid. When you plug in a charger, there’s a current charge level indicator and “playful” animation when you talk to Gemini. Notably (unlike Pixel Glow), third-party apps can access it to “build custom, interactive animations.”

title: Nexterity wants to automate the hard, dangerous part of pipefitting
snippet: The startup's robot can tighten or loosen four bolts at a time, and it fits in a Pelican case.
fullText:
Lindsey Elliott is big into bolts. At last year’s Bolting Symposium — the 13th annual — she said the highlight was playing Bolting Bingo against the many self-proclaimed “torque dorks” who were in the room.

A former engineer and planner at ExxonMobil, Elliott has spent years thinking about how to improve the infrastructure that moves oil, gas, and petrochemicals. Bolts are what she landed on. Specifically, the bolts that connect sections of pipe (technically called “bolted flange joints”). These bolts require hard, physical work to loosen and tighten and are the source of many pipefitters’ injuries. Like many trade industries, there’s also a labor shortage.

“Those people get really tired when they’re asked to work 12 hours a day for three months in a row,” she told TechCrunch. “I’ve talked to pipefitters across the U.S., across Canada, and just repeatedly have been told North American pipefitting productivity is notoriously low.”

The solution Elliott came up with at her startup Nexterity, which is one of the Startup Battlefield 200 selected to participate in TechCrunch Disrupt, is a remote-controlled robot that can handle this part of the job. It’s the kind of idea that could fundamentally change this particular blue-collar job if widely adopted, making the workers safer and more productive.

Think: more dork, less torque.

The robot comes in two main pieces that fit around a pipe. Powered by batteries, the robot can slide across the pipe once it’s attached and quickly loosen and tighten four bolts at a time. 

Elliott said Nexterity has developed a few different configurations of the robot to fit different standard pipe sizes, but they’re all small enough to fit in a Pelican case and be carried by a single worker. That makes them easy to deploy to new sites — flexibility that is crucial to Nexterity’s business model of treating the robot like rental construction equipment.

Elliott said she arrived at this particular design as a result of conversations she’s had over the last few years — not just at the Bolting Symposium, but also with members of the Pressure Vessels & Piping Division of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers.

“What I learned from the people, the torque dorks per se,” she said, “is that 80% of our pipes are between two to eight inches in diameter, or what they call NPS2 to NPS8. And so when you have that much repeatability, you have a fantastic candidate for automation.” 

It’s a pretty straightforward idea, but one that Elliott believes has a lot of upside. 

“I think it would shock a lot of people just how big this market is,” she said. “I mean, day to day, most of us don’t think about piping infrastructure, but even water, wastewater, water treatment, food and beverage, mining, nuclear, any kind of green and sustainable manufacturing facility — they all use the same kind of piping.” 

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

		

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

You can contact or verify outreach from Sean by emailing sean.okane@techcrunch.com or via encrypted message at okane.01 on Signal.

title: New Mac mini drops support for aftermarket storage upgrades
snippet: When Apple released the M4 Mac mini two years ago, teardowns quickly revealed a pleasant surprise: the internal SSD was not soldered to the logic board. This allowed for aftermarket storage upgrades, and we even showed you how to do it. With the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini updates, however, it appears the storage is soldered to the logic board once again. more…
fullText:
When Apple released the M4 Mac mini two years ago, teardowns quickly revealed a pleasant surprise: the internal SSD was not soldered to the logic board. This allowed for aftermarket storage upgrades, and we even showed you how to do it.

With the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini updates, however, it appears the storage is soldered to the logic board once again.

New Mac mini takes a step backward with soldered storage

In a blog post, the folks at Expand Mac mini revealed that the NAND is soldered to the logic board, similar to the M1 and M2 versions of the Mac mini. This means the SSD module is no longer removable.

Expand Mac mini sells storage upgrade modules for the M4 and M4 Pro versions of the Mac mini. As it stands right now, however, they say that “support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely.”

No slot means nothing to swap, and very little room left for us. In August we said we would extend our coverage once we had tested real hardware. This is the result, and not the one we hoped for.

We will keep looking for an opening, but support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely. If that changes, you will hear it here first.

For comparison’s sake, Expand Mac mini’s 1TB SSD expansion module for the M4 Mac mini costs $300. Apple charges $500 to upgrade the M6 Mac mini from 256GB to 1TB. Expand Mac mini’s 2TB module costs $420, while Apple charges $1,000 for the upgrade.

As for the Mac Studio, Apple’s repair guide still shows removable SSDs. We haven’t spotted any teardowns yet confirming that information.

title: Apple Pay just got even better with four new features and more
snippet: Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now. more…
fullText:
Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now. 

New design in iOS 27

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone. 

American Express rewards

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a new “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

Reload debit cards

iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

Bonus: Apple Pay at Walmart 

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.  

Walmart started rolling out Apple Pay (and broader contactless support) this week in Arkansas. The retailer says it launch for all stores in the United States by the end of this year. 

Wrap up

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

Apple today announced that Tap to Pay on iPhone is now available in eight additional Latin American countries, with support from six payment platforms across the region. Here are the details.

Tap to Pay on iPhone expands to eight new countries

In an update published to its Latin America and the Caribbean Newsroom, Apple announced today an expansion of Tap to Pay on iPhone across Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, and Peru.

Tap to Pay on iPhone allows merchants to accept in-person contactless payments using only a compatible iPhone and supported payment app, without the need for additional card readers or payment terminals.

Here’s the list of countries and payment platforms gaining support today:

Argentina: Mercado Pago

Colombia: SumUp, Symbiotic

Guatemala: Geopagos, Symbiotic

Panama: Geopagos, Symbiotic

Peru: SumUp

Apple also noted that Tap to Pay on iPhone “is compatible with contactless debit and credit cards from major payment networks, including American Express, Mastercard, and Visa.”

Apple originally announced Tap to Pay on iPhone on February 8, 2022. It was initially announced for the United States, with Stripe as the first payment platform set to support it.

Since then, it has expanded to 59 countries and regions, with Apple’s current list naming more than 100 payment service providers worldwide, including today’s additions.

snippet: If you’ve been missing the double-click of the Digital Crown that used to bring up the App Switcher on the Apple Watch before watchOS 27, it looks like the feature is making a comeback as of watchOS 27.2 beta 2. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
If you’ve been missing the double-click of the Digital Crown that used to bring up the App Switcher on the Apple Watch before watchOS 27, it looks like the feature is making a comeback as of watchOS 27.2 beta 2. Here are the details.

Apple working to bring watchOS App Switcher back

Earlier today, Apple rolled out watchOS 27.2 beta 2 for developers, less than a week after releasing beta 1.

Included in today’s beta is a tidbit that will likely please longtime Apple Watch users, including my colleague Zac Hall. Earlier this month, he wrote about how watchOS 27 had removed the ability to quickly switch between recently used apps by double-clicking the Digital Crown.

In his piece, he noted that there was no longer any way to quickly jump between recent apps, and wished Apple would restore the gesture before releasing watchOS 27, or in a future update.

While Apple didn’t bring back the App Switcher’s Digital Crown shortcut in today’s watchOS 27.2 beta 2, it did restore the App Switcher itself with a new gesture.

As spotted by the Apple Den Discord server and shared by user Bones on X, watchOS 27.2 beta 2 lets users press and hold the bottom of the screen while inside an app to bring up the App Switcher.

Apple has brought back the App Switcher!

On watchOS 26 and earlier, you could access the App Switcher by double-clicking the Digital Crown, then turning the Digital Crown to navigate through your recently used apps. You could also swipe left on an app and tap the "X" button to… pic.twitter.com/G5fa0TeTR9

— 𝓑𝓸𝓷𝓮𝓼 (@limpless_skelly) September 22, 2026

As Bones noted in their tweet, the App Switcher otherwise works much like it did before: after activating the App Switcher with a long press on the bottom of the screen, users can turn the Digital Crown to scroll through recently used apps, or swipe left on an app and tap the “X” button to remove it from the switcher.

While, like with any beta, there is no guarantee that this exact interaction will make it into the final release (likely to come next month), its addition in watchOS 27.2 beta 2 suggests that Apple is listening to user feedback and looking for a way to bring the App Switcher back.

title: iOS 27.2 beta 2 reveals new details about unnanounced iPhone anti-snatching feature
snippet: Apple continues to work on a feature that automatically locks an iPhone when it detects that the device has been snatched from its owner’s hand. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple continues to work on a feature that automatically locks an iPhone when it detects that the device has been snatched from its owner’s hand. Here are the details.

Apple still working on iPhone anti-snatching feature

Earlier this year, 9to5Mac first reported that Apple was working on a new iPhone security feature that can automatically lock the device when it detects that it has been snatched from the user’s hand.

While Apple has yet to officially announce the feature, new references included in iOS 27.2 beta 2 show the company is still actively developing it.

According to new code seen today by 9to5Mac, the feature, which is called “AutoLock” internally, can use the following signals to determine whether an iPhone may have been taken from its owner:

A sharp acceleration consistent with the phone being snatched;

A paired Apple Watch remaining unreachable for a certain period;

Loss of connectivity to a paired Apple Watch;

Prolonged loss of network connectivity;

The device remaining unlocked beyond a certain interval.

Additionally, new references include safeguards meant to prevent false positives, such as successful biometric authentication, certain foreground app activities that could otherwise be mistaken for signs that the device has been taken, and a backoff mechanism that can temporarily suppress further automatic locks after repeated lock events.

The code also suggests AutoLock uses a voting system in which a potential theft signal can request a lock, while safeguards such as biometrics, familiar locations, or certain app activities can veto it.

These new details add to the references already present in the code, including a location-based safeguard similar to Stolen Device Protection that accounts for whether the iPhone is in a familiar place.

It is worth noting that the feature is still under development and is not currently enabled or available as a user-facing option in iOS 27.2 beta 2. Rather, Apple has enabled the underlying AutoLock service in the background, while keeping the component that actually locks the iPhone disabled, possibly as a way to test the underlying behavior without actually triggering automatic locks.

This means that, for now, the new references only provide a look at Apple’s progress in developing the feature. Whether or when it will ultimately launch remains up to Apple.

We've examined tvOS 27.2 beta 2 and the rumored 4x HomePod wireless surround pairing with Apple TV 4K is now implemented, as shown below.

However, it's not yet fully baked, as there is currently no way to assign roles to each HomePod pair, i.e. front and rear speakers. It works… https://t.co/cufeJwx0PQ pic.twitter.com/IG3uqH32NU

— FlatpanelsHD (@Flatpanels) September 23, 2026

As seen in the screenshot above, the Apple TV 4K running tvOS 27.2 is configured to send audio to four HomePods total—two full-size models and two HomePod minis.

More details are shared by Rasmus Larsen on FlatpanelsHD’s website:

Via the Home app, you can now pair two sets of HomePods, four in total, wirelessly to Apple TV 4K. However, the feature is not yet fully baked, as you cannot assign roles to the four speakers, for example rear speakers – they play the same audio from the front and rear. It works with Atmos and surround sound from video sources, but menu and game audio only plays through the front speakers.

It’s been widely rumored for some time that Apple is working on a big overhaul and expansion of its Home product line. A new ‘HomePad’ device along with new Apple TV 4K and HomePod models are expected to launch in October.

Surround sound could be a great addition for HomePod and Apple TV users. But it’s also likely a good sign that Apple will indeed launch new Home products soon.

fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m bumping to Carly Rae Jepsen’s new double album (it’s great!), wishing I had more kidneys so I could afford the new M5 Ultra Mac Studio, marveling at Astra’s ability to decrypt 100-year-old WWI cyphers, and counting down the days until I can play Control Resonant.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

I’ve been covering Google’s multifarious hardware endeavors for nearly 20 years, from the early days of Nexus phones through this week’s Googlebook unveiling, and I see a few important parallels. Google has always wanted to assert some measure of control over the user experience, but that amount has ebbed and flowed depending on where its product sits in the funnel. 

	

The early days of Android were about growth, which meant leveraging established players like LG, Samsung, Huawei, and others to build its hardware while promulgating a free and open-source operating system that quickly supplanted giants like Nokia and Microsoft.

Alongside Android, Google nurtured Chrome OS (which later became, confusingly, ChromeOS) as its laptop (and occasional desktop) operating system, that, like Android, became synonymous with cheap-and-cheerful hardware, particularly in schools. And while Google did the work to rid itself of that budget reputation on the phone side (though, arguably, Samsung did the bulk of the heavy lifting), it never really managed to do the same on ChromeOS despite numerous attempts to build premium hardware.

Now, ChromeOS is being replaced by Googlebook, and its main appeal is quite simple to understand: “Hey premium Android users, we see you. Here’s a product that can bring you Apple users’ ecosystem benefits while retaining the openness and diversity of Android.”

A few questions jump to mind when I hear that:

Yes, there are billions of Android users out there, but are enough of them clamoring for ecosystem unity to replace their existing laptops in order to entwine their lives even further with Google?

Is that ecosystem unity actually additive in the same way that Apple has proven with iOS and macOS, or will it be more like the way Microsoft has tried to harmonize Android and iOS devices with Windows?

Will the legacy of Google killing off seemingly healthy products turn people away from Googlebooks?

Is this objectively the worst time to launch a new hardware brand?

Also interesting is that Google’s own hardware is absent from this ecosystem launch. Like Chromebooks before them, Googlebooks will be made by familiar companies like Lenovo, Dell, Acer, and ASUS, with internals from Intel, Qualcomm, and soon AMD — another reminder that Google is playing a very particular role here, that of software and AI vendor.

That Gemini Intelligence integration, which has been teased from the start of the Googlebook announcement, is another differentiator not only from macOS and Windows, but also from Chromebooks. Google is positioning the Googlebook as the best place to interact with Gemini, whose increasingly agentic aspirations now tap into every corner of Google’s product lineup. But it’s also appealing to developers and vibe-coders alike with a native Antigravity app and 12 months of Google AI Pro, a subscription that comes with a substantial amount of coding credit.

So is a Googlebook for Android users who want to code? Is it for fans of ChromeOS who want more integration with their phones? Is it for the Android faithful, the diehards who have been waiting patiently for their turn in the ecosystem sun? 

We don’t have long to wait: Googlebooks hit the market early next month.

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Kevin Michaluk, Clicks co-founder and former BlackBerry superuser.

Who are you?

Kevin Michaluk aka @crackberrykevin / CBK

What do you do for work?

How It Started: Founder at CrackBerry.com & Mobile Nations (spent 15 years in tech media); How It’s Going: Founder & President at Clicks Technology.

What do you do for fun?

Depends on the season! This summer picked up golf again (my obsession in my teenage years) and pickleball for the first time. I spend so much time working that some physical activities out of the house/office and away from screens for a few hours a week feels like a necessity for my mental and physical health.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

More intentional than ever. I wrote the first book on Smartphone Addiction back in 2008 and have been more acutely aware than most of the detrimental effects on individuals and society that smartphones, social media and tech can have. That’s part of the reason we launched Clicks in 2024 and Communicator this year. We’re building purpose built tech that helps people restore some of that balance with tech by building tools that respect their time. It’s not about being overly restrictive, but building experiences that people love and ideally lead to a healthier relationship with their tech. 

What are a few apps you can’t live without and why?

Whoop – I’ve had an on again / off again with fitness trackers over the years and have literally used them all… but this past year have grown to really love and rely on my Whoop. I jive more with their use of recovery score and strain goals over step count goals or trying to close rings, and I like that they have accessories to wear the tracker in. Sleeping with a ring or band on my wrist annoys me and ruins my sleep – with Whoop I literally own several pairs of their “Whoop underwear” that I put the tracker in and wear to bed. And as a guy who loves wearing real watches, I just don’t like wearing a smartwatch on my wrist that could be better occupied by a mechanical watch. And even Whoop’s new AI Chat feature I use more than I thought I would… it’s come in real handy for when I’m traveling internationally and trying to map out the best sleep and workout schedules to help me balance the time zone changes.

Shopify – I mean, when you’re building a company and one of your biggest sales channels is DTC, it’s hard not to spend a LOT of time in Shopify. 

TOP SECRET – No, that’s not the name of the app… but ask me about it again in early 2027 and I’ll share the details on the newest app I’m using that I actually can’t live without. It’s changed my life – I can’t imagine not having it on my phone. I’m not allowed to talk about it right now, but as an early private beta user can’t wait for others to start using it too! 

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Clicks Communicator, obviously!

What’s a recent song or album you loved?

My song of the summer was literally Summer on the Inside by warner case. Puts me in a good mood whenever it comes on 😉 

What’s a recent TV show you loved?

Reacher… cuz.. Reacher.

What’s a recent book you loved?

Grow by Mike Fata. Written by a local and successful Winnipeg-based entrepreneur and friend of mine (who I like to golf and/or drink Chianti with!), and it’s just an easy and motivating read for founders, whether aspiring or already in the thick of it.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

Watched MayDay on a whim (had no expectations when I hit play) and laughed a bunch. Ryan Reynolds meets Top Gun vibes.

What’s a recent game you loved?

Building Clicks! I think of business as a Team Sport. Every day is like a new match – with a new challenge or opportunity presented and you play with your teammates to try and win the day. I love the people I work (err…play?!) with and while it is a lot of work, it’s also a ton of fun.  (Ed. I’ll allow it.)

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Hanging with my wife and dog… don’t ask me which I love more! 😃

Thank you, Kevin, for reminding me that you can always turn onions into lemonade.

title: iOS 27 lets you create your own custom iPhone wallpapers
snippet: Apple introduces new iPhone wallpapers every year, and you can download iOS 27’s additions here. But iOS 27 also adds the ability to create your own custom wallpapers. Here’s how. more…
fullText:
Apple introduces new iPhone wallpapers every year, and you can download iOS 27’s additions here. But iOS 27 also adds the ability to create your own custom wallpapers. Here’s how.

Here’s how you can create custom wallpapers in iOS 27

This year as part of iOS 27’s overall theme of major AI improvements, Apple has given its Image Playground app an overhaul.

Image Playground now offers more powerful image generation capabilities and far fewer restrictions than before. It even lets you create images that are the perfect wallpaper size.

But you don’t even need to open the Image Playground app to create wallpapers.

iOS 27 lets you create your own iPhone wallpapers right from the wallpaper picker.

Go to Settings ⇾ Wallpaper ⇾ Add New Wallpaper or long-press your Lock Screen and hit the ‘+’ button to open iOS 27’s wallpaper gallery.

New in the gallery this year, you’ll see Image Playground as an option in the top row. iOS 27 also automatically adds some AI-generated images to the Featured wallpaper section.

For example, you’ll see suggested wallpapers that are based on your own photos, but in a new style. 

In my testing of iOS 27, with no effort on my part, my iPhone prepared beautifully stylized versions of some of my favorite photos that look great as wallpapers.

Wherever you see an AI-generated wallpaper in the gallery, Apple’s new Image Playground icon appears next to it. That way, it’s always clear where the image came from.

If you like one of Apple’s suggested AI wallpapers, you can choose it and be all set.

But iOS 27 also lets you create fully custom wallpapers by hitting the Image Playground button in the top row. Image Playground will ask you to describe your image, and let you optionally choose a style or base it on an existing photo or person.

When the image is created, it’s automatically the perfect size for an iPhone wallpaper.

title: Googlebooks will get full GeForce Now support ‘later this year’
snippet: Nvidia says Google’s new Gemini-infused laptops are slated to get GeForce Now support before the year is up, which is perfect because Googlebooks don’t exactly pack a ton of power. more…
fullText:
Nvidia says Google’s new Gemini-infused laptops are slated to get GeForce Now support before the year is up, which is perfect because Googlebooks don’t exactly pack a ton of power.

The entire Googlebook line was officially announced on September 21, spanning across Acer, Dell, ASUS, HP, and Lenovo. Each has its own draw, but they share the same baseline 16GB of RAM, up to 32GB. Each is equipped with a touchscreen and made from “premium materials,” and they genuinely look great. What qualifies as “premium” ranges from aluminum to carbon fiber. Of course, each has the instantly iconic Glowbar somewhere on the cover, flashing when the laptop is opened or closed.

In essence, Googlebooks run Android, for better or worse. Googlebook OS is almost a parallel operating system, but it and mobile Android go hand-in-hand by design. By nature, that means Google didn’t intend to pack these with discrete graphics cards that could power most games. But that’s why GeForce Now exists, right?

Nvidia announced that GeForce Now would be coming to Googlebooks in an official capacity before the year is up. The original statement only specifies it will arrive “later this year,” which leaves a gap of around three months.

	

That doesn’t mean GeForce Now won’t work with Googlebooks when they become available in October. Google Chrome and even Firefox now support GeForce Now natively through the browser. That means logging into the game streaming website will present a similar experience to a fully dedicated Googlebook app.

Still, an app will likely be a better experience tailored to the hardware outfit Google and its partners pack into the new laptops.

This was expected for a couple of reasons. Google has partnered with Nvidia in the past, and Chromebooks were one of the main targets for GeForce Now in the early days. On top of that, when Googlebooks were first shown off, the majority of titles seen were via GeForce Now and not running on native hardware.

GeForce Now also announced today that a slew of new titles are getting support this week:

Stick It to the Stickman

title: Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]
snippet: After a protracted wait, the first wave of Googlebooks is now official. Having spent a brief period testing, here’s what it’s like to use one. more…
fullText:
After a protracted wait, the first wave of Googlebooks is now official. Having spent a brief period testing, here’s what it’s like to use one.

I didn’t quite spend as much time with the software as my colleague Abner, so for a full set of impressions on these laptops running Googlebook OS, please read his extensive thoughts. This is a little more focused on the hardware side, with a sprinkle of software.

The good news right up top: My initial worries have almost completely been washed away, save a few minor complaints about two specific devices; there’s more here to like than I ever expected. Notice I said “almost” as there are still concerns in the back of my mind, but despite lots of, I guess, negativity surrounding and preceding this launch, the entire lineup of Googlebooks has exceeded my fairly low expectations.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

I do believe that this is largely due to my mixed experience with various Chromebooks across the entire price spectrum, combined with the ultimately lackluster or barebones “Desktop mode” that was added to Pixel devices over the past year.

This time, we have fewer SKUs to deal with, and of the five Googlebook devices, there appear to be fewer pinch points – save the pricing. These are not going to be cheap, with prices “starting at” $899 and, in most cases, are going to be more expensive. That is likely where a portion of you are going to stop reading and just dismiss these entirely. I can completely understand why.

Without glossing over or forgiving the frankly inflated asking price, I do believe this comes with one distinct benefit. There is less compromise in quality, which is something that worried me, given the mixed history of Chromebooks and the pitfalls of the cheapest model becoming the flag-bearer for the “default” experience.

I spent around 45 minutes prodding and poking the lineup, and there are two standouts.

Right off the bat, the Dell XPS and the HP Googlebook were the most impressive launch devices here. That said, each of the five laptops has its own merits.

ASUS’ Googlebook, Lenovo’s Googlebook 15, and Acer’s Googlebook 14 offer, in my opinion, are marginally lesser but still fairly decent takes on the first wave of hardware. The Lenovo in particular takes some design cues from previous Chromebooks and pairs with a bright HDR display. It was really easy to see despite lots of glare and jostling in the testing area.

I will state that I am personally not a fan of 2-in-1 laptops, but Googlebook OS, as it’s being styled, just turns the Acer model into arguably the best touchscreen laptop-tablet hybrid on the market. In fact, all of these laptops have excellent touchscreens that run at 120Hz. I was worried ahead of time that we’d get 60Hz screens, so it was very good to see a baseline of 120Hz.

Windows and ChromeOS have always struggled with touch inputs, while MacOS doesn’t allow for user interface control with your hands – or stylus. How many elite touchscreen experiences exist on a laptop? I wager until now, none. This is where Android, in my opinion, is being leveraged in the potentially best way possible. Swipes, taps, prods, it’s all just like using your phone or a tablet.

Just dipping back into a specific device in the lineup for a second, the matte display on the Acer Googlebook 14 was a great touch. It just eliminated glare almost entirely and reminded me of the recently released iPhone Duo. My only gripe was that it was covered in greasy fingerprints and smudges after a few minutes of usage.

Lenovo, ASUS, and Acer are utilizing Intel Core Ultra “Pantherlake” chips, while Dell and HP are going with the Snapdragon X Elite chipset. All come with at least 16GB of RAM for optimal performance. Some SKUs might offer up to 32GB of RAM, but my session made no mention of storage capacities, and there is no way to expand storage using external storage like a microSD card. There could be a really easy way to get people onside by offering these in future SKUs; for now, it’s business as usual.

More good news: The performance is excellent. Every Googlebook felt especially snappy. These are desktop-level chips running Android, which sort of is to be expected.

If anything, I was shocked at how responsive the experience was. It helps that each device has almost identical specifications. You can pick the laptop that suits your specific needs and still expect performance parity. Given my trepidation due to how Chromebooks have been treated by OEMs, this was very refreshing. It’s a good sign right at launch, but let’s hope Google holds more cards this time to almost force device makers to hit base specifications once cheaper models arrive.

The touchpads on all of the models are genuinely impressive. There’s some level of haptics, but MacBooks still reign supreme here. Every keyboard felt tight and responsive, and I liked stabbing away at the keys however briefly. None of the five models felt mushy or squishy under my fingers, and the layouts were instantly familiar to my battle-worn MacBook Pro battered fingertips. I didn’t have too long to test out the two unique keyboard G and odd Caps Lock keys, but they’ll no doubt take a while to get used to if you’re coming from Windows or Mac.

We saw ahead of launch that the lightbar is a key branding differentiator on the Googlebook. Sure, it looks nice, but it didn’t seem to do much beyond, well, look kind of cool. Google is planning on opening this LED strip up to developers in the coming months, so I’m sure we’ll get various takes on notifications, DND mode, and more that I probably haven’t thought of.

Correction: XPS laptops have been sold under the “Project Sputnik” banner with Ubuntu pre-installed in a partnership with Canonical that has been in place since 2012 and has become part of the Dell XPS Developer Edition series. Mostly focused on developers, the following incorrect statement has been removed, but is kept for posterity. Apologies for any confusion caused.

Something that I hope isn’t missed here is that the XPS Googlebook from Dell is the first such laptop from the company to come without Windows pre-installed. I think, given how mediocre the Dell Chromebook line was, this feels like a real statement of intent for a product line that is widely heralded as the best alternative to a MacBook. The company wouldn’t stake the XPS line on a mediocre product. It’s a gorgeous small-form-factor laptop, and one I really hope to spend some extended time with soon.

Can Android fill in the gap Chromebooks leave behind?

There are so many question marks over the Googlebook lineup, most notably who the platform is going to suit best or how it’ll fit into someone’s existing computing lineup. Some will ship with HDMI ports; there’s no room for a single SD card slot, or at least one that I remember spotting. I’d love to know what the experience is like using a secondary display or taking that experience elsewhere.

I feel like the software is much better than I had anticipated for a launch product. Yes, we’re missing a few top-level professional tools, but the full desktop Chrome browser might dispel some pre-launch detractors. I installed an extension I use every day, and it wanted to track my cashback while I was visiting a few of my favorite online shopping haunts. That reduced some of my initial fears of mobile Chrome on a laptop form factor.

What I cannot fault is the launch hardware. It is solid.

I went in with some preconceptions likely based on some of the leaks and, I’ll be honest, a mediocre unveil during the Android Show earlier this year. The devices have done a lot of the talking, which is an interesting prospect, as they already feel like a fluid expansion of Android into a new form factor.

Right now, I am likely not the target market. I need certain pieces of software, but ask yourself: do you have one key piece of software that is locking you into your current laptop or tablet? If that is the case, you probably were never looking at making a switch to a new desktop platform on launch day anyway.

My overriding early thought is that a Googlebook is an option for someone who has no allegiance to a desktop OS, but has a strong urge for their phone to expand into a bigger, more competent portable display. That might be a tiny portion of the market, but it could also be huge given that many people still use a phone for 95% of their day-to-day tasks. I don’t have a crystal ball or next week’s lottery numbers, but we have a new operating system to choose from, and I can’t be too negative about it. Any challengers to Windows, Mac, or Linux are good in my book. We just need things to start moving fast right out of the gate.

I think back to the early era of the smartphone. I imagined being able to take my phone, plug it into a screen, and have access to everything I need or use most. If that really worked, we’d all be using Samsung DeX, but we’re all still using separate laptops and desktops instead.

The modern smartphone is a hub for payments, photos, emails, entertainment, and the “right hand” of most people. Here’s what is different: The Googlebook takes your Android phone and turns it into a laptop. Whether you want it is ultimately up to you.

title: U.S. government urges Supreme Court to reverse Apple contempt ruling over App Store commission
snippet: Several legal and business groups, in addition to the U.S. government, filed briefs with the Supreme Court this week in the Apple vs. Epic Games lawsuit, urging the justices to reverse at least part of the contempt ruling against Apple. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Several legal and business groups, in addition to the U.S. government, filed briefs with the Supreme Court this week in the Apple vs. Epic Games lawsuit, urging the justices to reverse at least part of the contempt ruling against Apple. Here are the details.

A bit of context

In late June, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear Apple’s argument that a civil contempt ruling against the company should be reversed in its fight against Epic Games.

In essence, when Apple was compelled to allow developers to direct users to external purchasing options, the company did so while imposing a 27% commission on those transactions. When Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, the district court found the company in civil contempt.

Apple has been allowing developers to link to external purchasing options without charging a commission ever since.

Since then, the company has been trying to reverse that ruling, arguing that the actual text of the injunction did not prohibit it from charging a commission, and that lower courts improperly relied on the “spirit of the injunction” to find the company in contempt.

For reference, the original order read:

Apple Inc. and its officers, agents, servants, employees, and any person in active concert or participation with them (“Apple”), are hereby permanently restrained and enjoined from prohibiting developers from (i) including in their apps and their metadata buttons, external links, or other calls to action that direct customers to purchasing mechanisms, in addition to In-App Purchasing and (ii) communicating with customers through points of contact obtained voluntarily from customers through account registration within the app.

Last week, Apple filed its official opening merits brief with the Supreme Court, arguing once again that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not clearly prohibit the company from charging a commission on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its briefing, Apple also argued that allowing the contempt finding to stand would increase the risk of judicial overreach when courts enforce injunctions, leaving companies uncertain about what conduct an order actually prohibits.

U.S. government and other groups weigh in

While Epic Games has until November 13 to file its response, the court this week received a number of amicus briefs (filings from outside interested parties) from the U.S. Department of Justice, through the Solicitor General’s office, along with several legal and business groups weighing in on Apple’s challenge.

In its amicus brief, the Department of Justice argues that “[c]ivil contempt is […] appropriate only if the defendant’s conduct is clearly covered by the injunction’s express terms,” which it says was not the case with Apple’s decision to charge a 27% commission.

It goes on to echo Apple’s argument that civil contempt is improper whenever there is a “fair ground of doubt” as to whether an injunction actually prohibited the conduct at issue, concluding that the Supreme Court “should reverse the contempt finding as to the 27% commission.”

In the same brief, however, the Department of Justice says the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over its “plain button” restriction, arguing that the injunction clearly required Apple to permit both buttons and links, while Apple’s implementation effectively allowed only links.

On the remaining issues, such as restrictions on where external purchase links could appear, the Department of Justice says the Supreme Court should set aside the existing rulings and send them back to the lower courts to be reconsidered under the “fair ground of doubt” standard.

In addition to the Department of Justice, the Supreme Court also received amicus briefs from:

The Chamber of Commerce of the United States

Chamber of Progress

Former Federal Antitrust Enforcers

International Center for Law and Economics (ICLE)

Computer & Communications Industry Association, NetChoice, and Software & Information Industry Association

Washington Legal Foundation (WLF)

In short, they all support the general argument that Apple could not properly be held in civil contempt for conduct that the injunction did not clearly prohibit, and that courts should enforce injunctions based on their actual terms rather than their perceived “spirit.”

The ICLE adds that “choosing a profitable way to comply is still compliance,” while the Former Federal Antitrust Enforcers cited past precedent to argue that having judges determine what commission Apple may charge “is precisely the type of ‘direct price administration’ that ‘antitrust courts normally avoid.’”

Currently, proceedings are underway in the district court to determine how much, if any, commission Apple may charge on linked-out purchases, while the Supreme Court reviews the contempt ruling itself.

title: iPhone Duo video shows left-handed use for new model
snippet: iPhone Duo is less than a month away, but many prospective buyers are still wondering how well the device will work in left-handed use. Here’s a video that shows a left-handed example. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is less than a month away, but many prospective buyers are still wondering how well the device will work in left-handed use. Here’s a video that shows a left-handed example.

Here’s how iPhone Duo works in left-handed use

If you’re left-handed, the iPhone Duo may be exciting but also spark some questions. That’s because the new foldable is clearly designed for right-handed use primarily.

When using the outer display, iPhone Duo’s left side is one straight flat edge because it’s where the hinge is. But the right side has curved corners, inviting you to open it like a book.

The dock is also located on the right side of the display, and Apple hasn’t said if an accessibility setting will let you move it to the left.

So how will left-handed users fare with the iPhone Duo? 

Since everyone’s hand size is different, testing the device in an Apple Store will be the only way to know for sure. But I recently came across a video of iPhone Duo being used left-handed, and it’s the first time I’ve seen someone try it.

Here’s the video from Tom Hitchins (@bytereview) on Instagram:

Hitchins looks a little uncomfortable with the device, but as he explains in the comments, that’s because he’s actually right-handed. Thus, his left-handed test was for others’ sake.

The video says “works well enough” as Hitchins is able to reach from the left side all the way to the dock on the right. But you’ll want to test yourself to be sure.

I’m right-handed, but use my iPhone in my left hand so that my dominant hand is kept free. I suspect there are plenty of other right-handed users who do the same. So I’m a little unsure about the adjustment to using iPhone Duo in my right hand, but will report back once I’m able to test it.

title: Apple Wallet in iOS 27 adds feature that’s been on my wishlist for years
snippet: iOS 27 adds a variety of new features and changes for Apple Wallet, including one that’s been on my wishlist for years: the ability to import physical passes. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds a variety of new features and changes for Apple Wallet, including one that’s been on my wishlist for years: the ability to import physical passes.

iOS 27 lets you import physical passes, membership cards, event tickets into Apple Wallet

Apple Wallet offers a host of features to help you replace your physical wallet and keys.

It holds credit cards, driver’s licenses, transit cards, boarding passes, event tickets, car keys, home keys, hotel keys, and more.

And with iOS 27, the Wallet app takes another big step toward being the only wallet you need.

That’s because you can now import physical passes, tickets, membership cards, and the like into Apple Wallet.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:

iPhone and Apple Watch users will be able to create and store passes in Apple Wallet from physical cards, like loyalty or membership cards, eliminating the need to fumble through pockets and bags. With Siri mode in the Camera app, users simply point their iPhone at any physical card with a barcode or even screenshot a digital one, and they’ll be prompted to save it to Apple Wallet. Users can also create and add a pass directly from Apple Wallet. Once added, passes are ready to present as a barcode or QR code right from their iPhone or Apple Watch.

Digital passes are a lot more common today than when Apple Wallet first launched. But they aren’t available for everything.

I definitely still encounter businesses and events that utilize physical passes exclusively. And when I do, it adds a little anxiety to my life because I then need to remember to bring those passes with me at the right time.

But with iOS 27, everything can start going in the Wallet app, which is always with me. By putting everything in Wallet, the mental burden of remembering to bring something extra is suddenly gone.

title: Waymo is scaling fast: Here’s what the fleet data shows
snippet: In the past month, Waymo has expanded its fleet in Texas by 49%. There are other hot spots as well.
fullText:
Waymo’s commercial robotaxi ramp-up looks expansive, both in geographic reach and in ridership. And by almost every measure, it is — until you pay attention to where the bulk of those robotaxis are actually showing up.

The numbers over the past two years reflect the kind of commercial rollout you’d expect from a deep-pocketed company like Waymo, which spun out of Google and still counts Alphabet as its majority owner. In September 2024, Waymo was operating in just three cities — Phoenix, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. Today, it offers robotaxi service in 15 U.S. cities, with most of those commercial launches occurring in the past year. Ridership has skyrocketed, too, with Waymo now averaging 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week.

But a closer look at its fleet shows a company concentrating its efforts in just two states. About 80% of Waymo’s roughly 4,000 robotaxis are in California and Texas, and Texas is where the action is now: Waymo’s fleet there has grown by nearly half in the past three weeks, fueled by a new Chinese-built minivan the company is betting will help it scale, even as tariffs drive up its costs.

The other 800 or so vehicles are spread across cities in other states, including Arizona and Florida, another burgeoning hot spot. Most are the familiar white Jaguar I-Pace electric SUVs, but a growing number are the new minivans — a modified Zeekr RT that Waymo has branded “Ojai.”

Waymo’s focus on California is no surprise. It is headquartered in Silicon Valley, and much of its early testing and development work was conducted there. Plus, a segment of the population there is inclined to adopt tech at its earliest stages.

The recent growth in Texas is more interesting. Waymo has increased its Texas fleet by 49% in the past three weeks, according to state vehicle registrations and data from the Texas Autonomous Vehicle Fleet Tracker. As of September 24, Waymo had 1,102 autonomous vehicles registered in the state.

Waymo first launched in commercial service in Austin through a partnership with Uber in March 2025, letting riders hail its robotaxis through the Uber app. Since then, the company has expanded its robotaxi services in Dallas, Houston, and San Antonio.

Waymo’s Texas fleet remained relatively static for most of the summer, inching up from about 600 vehicles in June to more than 700 by the end of August. Then came September, when the fleet surged, driven by an influx of new Ojai minivans, which now make up about a third of Waymo’s Texas fleet.

Expect that share to grow.

The Ojai robotaxi, equipped with Waymo’s sixth-generation self-driving system, is supposed to help Waymo reach mass scale. Its interior is built to withstand heavy use, and it comes with an upgraded rider interface and Google’s Gemini AI, which acts as an in-car assistant for riders. 

Strip away that technology, though, and the Ojai is a minivan made by Zeekr, a brand owned by China’s Geely Holding Group (which also owns Volvo). The Ojai is built on Zeekr’s SEA-M platform, a shared vehicle platform designed for uses like robotaxis and delivery vans. The base Zeekr vehicles are shipped to the U.S. without any Chinese connected-car technology on board. Once they arrive, the vehicles are sent to Waymo’s Arizona factory, where they are outfitted with Waymo’s self-driving system.

The Ojai is supposed to drive down costs and ultimately help Waymo reach profitability. For now, though, tariffs are cutting any savings. Under current U.S. trade policy, vehicles built in China face steep import tariffs, raising Waymo’s costs for every Ojai it brings into the country.

Waymo appears willing to absorb that cost. New York-based research firm MoffettNathanson, which tracks Ojai imports using detailed shipping records, said in its September report that Waymo is on track to bring 5,100 of the vehicles into the U.S. by the end of the year.

Where will all those Ojai vehicles go? Texas is certainly on the list. But Florida, where Waymo operates in three cities, and newer markets like Las Vegas will likely see an influx as well.

title: The tiny magnetic e-readers from Xteink that attach to your Pixel are on sale right now
snippet: Qi2 or MagSafe have always been one of the wildest but useful additions to phones like the Google Pixel or iPhone, and the best accessory might just be another display on its own. Xteink’s magnetic mini e-readers, like the X4 Pro, are on sale while stock lasts during its autumn sale. more…
fullText:
Qi2 or MagSafe have always been one of the wildest but useful additions to phones like the Google Pixel or iPhone, and the best accessory might just be another display on its own. Xteink’s magnetic mini e-readers, like the X4 Pro, are on sale while stock lasts during its autumn sale.

I don’t personally believe there is a perfect e-reader size, but there’s absolutely nothing wrong with having a tiny e-reader on hand when you want to knock out another chapter. The Xteink X4 Pro and Classic models fit that mold with a corner-to-corner size of just 4.3 inches. Both fall under 6mm thick, so they don’t sit too pronounced when stuck to the back of your phone.

An e-reader doesn’t need to be fancy, just good. At $109 and $89 for the Xteink Pro and Classic, respectively, these are certainly good options for many users.

Right now, though, both have dropped by a $10 discount during Xteink’s fall sale. That puts the Xteink X4 Pro at $99 and the X4 Classic model at $79. It’s not a massive discount, but it’s enough to make the Pro version more approachable. It has a couple of advantages, like a front light for night reading and a bigger battery.

	

An illuminated display makes a huge difference, especially if you tend to read during your commute or want to put your phone down before bed and don’t want to keep the lights on while you fight to stay awake through what just so happens to be the longest chapter in the book.

A bigger battery helps, too. But it isn’t a massive game-changer with these low-demand devices. The biggest thing is the magnetic back, which doesn’t require a case if you have something like the Pixel 11. It can stick to the back of your phone at all times, or just when you need it. The point is, it adds a paper-like screen to your device so you can read in a little more comfort.

Xteink’s fall sale is first-come, first-served, and it’s expected to end on September 30.

title: Qualcomm announces the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Qualcomm today announced the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 to power the next generation of Android smartphones. more…
fullText:
Qualcomm today announced the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 to power the next generation of Android smartphones.

The big change this year is how there are a pair of chips. Qualcomm considers both to be “flagship” offerings that give “OEMs greater choice.” The Elite Gen 6 is seen as the follow-up to last year’s Elite Gen 5, while the Elite Extreme Gen 6 comes in a level higher.

Both are built on a 2nm process with an Oryon CPU that has two 5GHz Prime Cores and six 4GHz Performance cores. The 8 Elite Gen 6 offers 10% improved CPU performance and a 37% gain in power efficiency compared to the Gen 5. 

On the 8 Elite Extreme, CPU performance improves by 13% compared to last generation. A global VVC (H.266) codec on the Extreme allows for more power-efficient video. 

	

A “rearchitected” Adreno GPU offers 35% improved GPU performance and 40% power efficiency improvement over the Gen 5.

On the Extreme, there are AI-dedicated Adreno matrix cores that allow for more advanced models to run. GPU performance improves 44% compared to last year. There’s also 18 MB of High Performance Memory that compared to last generation offers a 12% power improvement. For gaming, Adreno Neural Fusion uses the new GPU matrix cores for AI super-resolution and frame generation, which makes possible up to 40% power savings in supported games.

The Hexagon NPU features a new Element Accelerator for transformer workloads to benefit LLMs. There’s 14% improved NPU performance and 20% improved AI performance-per-watt with the 12 scalar + 8 vector + 1 tensor + 1 element configuration.

On the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, a 50% larger shared memory allows for 30B+ parameters Mixture of Experts (MoE) models. The aim is to reduce trips to external memory, with 35% improved NPU performance and 33% improved AI  performance-per-watt. 

The Spectra ISP features what Qualcomm calls Intelligent Pixel Control to understand scenes on a per-pixel level. On the Extreme, you have support for 8K60 video and 4K240 ultra HD slow-motion capture. 

Both chips are paired with the Qualcomm X105 5G modem that is “newly architected” for greater downlink (10% increase) and uplink speeds. Specifically, six antennas can capture multiple data streams at once. This supports 3GPP Release 19 5G Advanced.

Motorola today announced the Signature 27 with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. More on that here.

Note: Qualcomm paid for travel and accommodations for this launch event, but had no input on editorial content.

title: Google Messages finally rolls out new long-press menu with precise copying
snippet: After testing got underway in January, Google Messages is finally widely rolling out a new long-press menu in conversations. more…
fullText:
After testing got underway in January, Google Messages is finally widely rolling out a new long-press menu in conversations.

This new design replaces the top toolbar that housed various actions. Google only surfaced three actions with everything else in an overflow menu.

Upon long-pressing on a chat message or image, Google will show a floating menu with Remix (photos), Reply, Forward, Copy (text), Star, Delete, Select more, Info, and Save (photos).

Each action is accompanied by an icon at the front for quick scanning, while Copy lets you highlight a specific part of the message by pressing down and dragging the bubble. Previously, you could only copy the entire message.

	

If you’ve selected the newest message in a thread, Google will somewhat center it with a bouncy animation and haptic feedback. Messages prominently blurs the background layer when this menu is active. The row of emoji and “Create” Photomoji shortcuts is unchanged.

As of today, we’re seeing the new Google Messages long-press menu widely rolled out with stable version 20260910_03_RC02. There is a server-side component, so be sure to Force stop from the App info menu if it’s not yet live.

title: Samsung open-ear Galaxy Buds On images show what they look like when worn
snippet: Once rumored to go by a different name, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds On open-ear designs have appeared with a little more detail in new images, suggesting these earbuds might become official sooner rather than later. more…
fullText:
Once rumored to go by a different name, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds On open-ear designs have appeared with a little more detail in new images, suggesting these earbuds might become official sooner rather than later.

The Galaxy Buds On have been leaked several times over the last couple of months, though rumors suggested the earbuds would go by “Galaxy Buds Able” instead of the “Galaxy Buds On” name. That information was gleaned from Samsung’s Wearable app in early July, though the first of the two names seems to be an internal moniker.

New images of the Galaxy Buds On have surfaced (via Android Headlines). Previously, we’ve seen detailed renders and icon images, but nothing that looks like it could be official from Samsung. The new photos look a little cleaner, and one looks likely to be from the marketing team.

The Galaxy Buds On images also show what they look like when worn properly – that is, clipped around the ears rather than resting in them. It’s also a different style from the open-ear design worn over the ear. They look uncomfortable, but the design is already plentiful in certain regions, suggesting it’s a popular form factor.

	

It’s hard to pick up any details from the earbud images or to determine which port is the driver and which is the microphone for ambient noise detection. Even if that were determined properly, there’s no telling how they’ll sound prior to release.

The Galaxy Buds On were reported to have a few interesting features when previous images were leaked, such as an “Auto Volume” setting and head-nod and shake gesture control. Samsung Galaxy users will also have voice memos automatically transcribed to text.

Other devices like the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra have been circulating alongside the Galaxy Buds On, suggesting Samsung is gearing up for another launch soon. When that is, there’s no telling right now.
