title: Apple Watch Series 12: My three favorite new features so far
snippet: I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 last week, and so far after a few days of testing there are three standout features for me. more…
fullText:
I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 last week, and so far after a few days of testing there are three standout features for me.

#1: S11 chip makes everything fast

The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip update, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri has been sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

#2: New health features and complications

The new Health Sensing System should make Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the new health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:

Heart Rate

Daily Steps

Readiness

These let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. 

I’ve been testing heart rate and step complications, but my Watch needs more data before readiness is available. Overall though, these are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

#3: Faster charging

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

More battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:

Apple Watch Series 12: 15 minutes charge gets up to 12 hours battery life

Apple Watch Series 11: 15 minutes charge gets up to 8 hours battery life

I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off quickly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

For more Series 12 thoughts, check out my colleague Chance’s full review here.

Apple Watch Series 12 is now available starting at $399.

title: Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra leak shows another side, confirming minimal changes
snippet: The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra showed up in a leak in August, but a new one has surfaced as the October launch date gets closer. The most recent images further confirm little about the design will change. more…
fullText:
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra showed up in a leak in August, but a new one has surfaced as the October launch date gets closer. The most recent images further confirm little about the design will change.

The last leak image we saw of the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra confirmed the new tablet will carry on Samsung’s recent camera notch design change. It takes on a teardrop shape, minimizing its scree footprint. That, along with the S Pen changed with the release of the Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra.

In comparing leaks with new ones courtesy of Evan Blass on Twitter/X, it still seems like nothing on the outside is being altered. The new leak provides side and rear views – something the previous leak left out. But it only further confirms the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra will carry on the Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra’s build design.

That even goes for the S Pen charging location, which docks to the top right, when the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is in its landscape orientation.

	

That carry over from last year isn’t a bad thing, and tablets have sort of stagnated for some time. That’s part of the reason foldables have become so popular in recent years.

But Samsung has stuck to this design philosophy for some time. It might be nice to see some change that improves on bezels, or battery life. Of course, this leak only shows off what’s on the outside.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is expected to launch on October 7.

title: iOS 27 gives Apple Mail my most wished for feature upgrade
snippet: Apple’s Mail app in iOS 27 includes the feature upgrade that’s been at the top of my wishlist for years: search that “just works.” more…
fullText:
Apple’s Mail app in iOS 27 includes the feature upgrade that’s been at the top of my wishlist for years: search that “just works.”

iOS 27 overhauls search in Apple Mail to make it more relevant and accurate

Apple’s Mail app has long been plagued by lackluster search. 

I suspect that statement won’t be controversial at all among years-long users of the app. In fact, some might say “lackluster” is too kind a word to use.

But Apple says iOS 27 finally brings the Apple Mail search upgrade the app deserves.

From Apple’s website detailing iOS 27’s new features:

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

Here’s how this new ranking system in Mail will benefit users.

When you first open search in iOS 27’s Mail app, there’s a banner at the top that highlights “Expanded Search Results.” It explains: “Mail can look for more results based on what you mean, not just the words you type.”

Essentially, Apple is bringing search into the 21st century. Or you could say, it’s making search work the way it always should have.

I’ve used iOS 27 in beta for several months, and in my experience it’s definitely an upgrade over the old system. There hasn’t been a single time that I’ve tried searching for something and couldn’t find it. But understandably, your mileage may vary.

The improved search relies on proper indexing, so if your iPhone is still performing indexing (check the Settings app to see if it’s “Optimizing Search & Siri”), you may need to wait a bit before search works as well as it should.

What’s your take on Apple Mail’s search capabilities today? Have you tried the iOS 27 version yet? Let us know in the comments.

title: MagSafe Monday: BLAVOR’s solar power bank is built for fall camping trips
snippet: The weather is turning cooler, and it’s time for camping and football tailgates. BLAVOR’s 20000mAh Solar Power Bank is built for this time of year. It has four built-in cables so you can leave your bag at home, a solar panel for recharging, and a wireless pad on top for your iPhone and Apple Watch. Let’s take a look at it. more…
fullText:
The weather is turning cooler, and it’s time for camping and football tailgates. BLAVOR’s 20000mAh Solar Power Bank is built for this time of year. It has four built-in cables so you can leave your bag at home, a solar panel for recharging, and a wireless pad on top for your iPhone and Apple Watch. Let’s take a look at it.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Four built-in cables

This is what sold me on the concept overall. The unit has four cables built directly into the housing (two USB-C, one Lightning, one USB-A) plus three separate ports, so you can charge six devices at once without carrying a standalone cable, which makes packing a lot easier.

The USB-C port supports 20-watt fast charging, which BLAVOR says gets a typical iPhone to full in around 50 minutes (Pro vs Pro Max will obviously change). On the capacity side, 20000mAh works out to roughly 4 charges for an iPhone 17, 2.7 for an iPad mini, and 37 for an Apple Watch. Those are BLAVOR’s numbers, but the ballpark is right for a bank this size battery overall. A lot will depend on temperature, if you are using it while charging, etc.

Wireless charging, but no MagSafe

There’s a wireless charging area on top that works with both the iPhone and the Apple Watch, but it has no magnets. This is plain old-school Qi, not MagSafe or Qi2, so your iPhone sits on the surface rather than snapping to it. Set the bank down on a table, and your iPhone stays put. I won’t stay connected in a bag, etc Ideally in a future one, I’d love to see MagSAafe

BLAVOR only advertises the 20-watt figure for the wired USB-C port, so treat the wireless pad as a convenience charger, not your primary way to charge. If you want high speeds, use one of the four cables already attached to the battery.

Solar charging is a great addition, but it won’t let you charge the battery from empty to full. A panel this small cannot recharge a 20000mAh cell in a day of sun. What it can do is keep the bank from dying over a long trip and give you an emergency option when there’s no outlet nearby. I would think of it as more of a backup option.

BLAVOR packed seven extras with the battery: a flashlight with three modes, a camping light with three brightness levels, a compass, a thermometer, a carabiner, and actually rope. It’s rated IPX5, which means splash and rain-resistant.

Wrap up

This is not the battery you will use on the plane. This is a great option for camping, tailgating, etc. It’s a good, nice one with plenty of wired options and really handy for an emergency recharge via solar. Super unique concept, and it’s something I’ll keep in my camping bag, etc.

You can buy the BLAVOR Solar Power Bank from Amazon or directly from BLAVOR.

snippet: Meta's lawyers have argued that certain evidence should be withheld from public view on the grounds of attorney-client privilege in the ongoing lawsuits over alleged harm to teens' safety and mental health. fullText:
Skip to main content

Lawyers suing Meta called the hats an example of its ‘culture of privilege abuse.’

Lawyers suing Meta called the hats an example of its ‘culture of privilege abuse.’

by  Richard Lawler

Sep 24, 2026, 11:50 PM UTC

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

Richard Lawler

 

is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Meta’s lawyers have argued that certain evidence should be withheld from public view on the grounds of attorney-client privilege in the ongoing lawsuits over alleged harm to teens’ safety and mental health. Lawyers suing the company said this week that the label has been applied far too broadly, while pointing to a recently unsealed document showing that the team behind launching Instagram’s Teen Accounts in 2024 put in an order for baseball caps that simply said “a/c priv.”

Image: 4:22-md-03047, document 3509-4

The lawyers suing Meta argue the Project Nido (an internal name for the Teen Accounts team) swag is part of “culture of privilege abuse at Meta” aimed at keeping the research it’s conducted internally on teen harm out of the public eye, an issue that Mark Zuckerberg discussed after internal data on Instagram’s effects leaked in 2021.

US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers already called some of Meta’s privilege redactions “entirely inappropriate” in an order last month.

She pointed out one example where Meta’s lawyers tried to cast a discussion about a slide deck and whether or not to publish certain data as a discussion of attorney legal advice, deciding that based on testimony from the trial, their reticence about publishing was more of a business decision focused on preventing leaks.

Meta de-designated about 65,000 previously withheld or redacted documents in April 2025, after discovery, which the plaintiffs say came too late for them to use in depositions. Now Meta has requested time through the end of this year to re-review other privilege redactions it’s made, while the plaintiffs’ lawyers say a neutral party should be appointed to lead the review, paid for by Meta.

title: iPhone 18 Pro’s best Dynamic Island feature is one Apple barely mentioned
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro is here (read our review), and its Dynamic Island is better than ever. My personal favorite change is something Apple barely mentioned: an improved dual Live Activity mode. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro is here (read our review), and its Dynamic Island is better than ever. My personal favorite change is something Apple barely mentioned: an improved dual Live Activity mode.

Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro lets you see more information when running two Live Activities

Apple debuted the Dynamic Island in 2022 on the iPhone 14 Pro. And while software support for Live Activities has expanded a lot since then, the actual Dynamic Island hardware has stayed unchanged.

But with iPhone 18 Pro, Apple managed to shrink the Dynamic Island for the first time. 

By moving certain Face ID components under the display, iPhone 18 Pro adds slightly more usable screen real estate than previous iPhones had. 

More importantly though, the Dynamic Island can now display more Live Activity information than before.

In Apple’s announcement earlier this month, it spotlighted how three Live Activities can now run at a time—up from the previous limit of two.

That’s a nice upgrade, but the change I’ve found even more beneficial (and I’m not alone) is that your second Live Activity can be a lot more informative on iPhone 18 Pro.

That’s because if you’re only running two Live Activities, there’s more space available than before, and Apple uses that space to give the second Live Activity additional info.

So if you’re listening to media while running a timer—something I do all the time at the gym—now you’ll actually see the remaining time in the Dynamic Island. Before, it only showed a timer icon.

I look forward to seeing how apps make their Live Activities even more useful for iPhone 18 Pro users.

Do you have an iPhone 18 Pro? What do you think of the new Dynamic Island? Let us know in the comments.

On GitLab, Valve has released Lepton as an open-source repository, allowing developers to use the tool primarily for porting games to the Steam Frame. Valve explains:

Lepton is a tool for use with the Steam client which allows games which are exclusive to Android to run on the Linux operating system. Most users should use Lepton provided by the Steam Client itself.

…Lepton is intended to help game developers bring their VR Android games to the Steam Frame. Other usecases are possible, but were not the focus of development and may lack polish.

The Verge points out that some developers are already using Lepton to port Meta Quest games (the Quest runs Android) to the Steam Frame.

title: iCloud storage notification glitch puts unremovable red badge on Settings app [U: Fixed]
snippet: Update, September 23: Apple says this has been fixed for all users. Original story below. There’s an annoying little iPhone notification glitch impacting some users on iOS 27. For those affected, the Settings app gets a red badge prompting an alert to ‘Activate iCloud Storage’. However, tapping on this alert simply navigates to the iCloud storage purchase screen and the alert does not go away after dismissing it. This glitched notification appears even when the user has plenty of available iCloud storage already, like if they are on a 2 TB family Apple One plan. more…
fullText:
Update, September 23: Apple says this has been fixed for all users. Original story below.

There’s an annoying little iPhone notification glitch impacting some users on iOS 27. For those affected, the Settings app gets a red badge prompting an alert to ‘Activate iCloud Storage’.

However, tapping on this alert simply navigates to the iCloud storage purchase screen and the alert does not go away after dismissing it. This glitched notification appears even when the user has plenty of available iCloud storage already, like if they are on a 2 TB family Apple One plan.

While Apple sometimes does use the Settings app as a way to promote offers (like Apple TV trials) and remind users about AppleCare warranties, this particular notification appears to simply be a mistake rather than some underhand way to shove an iCloud upsell in front of customers.

The notification appears on devices running the release version of iOS 27 and iOS 27.2, as well as iOS 26.7. 

Some users have reported that signing out of their Apple Account on their device and logging back in causes the alert to go away. But hopefully Apple can also resolve this quickly with a backend change.

Update: Apple Support recommends logging out and back into your Media & Purchases account on the device. Go to Settings -> [name] -> Media & Purchases -> Sign Out, then sign back in.

fullText:
Apple today updated its official list of digital camera RAW formats supported across its platforms, adding support for 11 models from several manufacturers. Here are the details.

Apple now supports RAW files from 562 cameras

Apple’s operating systems offer system-level support for RAW images captured by many third-party cameras.

In a nutshell, this lets compatible apps work directly with those cameras’ RAW files, allowing them to better adjust elements such as exposure, color, and so on.

That is in contrast with formats such as JPEG, which don’t allow for the same post-processing editing flexibility, since much of that image processing is basically baked into the final image.

Apple maintains support articles listing digital cameras with RAW formats supported by its current (and past) operating systems. The list was updated today, adding 11 digital cameras, bringing the total to 562 models.

title: A Chrome bug is slowing extension load times to a snail’s pace on macOS, Google is aware
snippet: Google Chrome extensions are reportedly taking too long to load on macOS devices, when they should reasonably only take a couple of seconds, due to a bug in the latest updates. Google is aware of the issue. more…
fullText:
Google Chrome extensions are reportedly taking too long to load on macOS devices, when they should reasonably only take a couple of seconds, due to a bug in the latest updates. Google is aware of the issue.

The report comes courtesy of PiunikaWeb, which noted a thread entry on the Chromium issue tracker divulging the issue. The issue seems to affect macOS instances of Google Chrome, rather than Windows or mobile versions. The affected extensions are reportedly taking up to 60 seconds to load, when extensions should open instantly. 

Users began reporting extensions lag in Google Chrome last week, and one of the main third-party tools it seems to affect is password managers like 1Password. The credential management app offers an extremely handy Chrome extension for password autofill across any site that requires you to remember your reasonably complex password. According to the company, it’s aware that a Google Chrome update seems to be slowing extension performance.

Hey Don! There is a known issue in Google Chrome itself right now that can cause extension popups to take much longer than usual to open, and we’d like to figure out if that’s what you’re running into here.

When 1Password is slow or won’t open, do you notice the same thing with…

— 1Password (@1Password) September 16, 2026

It doesn’t seem to only affect 1Password. Some replies indicate other extensions are being affected by the bug, though it doesn’t appear to be consistent.

	

What seems to be causing this disparity in extension load times is mismanaged process priority on Google Chrome’s end, though that hasn’t been verified by Google. Specifically, this seems to happen on macOS 26, and for whatever reason, Google Chrome deems certain extensions a low-priority operation, effectively pushing them to the background while it diverts resources to other tasks. The result is a much longer load time for users.

Google is aware of the issue, posting a reply to the official community page. Here’s what Google’s team says:

We’re continuing to investigate this issue as a priority, and I’ve also asked the team to consider all options including if we can roll the experiment out any further. We’ll make sure to share further updates on this thread as we have them.

Some users have noted that, in the meantime, enabling the PMLoadingPageVoter flag fixes the issue. It’s worth noting that enabling/disabling flags in Google Chrome carries some risk, so please only do so with that in mind.

title: Big Pixel VIPs widget redesign starts rolling out
snippet: Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop. more…
fullText:
Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop.

Previously, the widget could be expanded to take up your entire screen. This redesign limits Pixel VIPs to two layouts.

The 5×1 layout shows just one row of your prioritized contacts (up to four) at a time with the ability to scroll for more. This view pairs circular profile avatars with just first names, rather than including surnames as before. The change results in a more consistent widget appearance.

Old vs. new

	

The 5×2 configuration is now the max size for the Pixel VIPs widget. Depending on the number of contacts, Google will display rectangular cards that feature pill-shaped buttons to quickly call or message.

Meanwhile, unread messages will result in a circular badge appearing in the top-right of the circular profile or the messaging icon, which would benefit from being a little bit more noticeable in the latter configuration.

This is rolling out via a server-side update that is not yet widely available. It’s only appearing on one of our Pixel devices today.

Version 2.0 rolled out earlier this week with a fullscreen design that replaces the bottom sheet approach. There are also some tweaks to the feed, while a dock at the bottom of the screen lets you quickly switch between your VIPs.

title: Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro case is a keeper
snippet: Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them. Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather. more…
fullText:
Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them.

Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather.

So it was when I put on the new “Red Ochre” variant of the leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case from Bellroy. The Melbourne-based company has long been an official Made by Google partner, which means it’s always among the first case manufacturers to unveil its wares each August.

I’ve had the case on my phone for just over three weeks now, and I look forward to picking it up each time. Bellroy’s leather is thin and rigid, and is treated to prevent wear, which means that it takes longer than, say, a piece of Horween leather from Nomad, to age. But it also means it will look new for longer. Barring a few minor scratches, the case has survived more than a few child-related drops with aplomb.

	

On the structure side, the leather is reinforced with a rigid plastic frame that protrudes a millimeter or so above the display, and is covered internally by a microfiber lining. Magnets are present on the back for PixelSnap compatibility, and the buttons are made from anodized aluminum, which gives them a satisfying tactility akin to the phone’s buttons themselves.

At $59, this is not a cheap case, but to my eyes it’s the right combination of form and function. I love the color, though there are three others available — Black, Artichoke, and Pewter — if the more traditional saddle color is a bit too bright.

My weakness is a great leather case for any phone, but unlike iPhone and Galaxy cases there aren’t many good Pixel options. There’s this $40 option made by Snakehive that I plan to pick up, but it lacks coverage on the top, bottom, and right button side, which I dislike. Still, it appears to have more supple leather than Bellroy’s, which should patina more quickly, so I’m looking forward to putting them head-to-head in the future.

Until then, I’m quite happy with Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case, and plan to keep it on my phone until something else newer, shinier, and patina-ier comes along.

title: 5 iPhone Duo Features I’m Already Dying to Try
snippet: Commentary: After getting hands-on time with Apple’s new foldable phone, here are the questions I’m most eager to answer in testing.
fullText:
First impressions last a lifetime, and the iPhone Duo certainly made one when I got my hands on it at Apple Park earlier this month. But along with the intrigue came a handful of questions that I can’t wait to explore once the Duo becomes my everyday phone.

Apple’s passport-sized foldable iPhone, which opens for preorders Oct. 16 and launches Oct. 23, is designed to be versatile. You can quickly text or check notifications on its 5.4-inch cover screen, then unfold it to watch videos or multitask on the 7.6-inch inner display. Rotate it to portrait orientation, and it’s well suited to scrolling through vertical social content. Judging by how much I enjoy using Samsung’s similarly sized Galaxy Z Fold 8, I have high hopes for the iPhone Duo.

		

			

In my short time with the Duo, I got a glimpse of how Apple’s hardware and software work together to differentiate the phone in an increasingly competitive foldable market. But with this being Apple’s first foray into the space, I have plenty of questions I look forward to answering once I can test the phone.

Here are the five features I’m most eager to explore on the iPhone Duo.

How streaming will be optimized for the displays

One of the biggest draws of a foldable phone is the ability to watch videos on a larger inner display. 

Traditional book-style foldables such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold tend to have taller designs that resemble a slab phone when closed. When you open the phone to watch widescreen video, the content is letterboxed, leaving massive black bars at the top and bottom of the display. With a passport-sized foldable such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8, whose 4:3 aspect ratio is better suited for content consumption, those bars are significantly reduced, allowing more of the inner display to be used for video.

Apple demonstrated how Netflix will be optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

At Apple’s product unveiling, the company demonstrated how Netflix is optimizing its app for the iPhone Duo, ensuring content is well suited to both the phone’s cover and inner displays by reducing those black bars. The Duo sizzle reel shows similar customizations for Apple TV. The question is how other streaming services will customize their apps for the Duo’s 1.4:1 aspect ratio to deliver a more immersive viewing experience.

One standout feature of the iPhone Duo compared to other foldable phones is its matte main display reduces glare and the appearance of a crease. That can make it easier to watch videos under various lighting conditions, and I especially look forward to testing that under the bright California sun. It’ll be interesting to see whether colors look significantly more muted as a result of that matte screen, or if I hardly notice a difference. In my limited time with the phone, I didn’t sense there was a huge tradeoff when it came to the display’s vibrancy, but I also look forward to exploring that more.

Another element that could make on-screen content feel more immersive is the Duo’s “disappearing” under-display inner camera. While phones such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 have a noticeable hole-punch cutout on the larger display, the Duo essentially hides its camera when it’s not in use. That means fewer visual distractions when watching TV shows and movies, while also keeping a tiny black hole from getting in the way of documents and other content on the larger screen.

The camera cutout on the inner display can “hide” when not in use.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Notably, the Duo’s speakers sit on opposite sides of the foldable phone, with one set on the upper left half and the other on the bottom right. The Galaxy Z Fold 8, on the other hand, places both speakers on the left side. I was initially thrown off by the Z Fold 8’s slightly lopsided audio, but I’ll admit I quickly stopped noticing it as I continued to use the phone. Still, the Duo could have a noticeably improved sound experience because of its more balanced speaker setup, paired with Apple’s Spatial Audio. 

It’s also interesting that the Duo’s volume buttons sit at the top of the phone when it’s held in landscape, therefore making the controls easier to access when the phone is rotated to portrait. That may be a slight adjustment for me at first, but I’m curious if I’ll end up preferring that arrangement as I swipe through endless reels.  

The multitasking experience 

The Duo supports drag and drop functionality when multitasking.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Another major perk of foldables is the ability to multitask. Unlike the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which allows for multitasking with up to three apps, the Duo is limited to two. That’s not much of a letdown for me, since I usually stick to running two apps simultaneously on the Z Fold 8 to prevent overcrowding.

Like other foldables, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8, 8 Ultra and Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you can easily drag and drop content across apps on the Duo. I played with this a little bit during Apple’s event by quickly attaching photos to text messages, but I’m curious how many other apps, both internal and third-party, will support this capability. 

Apple Pencil support could really make the Duo feel like a tablet

The iPhone Duo has frequently been referred to as a hybrid between an iPhone and an iPad Mini, and one aspect that makes that especially true is its support for the Apple Pencil stylus. That support is slated to arrive later this year via a software update.

Rumors pointed to Apple designing a smaller Apple Pencil for the Duo, which never materialized due to “technical problems” before mass production, according to Bloomberg. Instead, Apple opted for its USB-C Pencil (but notably not the Apple Pencil Pro). 

The iPhone Duo is designed for both horizontal and vertical content.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

I’ve never owned a tablet; I haven’t been able to muster a strong enough reason to spend hundreds of dollars on what I see as a larger and less capable version of a smartphone. Foldables are a happy medium for me, allowing me to use a compact or standard-size handset that doubles as a larger canvas for watching, working and multitasking. Stylus compatibility could elevate the Duo above competitors such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which doesn’t have S Pen support. 

That said, I hardly ever reach for the stylus on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, because typing and swiping with my fingers feels so much more intuitive. But having the option to use the Apple Pencil with the Duo is a plus either way. I’ll have to see if it opens my eyes up to a world of tablet-like productivity I’ve been missing out on.

Camera performance

The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel rear cameras.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Foldable phone cameras have long had a bad rap, given that early models had less room for larger image sensors and lenses. This resulted in images that were significantly downgraded from what you’d get on a flagship, despite the high sticker price.

That gap has narrowed in recent years as both camera hardware and foldable design have evolved to become sleeker and more capable. Phones such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold have impressive cameras that may not be quite on par with their non-folding premium counterparts, but that still deliver great images.

The iPhone Duo appears poised to offer up similarly high-quality shots, with a 48-megapixel main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. Like the Z Fold 8, though, there’s no telephoto camera. I was mentally prepared for this omission, given my experience with Samsung’s passport-sized foldable, and I don’t really mind the absence of a telephoto lens on that device. That said, it is disappointing when a phone in the $2,000 range doesn’t have the most specced out rear camera setup.

The biggest looming question is how good the iPhone Duo’s internal selfie camera will be. In its tech specifications, Apple simply refers to it as an “under-display FaceTime camera” that supports 1080p video recording at 30 or 60 frames per second — but no official word on the megapixel count. This implies it may be a step down from the 12-megapixel selfie camera on the front of the Duo. 

The Duo’s inner selfie camera is geared toward FaceTime videos.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

To be fair, apart from when I’m testing a foldable phone’s cameras, I rarely ever opt for the inner selfie camera because it doesn’t feel like a natural way to snap an image, especially when the cover screen camera is right there. Plus, to get higher-quality images, you can use the Duo’s Smart Take feature to see a preview of your shot on the cover screen when using the rear cameras. So there are better options for taking a photo than using the inner selfie camera. 

I look forward to seeing how all the Duo’s cameras perform once I take it out and about beyond the confines of Apple Park.

How good will battery life be?

For some people, battery life will be the make or break element. How long will the iPhone Duo last as you endlessly scroll, stream and snap photos?

Apple says the iPhone Duo will give you up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours when using the outer screen. When evenly splitting your time between both, the company says you’ll be able to go 24 hours before needing to charge. 

With more traditional book-style foldables such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Pixel 11 Pro Fold, I tend to stick to the cover screens because they’re so similar to the dimensions of slab phones that I forget there’s a larger display inside. Palm-sized phones such as the Z Fold 8 help to remedy that by giving me more incentive to unfold the device and use a larger canvas, and the Duo falls in that camp. 

When splitting time between the iPhone Duo’s displays, Apple says the phone should last about a day before needing to be charged.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

With that in mind, I’m curious how well the Duo’s battery will hold up as I frequently hop between the cover and main displays. Unlike Samsung’s latest foldables, the iPhone Duo doesn’t have a silicon-carbon battery, which can increase energy density and speed up charging time. Still, Apple says the iPhone Duo can charge up to 50% in around 20 minutes with a 60-watt adapter or higher.

The Duo does have the advantage of MagSafe support with Qi2.2 wireless charging up to 25 watts, like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. By comparison, the Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultra don’t have built-in magnets, so you’ll need a Qi2-compatible case to tap into wireless charging. While it’s probably smart to slap a case on your nearly $2,000 iPhone Duo, it’s nice to know it’s not necessary for painless wireless charging.

Now, the countdown is ticking. Until I can put the Duo through its paces in the real world, the verdict on this — and the many other questions that are bound to arise — remains out.

snippet: This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel. more…
fullText:
This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel.

The silent or mute icon goes from a crossed-out speaker to a bell.

This might be an accidental regression as Google switched from the bell to the speaker in Android 14. Notably, this change was not present during the Android 17 QPR1 Beta cycle and only went live with the stable OTA this week. 

The speaker icon is still live in 17 QPR2 Beta 5. (Meanwhile, the switcher at the top of the volume slider still uses the bell.)

	

Another icon change further complicates whether this tweak was intentional. The VPN icon is now much thicker and filled in, with this update also only appearing with the stable release.

We’ll know this was a mistake if Google changes it back in future releases, though any fix may not arrive until the sizable QPR2 update in December. Android 17 QPR1 is not yet available for the Pixel 11 series.

title: How NASA and Nikon Captured Those Stunning Artemis II Moon Photos
snippet: It’s not all about the latest camera gear – the astronauts relied on both old and new tech that anyone can buy off-the-shelf.
fullText:
Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen takes photos of the moon through a window shroud using a Nikon camera. The picture of him was captured using an iPhone 17 Pro Max.

																			NASA
												
			
				

When NASA’s Artemis II mission put humans at the far side of the moon for the first time in 44 years, it often felt like we were there in the capsule with astronauts Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen and Reid Wiseman. That’s almost entirely due to the frequent transmission of imagery from the flight, from live feeds to high-resolution photos that let us look at the moon and life in space like never before.

But getting those photos and videos isn’t as easy as tossing a camera in a bag for an Earth-bound vacation. To capture the high-resolution images that made us gasp here on the ground, the astronauts shot with Nikon DSLR and mirrorless cameras. Artemis II used GoPro Hero4 cameras for interior and exterior video feeds, and the crew took many notable photos inside the capsule using iPhone 17 Pro Max phones.

As NASA moves toward the Artemis III mission in 2027 and an expected moon landing in 2028 there will undoubtedly be a huge demand to document and share everything that goes on. To get a better understanding of what’s involved with making sure astronauts can capture those historical and candid moments, I spoke to Michael Corrado, Nikon senior manager of Pro Services.

“Just to see these pictures come back from space, we couldn’t be more humbled as a company,” Corrado said. “And as an individual, my dad was part of the space program… so it’s in the legacy here.”

NASA astronauts Christina Koch (below) and Victor Glover (above) share a window inside the Orion spacecraft during the sixth day of the Artemis II mission. Flight Day 6 was the crew’s lunar flyby day, during which they rotated roles taking photos, making annotations, and recording their observations of the lunar surface.

Corrado also walked me through the rigorous process NASA requires to certify equipment for space travel, why astronauts primarily rely on decade-old tech and how future flights will look different.

It also struck me that even these Nikon professionals, who have worked with NASA astronauts and teams for decades, were still gobsmacked by the imagery that comes back. “We were just sitting there in awe of what we were seeing every day,” Corrado said.

		

			

How to launch a camera into space

The Artemis II vehicle – the Orion spacecraft and Integrity capsule – represented some of the latest space flight technology, but not all of the cameras were cutting-edge.

For video, NASA used several GoPro Hero4 cameras mounted inside and outside the Artemis II spacecraft, a compact action camera model that came out in 2014.

The workhorse of the mission was the Nikon D5 DSLR, a model first introduced to the consumer market in 2016. Also on the flight was the half-decade-old Nikon Z9 mirrorless camera body, introduced in 2021.

A photographer here on Earth might pass over the Nikon D5 as an outdated camera, but Corrado suggests that NASA doesn’t view it as “old technology.”

“I’d use the word ‘trusted’ technology more than anything,” quipped Corrado.

Artemis II commander, Reid Wiseman and Canadian Space Agency mission specialist, Jeremy Hansen (background), training in a mockup of the Orion capsule at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in July 2025.

James Blair/NASA – JSC

Nikon’s cameras are the only ones fully certified to fly on NASA missions, a spot on the equipment roster the company has maintained since the later Apollo missions in the 1970s. Of the Artemis II lineup, only the Nikon D5 carries the certification badge; the Nikon Z9 is still being evaluated – in that case under real-world conditions.

Certification is as much about safety as it is about performance. Camera batteries can be flammable, and flame is the last thing you want in a space capsule.

But the camera’s electronics also need to be shielded against radiation. We enjoy a buffer from Earth’s atmosphere, but radiation in open space is another matter. So, although the cameras on the mission are mostly stock models, they’ve been reinforced with internal shielding.

“Back in the day, we used to strip things off the camera [like] the leather,” Corrado said, referring to the missions in the 1970s. “They were almost naked cameras that went up. But none of that has to happen with the D5 and the Z9.”

There also wasn’t a lot of equipment. When I go out to shoot a sunrise, I’ll typically bring a backup camera in case something goes wrong with my main body. Traveling 250,000 miles from the nearest camera store, I’d expect there to be backups, but since weight is such an issue during spaceflight, Corrado noted that no backup bodies accompanied the astronauts on Artemis II.

Getting the shot in-camera, in-capsule

Today’s cameras are advanced enough that their automatic modes can cover almost any photo situation, and if a shot isn’t quite right we can edit it easily in software. In a dark scene, for example, a camera will increase the ISO to compensate and introduce digital noise, which can then be cleaned up in Lightroom.

The photos that came back from the Artemis II mission, though, revealed that the astronauts never leaned on that type of automatic crutch. The dark shots – it’s space, after all – sometimes had high ISOs but not to the point of introducing excessive noise.

Photographic documentation of Artemis Lunar Imaging Orion Crew Configuration with Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Andre Douglas

In an extremely harsh lighting environment, they knew how to take advantage of the wide dynamic range of the D5 and Z9 cameras to avoid moon surfaces blown out too white to preserve surface details. Photos from the dark side of the moon, the first captured in 55 years, reveal formations that scientists will be studying for years.

One of my favorite images is a shot of the back of the moon with the Earth rising behind it. You can see details of clouds and the peaks of continents on the illuminated portion of the planet, versus a sliver of bright white like you’d get when taking a snapshot of the moon from your backyard.

Earth sets at 6:41 p.m. EDT, April 6, 2026, over the Moon’s curved limb in this photo captured by the Artemis II crew during their journey around the far side of the Moon.

Keep in mind that the images NASA published during the mission are the ones captured in-camera, not edited raw images, again demonstrating the astronauts’ photographic skills.

HULC-ing out with the Nikon Z9

After years of service, the Nikon D5 is likely looking at NASA retirement. “We worked for years to get the D5 certified for use in space,” Corrado said, “and now it has probably seen its last launch.”

The Z9 is taking over for the future, which means it’s currently going through the official certification process even though it’s been around the moon.

In fact, Artemis wasn’t the first time the Z9 has gone to space. Astronaut Don Pettit used it for about eight months on the International Space Station. Corrado said there are currently 20 Nikon Z9 cameras on the ISS.

NASA astronaut and Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch, seen here on the fourth day of the mission, prepping for lunar flyby activities after completing aerobic exercise on the flywheel device. Photo captured on a Nikon Z9 mirrorless camera.

“Life is different when you wake up to an email that you think is spam that says ‘Greetings from orbit’,” said Corrado. Pettit’s real-(off)-world experience and questions made their way to Nikon’s engineers. He noted that the feedback typically results in firmware changes specific for NASA.

The hardened Z9 that will reach the lunar surface in 2028 will be wrapped in a thermal blanket as part of a system called the Handheld Universal Lunar Camera (HULC). The cover will protect the camera from the moon’s extreme temperature fluctuations.

Looking to the next moonshot

It’s not fair to see the visual riches of the existing Artemis II photos and still have a wishlist, but I think depth is one element missing. Wiseman talked about witnessing land formations on the moon’s surface, saying, “It’s just everything from the training but in three dimensions and absolutely unbelievable.”

The Artemis II crew captures a portion of the Moon coming into view along the terminator – the boundary between lunar day and night – where low-angle sunlight casts long, dramatic shadows across the surface.

That makes me wish the crew had captured footage using the Spatial Video feature on their iPhones (I’ve found no evidence that they did). Imagine putting on an Apple Vision Pro and seeing the moon in an immersive way that’s even closer to what the astronauts experienced.

Stereoscopic footage could be recorded in the future, though. Nikon is working on a depth camera, for which it was granted a patent in 2025. “We’re still working with NASA very closely… together on these technologies,” Corrado said.

No matter what form the future images from Artemis III and future Artemis flights take, they’re sure to be stunning thanks to the astronauts’ training and the crews at Nikon and NASA working to equip them with the hardened camera equipment the missions require.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Jeff Carlson
						

						

							Senior Writer

title: The Googlebook has an opportunity to build Android like nothing else [Video]
snippet: Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it? more…
fullText:
Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it?

I’ll state right up top that I’m already cautiously optimistic. We need a competitor player to Mac and, in particular, Windows. Microsoft, as of late, has been nothing but combative with the people who use the firm’s operating system every single day. A new player is needed. I’m still not fully convinced yet by Googlebooks, but there is an opportunity, a big opportunity that hinges on quite a few things falling into place.

Considering how many new products are released every year, it’s quite surprising how few operating systems are unveiled. I suppose there is a caveat that Android has existed for a long time, but there have been no true attempts to make it work as a “proper desktop” experience, save Samsung’s DeX system, which was an internal attempt to make it work with Galaxy phones and tablets.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

DeX is a fine take on things, but it is limited by virtue of being an experience trying to emulate a desktop experience. Googlebook OS is Android reimagined for the desktop era.

I’m still not sure if this is too late or if there is enough interest. Google’s move comes at a very interesting time. Maybe its impending launch was the reason that Chrome OS has languished in recent years, having had lots of early promise and a surging user base, particularly in the education sector.

I have had the benefit of trying out Googlebooks, but in the lead-up to launch, I’ve been thinking more broadly about why now, and whether there is any real, tangible reason that Google would fully adopt Android across phones, tablets, and, now, desktops/laptops.

Bear with me, though, as a lot of assumptions have to be made for my points to fully hit home. I know that isn’t ideal, but just indulge me in this thought exercise at the very least.

The high-end might not be the ‘tip of the spear’

We’ve just seen a slew of expensive hardware unveiled under the Googlebook branding. These are the “optimum” hardware experiences, and I do think many are overpriced. That’s not where I see the benefits.

Compared to previous Chrome OS versions, Android devices are better optimized for low-power, low-resource use. A bad Chromebook is almost always worse than a bad Android device, at least in my experience. It’s harder to hide bad performance on a laptop or desktop because you’re used to certain power thresholds. On a tablet or phone, that isn’t as pronounced because things are almost always more lightweight.

It helps that many Android SoCs are powerful enough now to rival mid-range desktop processors or at least those found in notebooks.

Android seems to scale much better now than a few years ago, but as Apple has shown recently, you can run desktop-level applications on mobile SoCs. I could easily see a laptop running absolutely fine with a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 from a few years ago and doing so with very low power consumption.

Just a few years ago, when Google Stadia was still around, the idea of a “gaming Chromebook” felt silly and wasteful. Those machines relied entirely on the cloud, meaning you were paying a premium for a laptop that couldn’t actually play games without perfect Wi-Fi. However, if we get gaming Googlebooks these could be a very different prospect. 

Hardware has evolved to the point where modern mobile processors easily outperform last-generation consoles like the PlayStation 4, bringing entry-level gaming power straight into a laptop chassis without needing an internet connection.

At the same time, the software side has improved drastically. Android gaming is no longer just for casual mobile apps; it now features massive, high-fidelity games that look and feel like console titles. Combined with the ability to emulate older PC and console games locally, a gaming Googlebook becomes a genuine, self-sufficient gaming machine you can actually take anywhere, and one that doesn’t require a wall outlet to play for hours at a time.

Unlike Steam Machines and the Steam Deck, Fortnite is there right from day one.

Something else to consider that I think has been glossed over by basically anyone, because we’re so accustomed to mouse and keyboard interactions with a laptop or desktop.

No other desktop-level operating systems have been developed from the ground up with touch interactions in mind. This is one of the other major USPs for Googlebooks; I’ve already said it multiple times in this rundown that Android only needs to close an application gap. That is exponentially easier than trying to shoehorn a legacy OS into a new form factor.

Apple has kept iOS, iPadOS, and MacOS all as separate OS builds. Google’s “everything is Android” approach could be a masterstroke. I’m resting heavy emphasis on “could” in that equation.

Why? Well, there is a generation of people out there who have grown up effectively “mobile first.” Kids who are now young adults, the “iPad kids” that are now getting to a stage where they are looking for a product that is familiar, comfortable, and does everything they need.

They’ve grown up already using tools like Capcut rather than Adobe. Playing mobile games or mobile ports of the biggest games, like Roblox. Traditional desktop paradigms have never catered to those young people. Googlebooks and the Android experience, rightly or wrongly, extend the familiar to a new form factor. It’s a play that I haven’t seen many discuss, but that could work if the price is right.

‘Desktop-level’ could bring even wider benefits

For the older folks, we have a bee in our bonnets about “desktop-level software”. It’s still essential that we get some things ported over sooner rather than later.

If, for instance, Blackmagic or Adobe port over their respective software packages, Davicini Resolve or Creative Cloud apps to Googlebook, that’s great. 

There’s a hidden secondary benefit, though. The next wave of foldable phones with potential support for desktop apps or desktop app scaling now have access to professional-grade applications in a form factor that is multiple times more portable than a traditional laptop. This extends to tablets, too.

I’m quite bullish that Android tablets could be one of the biggest beneficiaries with the introduction of the Googlebook, that is, if the company is willing to allow more power tools to come to the other versions of Android that the Googlebook OS is based on.

You can rebuke much of what I have said for any number of reasons, but everyone can agree that so much hinges on which brands are willing to start building for Android. Closing this “app gap” is arguably the most important component of the Googlebook during its first year.

I’m cautiously optimistic about the Googlebook program. A fully flexible, malleable operating system that spans regular smartphones, foldables, tablets, laptops, and potentially desktops could do something no other OS has offered before. Scalable in ways that not even Apple has been able to do, but has half-stepped toward since making iPadOS a midway experience or bridge between iOS and Mac.

If Google invests in and enhances Android across the entire stack, every existing and future device will evolve at a rate that wasn’t possible before. Scalable for any screen size. Apps that can be desktop-level while still being mobile native.

There is a big “if” here, and that is the only reason I’m not fully invested yet. The current, glaring software gaps need to be plugged – and plugged fast.

There is a parallel that might prove to be a good omen. Linux has had a massive swell of users over the past year, driven by Valve and, in particular, Steam OS. The success of the Steam Deck has proven that an alternative to Windows can work for gamers.

I’m not sure if we’ll ever get a compatibility layer in Android for various Windows or Linux applications, but who knows. It is not out of the realm of possibility, and if it happens, it’s going to be a major turning point. Google just has to be sure that this is a long-term project, and improving on Chrome OS is a must.

Proton has done wonders for Valve over the past 3 or 4 years. This is a blueprint Google could follow. I do think getting native ports for a few of the biggest applications is all it will take to get more on board. A small swell could quite easily become a bigger wave of app conversion.

A few years ago, if you’d asked me if my gaming PC would ever run an OS other than Windows, I’d have said “never”. I sit here 18 months after ditching it in favor of Linux’s performance gains.

That experience has taught me to be less dismissive of Android on desktop than I was some months ago, and my time playing with the first run of Googlebooks has me excited for what might be coming next for Android.

title: Android Auto update might fix cellular signal icon – is it back for you?
snippet: For months now, there have been reports of Android Auto’s status bar having a broken icon for cellular signal, but the latest updates seem to finally put an end to the debacle. more…
fullText:
For months now, there have been reports of Android Auto’s status bar having a broken icon for cellular signal, but the latest updates seem to finally put an end to the debacle.

The bottom/side bar on Android Auto shows your apps, the time, and your phone’s current battery and cellular signal status through icons. But, for around 4-5 months now, there have been reports of users seeing the cellular signal icon go missing at random, only to come back just as randomly for some. 

When it’s missing, it leaves a funny-looking gap in Android Auto.

Image via Reddit

With Android Auto 17.8, it seems Google may have finally addressed this problem more widely.

	

A number of users on Reddit all report that the latest update has suddenly fixed the cellular signal icon on Android Auto. That said, reports are limited to just a handful of users, one of which cleared their app cache following the update’s installation.

So, we’ll open this one to you. Has your cellular signal icon returned on Android Auto? Sound off in the comments and let us know.

title: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better
snippet: iOS 27 introduced Dual Capture support for FaceTime, letting you show your front and rear camera views at the same time. And in iOS 27.2, that upgrade is expanding to now support Group FaceTime calls. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduced Dual Capture support for FaceTime, letting you show your front and rear camera views at the same time. And in iOS 27.2, that upgrade is expanding to now support Group FaceTime calls.

Group FaceTime calls support Dual Capture in iOS 27.2 on compatible iPhones

FaceTime is a popular iPhone feature that, at its core, hasn’t changed much since first coming on the scene many years ago.

But iOS 27 introduced the first substantial upgrade in a while: Dual Capture support.

With Dual Capture, you can have your front and rear camera views active at the same time during your FaceTime call. Just hit the ‘Flip’ button on the viewfinder and whoever you’re talking to will see both of your camera views simultaneously.

Note: Dual Capture requires an iPhone 17 or later, and participants in the call need to be running iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 to see the dual camera streams.

iOS 27.2 is currently in beta, but it comes with a great upgrade for Dual Capture: Group FaceTime calls are now supported too.

In iOS 27.0, you can only use the feature in one-on-one calls. But if you join the iOS 27.2 beta, or just wait a few weeks for the public launch, you’ll get Dual Capture for all of your Group FaceTime calls as well.

Have you used Dual Capture in FaceTime yet on iOS 27? How did it work for you? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by CleanMyMac by MacPaw. With the release of macOS 27 Golden Gate, use CleanMyMac first to free up space, optimize your system, and ensure your new Mac runs at 100% on day one. Learn more.

macOS 27 Golden Gate is a huge upgrade over macOS 26 Tahoe, and not just because of the smarter design decisions. Just like iOS 27 for iPhone, the Mac adds a Liquid Glass appearance slider. This lets you dramatically change the look of your Mac across the system.

The slider

Liquid Glass is Apple’s design language that started with iOS 26 and macOS 26 Tahoe. Initially, Liquid Glass started with a single look. Apple later added a setting to make Liquid Glass less clear.

Starting with iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, Liquid Glass is no longer limited to just two styles. Instead, Apple has introduced an appearance slider. This lets you make Liquid Glass much more clear than before. You can also give Liquid Glass a more opaque look that still looks modern.

macOS 27 Golden Gate defaults to a medium setting. The system also invites you to adjust the slider during initial setup. You can also adjust the slider later in System Settings > Appearance.

The Liquid Glass slider provides a live preview of what to expect from each setting. Three notches suggest most clear, medium, and most opaque. However, you can assign it to any level in between notches as well.

The Dock

The Dock is the most prominent component that changes appearance based on the Liquid Glass slider setting.

It can range from showing your desktop wallpaper in clear definition to being a more opaque and defined material.

Here’s a closer look:

macOS desktop widgets can be full color, dim, or change automatically. The Liquid Glass slider changes how the dim widget appearance looks as well.

Apple Music and Podcasts

Apps like Apple Music and Podcasts that have system Now Playing bars have a very different look based on the Liquid Glass slider position.

Here’s the Now Playing bar Podcasts, for example:

And here’s Music: 

More

The slider also applies to sidebars, toolbars, and toolbar buttons. This changes the look of Photos, Safari, and other apps with window chrome.

The one thing about the Liquid Glass slider in macOS 27 Golden Gate is that a single slider controls all Liquid Glass appearances across the system. That means you get one look for the Dock, widgets, and window chrome. 

What’s your preference? More clear, more opaque, or somewhere in the middle? Personally, I really love how nice and mature the more opaque option looks on my Mac. Still, it can be fun to experiment with more clear, and I’m glad macOS 27 Golden Gate gives everyone the option to decide.

Share your thoughts in the comments!

title: Nest Doorbell has been triggering Gemini’s American accent, no matter what language you speak; fix coming
snippet: Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect. more…
fullText:
Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect.

According to one user on Reddit, Gemini has been responding to them in American accent only when its referencing their Nest Doorbell. That’s nothing out of the ordinary on the surface, but this user’s complaint revolves entirely around the fact that they’re French, speak French, and live in France. Even still, the Nest Doorbell seems to trigger Gemini’s US English.

It isn’t just affecting one user, or one device. A commenter expressed the same concern in the Netherlands, and another in the UK. For the user in the Netherlands, their Bosch washing machine alerts default to US English instead of Dutch. It sounds like every other interaction with Gemini happens in the language of choice, but certain appliances bring out a different Gemini voice altogether.

According to a response by an official Google account, the issue is being worked on. No fix has been rolled out, but Gemini will likely stop responding in its American accent soon enough, unless you specifically want that.

	

It might have been be a bug developed after the September Google Home update with changes to Gemini for Home. Spoken notifications seem to work as intended, but for whatever reason, Gemini chooses to give the user context in an American accent instead of the language or accent set in preferences. the only change note that refers to Gemini is one that improves follow up question behavior. Beyond that, there’s nothing pointing towards an obvious cause.

Something is clearly broken along the pipeline of information, but it’s manifesting in one of the most hilarious ways.

It’s a strange one, but Google is aware of the issue and claims to be working on it.

title: Apple Notes adds a power user feature in iOS 27 that’s rare in other apps
snippet: Apple Notes in iOS 27 adds a variety of new features, including one that power users are sure to appreciate: section links. more…
fullText:
Apple Notes in iOS 27 adds a variety of new features, including one that power users are sure to appreciate: section links.

Apple Notes lets you link to specific sections of your note in iOS 27

There’s no shortage of third-party notes apps on the App Store. You can find everything from barebones note-takers to powerhouse productivity suites.

Apple Notes has long excelled at offering a minimalist, user-friendly interface while also providing tools that power users love.

And in iOS 27, Notes has an exciting new addition in the latter category: section links.

Whenever you select some text inside a note in iOS 27 and open the edit menu, tapping ‘Add Link’ will reveal a new option: Link to Section.

Inside this menu, you’ll find a full list of all the headings and subheadings in your note. Tap one, and Notes will create a link to that specific section. You can choose to use the section title as the link’s text, or your own custom text.

Section links are great for navigating long notes, as they make it quick and easy to jump to a specific area.

With section links you can create a full-blown table of contents at the top of your note, or just use them sparingly for sections you revisit a lot.

Most iPhone owners probably won’t ever use the feature. But for power users who value more flexibility in their notes app, section links in Apple Notes are a welcome new addition.

title: Apple retires the Apple Park Visitor Center’s unique AR experience
snippet: Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.” That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park. more…
fullText:
Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.”

That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park.

When Apple opened the Apple Park Visitor Center to the public in 2017, here’s how the company touted the AR experience:

Inviting guests to explore Apple Park in an immersive and engaging way, a 3-D model of the campus is brought to life by augmented reality technology.

Visitors can learn about the world’s largest naturally ventilated building and view one of the largest on-site solar energy installations in the world. Visitors can also choose to lift the entire roof off the building to peek inside to the collaborative office pod layout.

Until this change, the Apple Park Visitor was divided into three sections: the AR exhibit, a traditional-style Apple Store, and a cafe.

Source: RedNote

Now, Apple has retired the AR exhibit and transformed that space into an extension of the more traditional Apple Store. As spotted by MacRumors, this includes Avenues along the wall showcasing accessories and redesigned display tables featuring Apple products.

The rest of the Apple Park Visitor Center, including the cafe, remains unchanged.

9to5Mac’s Take

The AR experience at the Apple Park Visitor Center was unique, but after nine years it was starting to feel like that space could be better utilized in other ways. 

I wish Apple had tried something other than converting it into a traditional retail store, but at least the cafe remains as a unique fixture of the Apple Park Visitor Center.

title: Apple Photos in iOS 27 gets camera roll feature it’s long needed
snippet: iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’ more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 Photos app contains only photos and videos you shot in Camera app

Apple’s Photos app has steadily expanded its feature set over the years. In addition to being home to the photos and videos your iPhone captures, it also includes content that’s been shared with you, Memories, screenshots, saved media, and a lot more.

The Photos app used to offer a ‘Camera Roll’ feature that was similar to what the ‘Recents’ album does today. It included images you captured as well as ones you saved.

But what’s been missing for a long time is a feature that actually just shows photos and videos that you’ve taken—in other words, something that could more accurately be called your ‘camera roll.’

iOS 27 delivers that long-missing feature, and it’s called ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 is a new Photos collection that does exactly what it sounds like. It includes only media that’s been captured by your Camera app.

So photos and videos that you shot on your iPhone are collected there. But you won’t see screenshots, images your friends sent you, or any other types of content.

In addition to the dedicated ‘Captured by Me’ collection, you can also use a ‘Captured by Me’ filter in your main Photos library.

Whichever way you use the feature, ‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 fills an important gap in Apple Photos’ feature set.

title: What I learned after 30 days with the Pixel 11 [Video]
snippet: It has been almost 30 days since Google officially launched the Pixel 11 lineup, and the 11 might be the most sensible device of the bunch. Here’s what I have learned, having used it for the full month post-launch. more…
fullText:
It has been almost 30 days since Google officially launched the Pixel 11 lineup, and the 11 might be the most sensible device of the bunch. Here’s what I have learned, having used it for the full month post-launch.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Less nip, more tuck

It’s hard to be annoyed too much about the Pixel 11 design, but I can 100% get a little bored. When you get a new phone, you may subconsciously want at least a few changes to help it feel “different.”

However, if you’ve not used the Pixel 9 or Pixel 10, you probably won’t even care. I know I’m not in the minority in loving the Pixel design, but there’s certainly a feeling of Groundhog Day after a while. What I’ve realized is that, as someone who has used the last three generations, to me, a case has felt more important than ever.

	

After a month of use, the flatter camera visor is one of the few “big” changes that feels more consequential. My dream would be a boxier shape akin to the Pixel 10a, but with a case on the phone, you can achieve that, or close to it.

A tangible change I hadn’t expected was the NFC chip moving closer to the top edge. In tandem with the smaller camera protrusion, I’m not clashing my phone against terminals or turnstiles, plus wireless payments are a lot faster, or at least feel more accurate.

I’m so glad we have stronger Pixelsnap magnets because you’re confident an accessory will stick, which is especially important because the slippery, glossy finish on the back glass was problematic with the Pixel 10 at times. I do wish that the phone didn’t sound so hollow to the tap, for a $900 phone, it can feel a little cheap, even though it has a great frame and mass. Little nitpicks, but I do care about extra attention in these areas. Maybe next year it’s time to address these admittedly minor build complaints.

As far as the design is concerned, the Pixel 11 builds on what was good; the good news is that there is very little bad. I hoped that we would get display brightness changes, but maybe it’s the endgame for this specific size and shape. I’m very unsure how Google will make major changes next year if we do get a proposed redesign. The only way I can see changes is in the materials used, some dimension shavings, but little else that can really refine the post-Pixel 9 formula. 

Does Gemini Intelligence matter?

I mean this in the most positive way possible. The Pixel 11 is more of the same, yet there are a few things that start to feel like they haven’t become game-changing in the ways that Google seems to expect. I’m not actively using many of the new functions that the Pixel 11 shipped with. I say “actively” as the hands-off background automation approach is what Google should excel at and isn’t quite doing so everywhere yet.

Proactive Assistance is on the cusp of being a truly exceptional upgrade for Magic Cue. I’m in the UK, so Google Messages is an app that I love, but don’t use with many contacts. I say this because when I’ve had suggestions for things like my passport number or my flight number on a trip, the instantaneous pop-up suggestions seem so perfectly integrated that it feels like Magic Cue on steroids.

We desperately need to get this into third-party applications as soon as possible. It would save me so much time and effort in WhatsApp chats that I’m sort of frustrated it isn’t system-wide yet.

Now that I’ve been using Rambler for an extended period, I’ve made a U-turn on its inclusion, and I’m trusting it more to take notes, send long messages, and dare I say it, compose a few important emails…It’s a sleeper function that I’m enjoying greatly as a lazy typer. I even drafted a few paragraphs of this extended review using Rambler. Add in live transcripts, and it’ll become a “must have” for the lazy among us.

I completely forgot that Pause Point was already on Pixel 11. I’ve tried it a few times, and I don’t know why it isn’t being touted as a bigger deal. It’s one of the few Digital Wellbeing tools that feels like it could curb your phone usage. The rest of the AI stack? It all still feels a little filler. I’m still using Pixel Screenshots on an almost daily basis, but I’m still not finding ways to use many of the major functions that Google keeps touting because of the aforementioned first-party app requirements.

I mentioned modem issues in my initial review; these were temporary. Fully resolved, there is no doubt in my mind that the modem handles signal way better than the Pixel 9 and 10, and VPN connection woes are gone with the last couple of OTA updates, too.

Finally, a quality camera…again

I’m so glad that Google paid attention to some of the major complaints with the Pixel 10 and put in a “proper” big main sensor rather than short-changing buyers with an A-series sensor. The quality jump just gives me confidence that you’re properly equipped for every eventuality.

Next year, I’m fully hoping for some improved ultrawide and telephoto hardware.

To the surprise of nobody, Camera Looks is my outright most used function across every facet of the Pixel 11 this year so far. In the back of my mind, with just about any Pixel, having consistency has been both a blessing and a curse. I spoke about this last year when switching away to Zerocam on the Pixel 10 Pro. I wanted less processing done on my behalf, and Camera Looks just answers that with aplomb.

I have completely switched to using the “Shadows” look. It’s my default setting, and like when using Zerocam, I’m being more picky about what photos I’m taking with this phone. My only gripe is that the recipes you can cook up would be great if saved for specific circumstances. Being able to save these as custom looks with unique names would be a godsend and a real timesaver.

If you just want pure consistency, stick with the default settings and enjoy another great camera with better zoom, a quality main sensor; the rest is just more of the same – which is to say very good for this price bracket.

I wish I had more reasons to use Magic Camera, as my colleague Daniel Bader so aptly states, this is the ultimate family camera function. The outputs are great, and getting both video and photo at the same time is perfect, as you preserve the moment no matter what. 

As I say, maybe I need to force myself to use it more often. I’ve barely touched it since my first week of testing, but I’m more at home playing with regular photos and don’t often need snapshots from Magic Camera. There are people who are going to use this practically every day. I am not one of those people.

Loving the longevity

I can’t say I’ve had a problem with a recent Pixel phone, but the 11 is really solid. I’ve been on a few weekend trips already with this phone, and it hasn’t let me down. Side note: I actually like the AI summaries for battery usage. It feels better tailored than just the list of apps. It’s fairly recent, but I like this tweak and hope it improves over time.

There’s only so many times I can complain about the charging speed before you sort of come to terms with it. At least the Qi2 charging speed has increased to 25W, which isn’t a million miles away from the wired charging speed now. Just give us a little more, and I’ll be happier. That said, I started charging overnight again quite recently, so my complaint is a little moot.

For what it’s worth, the Pixel 11 lasts longer than my Pixel 11 Pro, which is solid and dependable. It’s been a long time since a Pixel had a terrible battery lifespan, put it that way.

What’s it like to own the Pixel 11, and is it worth it?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

2026 feels like a sobering year for technology. Not only has real progress slowed drastically in the areas outside artificial intelligence, but we’re expected to pay more for the privilege.

There is a good phone underneath the price hikes. One that, yes, hasn’t changed all that much.

Luckily for most people, the Pixel 11 isn’t as compromised as the Pro models. For a long time, I felt that this was where Google did the best work outside of the A-series. A solid base for all the functionality and features a “normie” would and could want from their mobile companion.

Because the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL have some cost prohibitive compromizes, there’s a cost incentive to go for the base model once again. I still struggle to fully recommend that anyone buy the Pixel 11, but it’s the most sensible of the bunch.

We’ll revisit the Pixel 11 again in the next few months to determine what has held up and what hasn’t, so if you prefer even longer testing periods, then check back in another 60-ish days for an updated verdict.
